div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

A DIAMOND merchant may speak of his goods being of the purest water, but the milkman may not. FIFTY-SEVEN Yehrg ago people were gazing in wonder on their first gas light. To-day they are gazing in wonder On their last gas bill. VITAL statistics show that men bear pain with less fortitude than Woman, that they die earlier and oftener, and are a scurvy lot anyhow. TEACHER: "Who was it that first said 'Property Is robbery?" Boy: • I don't know; I suppose it was some fellow who did't have any."' Buss—to kiss. Sillybus—to kiss the hand instead of the lips. Erebus—to kiss in the dark. Blunder- buss—to kiss the wrong person. Omnibus—kisses all round. WHEN the grocer retires from business he weighs less than he did before. IT is said that no one can arrest the flight of Time, but who is there who is not able to stop a minute? "MAMMA," inquired Flossie, "didn't the clergy- man say that I got my eyes from you ? " "Yes, dear." "And you really used. to have four eyes, mamma?" SNUFF-TAKING Professor to class—" The great art in correspondence is to write as you speak.' Young lady pupil—" But, sir, how is it when people sneak through the nose?' FOND mother—" Jane, give the baby some lauda- num and put it to sleep, and bring me my parasol. I am going to a meeting for the 'melioration of the condition of the human race." "I HAVE such an indulgent husband," said little Mrs. Doll. "Yes, so George says," responded Mrs. Spiteful, quietly. "Sometimes he indulges too much, doesn't he 2" They no longer speak to each other. A WIT at court was asked by the king to produce a pun. "Will your majesty, then suggest a subject ?" "Make one on myself," said the king. "Bat," replied the wit, "your majesty is not a subject."' TEACHER "There are three kingdoms—the animal, the vegetable, and the mineral. Where does the sugar belong 2" "Pa puts 4in the water before he pours in the whisky," replied little Johnny Yerger. "THAT'S it!" exclaimed Mrs. Bascom at the con- cert, as the singers came out again in response to an encore. "Make 'em do it over again until they 'get the ihing right."' THE little one, being a guest of her grandma, at Boston, had been liberally feasted, when a second dish of pudding came on., Looking at the steaming dish, she exclaimed with a sigh, "Grandma, I wish I was twins." CITIZEN, 'to coal-dealer—" I want a ton of coals." Coal-dealer—" All right. Shall we send up right away ?" Citizen—" Oh, no! If it's anything like the last, I'll just call for it on my way home, and carry it up in my overcoat pocket.' WANTED to know :—lf keeping up a ball till,day- light does not betray a party spirit? Wanted fur- ther to know—How to split a difference? And finally—lf it be true that the first apple was eaten by the first pair. Mn. FEATHERLY (making an evening call)— "Bobby, won't you come and sit on my knee ?" Bobby (accepting the proffered seat)—" All rights, Mr. Featherly. Pa told me to day that yes vasigiclu to be sat on once in a while." "DID you hear about the burglar who was arrested this morning 2" "No What for?" "For breaking into son..''." "Is that so ?" "Yes. He'd got through two bars, when someone hit him with a stave." Funeral private. YOUNG LADY—" We had a delightful time at the Concert Music Hall, last evening, Mr. Dumley. It was a Meyerbeer night, you know. Are you fond of Meyerbeer ?" Mr. Dumley (hesitatingly) —" Ye-es, but I think I would just as soon have Bass."

HOSTESS (excitedly), as guests are about to take their seats)—" Mercy 1 There are thirteen here ?" Chorus—" Never mind 1 Don't be afraid; don't be superstitious 1" Hostess—" Oh, it's not that. But there are only twelve plates, laid. How awk- ward!" ELTRIPIDES once gave Socrates a work by Beraclitus, and asked him what he thought of it. "What I understand," he replied, "is very good, and so, I daresay, is what I don't understand; but it wants a good diver to get to the bottom of it." "THIS is- about the slimmest dinner I ever sat down to," he said, as he surveyed the table; "but s'pose I ought to make certain allowances." " Yes, John," replied his wife, "if you would make certain allowances you"would have no occasion to find fault with your food." THIS is what ran through the audience when ffanki-Poo kissed :Yum-Yum :—" Oh, what a beauti- ful scene, and how they are enjoying their heaven of bliss." This is what Yum-Yum said to Nanki- Poe :—" Onions and beer again. Kiss me on the ear, or I'll have you fined." JUDGE--" Prisoner, you are accused of entering this lady's shop, taking therefrom a bundle of cigars, and leaving without paying for them. What have you to say in your defence ?" Prisoner—" I didn't know the price:" Judge—" You should have asked." Prisoner—" I didn't like to, your lordship, I am always so bashful before ladies." A MIN went into the country last Sunday for a, walk. He carried his overcoat on his arm, but find- ing it burdensome, hung it on a fence. Taking a card from his pocket, he wrote—" Do not touch this coat; infected with small-pox." He came back two hours later and found the card, upon which was written, underneath his warning, "Thanks for the coat, I've had the small-pox." . Two Francisco policemen tried to arrest a China- man. They found it necessary to leave him a moment, and so handcuffed him with his arms each side of a lamp-post. When they returned their prisoner was gone. He had climbed up the post, and swung his arms over the top. "IT is a curious thing in public life," said Wiggins, as he laid his newspaper on the .table, "that a windy, loud-mouthed impostor often succeeds, while men of great merit are passed over." ." Not at all," replied Bodley ; "It's the most natural thing in the world to put the blower before the grate." LOITISIANA postmaster, who is assisted •in his duties by his young bride—" Why, Mary, what are all these postal-cards doing here They should have gone in the last mail 1" Young bride, who was a Massachusetts schoolmistress—" Oh, I have just put them aside until I should have time to correct the spelling 1" "JOHN," said the minister to the sexton, "that pulpit cushion is worn out. I wish you would see hat a new cover is put on it." "Yes, sir," said John griaily; "1 know it's wore out, an' it's the third • this year. It ain't my place to make remarks, sir, but in my opinion there is such a thing as carrying religion a leetle too far." WHEN two young people of dissimilar sex, with a singleness of purpose and a doubleness of affection, ' sit up with each other, and po on, and when the cloc4k strikes a dozen, he says—" Is it possible ?" and she says—" Why, I didn't know it was so late I" you may draw your conclusions that very soon a united couple will be buying some furni- ture. _ _ _

POLICEMAN—" Look'r you! What are ye doin' 'round here this time o' morninr?" Stranger (boldly) —" I'm tending to me bisness. What yer suppose?" Policeman--' Oh, ye are Where did that chicken come from I" Stranger (with more under his coat) savagely—"lt come from an neg, av coorse? What'n blazes did ,yer think it come from 2—a sody foun- tin' 7" MINISTER—' Ofiwhat were you accused? Convict —" Stealing°, watch. I made a good fight about it. I had two lawyers and proved an alibi with sixteen witnesses. Then both my lawyers made strong speeches to the jury. No use. I was sent up for four yours." "I don't see why you were not acquitted." "Well, I confess there was one weak point in my defence. They found the watch in my pocket." LAWYER—" Miss Someage, you are the plaintiff in this suit for breach of promise, I believe 7" "Yes, sir." "And Mr. Squint, here, is the defendant." "Yes, sir." "Well, Miss Some,age, you may tell the court how and when he promised to make you his wife." "It was on the 3rd of September last, sir. I went into his photograph gallery and agkked him if he would take me, and he said he-would.' A MAN in a Western town hanged himself to a bedpost by his suspenders. The coroner's jury, which was composed of mothers, decided that "The deceased came to his death by coming home drunk and Mistaking himself for his pants. div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

One of the new lords, Sir Francis Sandford, has chosen the title of Lord Sandford, of Sandford, Shropshire; the other, known in the " beerage " as Guinness, will sink all memories of stout in the peer- age under the title of Lord Farnleigh.

The Irish papers are announcing that if Mr. Parnell presently marries Mrs. O'Shea he will gain a large fortune by the union. This is a mistake, for every shilling which comes to Mrs. O'Shea under the will of the late Miss Wood will pass to the trustees of her marriage settlement with Captain O'Shea.

Cremation is more and more becoming the fashionable mode of disposing of the dead. The body of the late Mr. Lloyd was cremated, so were Baron Huddlestop's remains ; and Mr. Kinglake's body was similarly disposed of at Woking, on Thurs- day. Here we have journalism, law, and literature represented. '

Mrs. Gladstone attainet her seventy-eighth birth- day on Tuesday. She was, our Chester Correspon- dent says,the recipient of a great number of presents and congratulatory letters, as well as a telegram from the Princess Louise. Mrs. Gladstone is in excellent health.

Among the numerous congratulations received by Mr. Gladstone on his birthday was a unique and lengthy address in seven languages presented by Prof. J. J. Johnson, ot Rochester. The Greek and Latin versipns were written in poetry, while the English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish were in elegant and idiomatic prose. The author had previously dedicated to Mr. Gladstone a French and English translation of Horace's " Ars Poetica."

The Queen is to leave •Windsor Castle for the Continent on Tuesday, the 24th of March, accom- panied by Princess Beatrice and Prince Henry ot Battenberg. The Royal party will proceed from Windsor to Portsmouth Harbour, and are to embark there for Cherbourg in the Royal yacht Victoria and Albert. The Queen will travel direct from Cher- bourg to F!orence, by way of the Mont Cenis Tun- nel, Genoa, and Pisa, arriving there on Thursday, the 261,13.

Mr. C. P. Villiers, the veteran M.P., who has just I celebrated his eighty-ninth birthday, writes :-7—" I have, indeed, exhausted the time usually allowed to mortals .for remaining in this world, but amongst the few consolations that I derive from reflecting on the past there are none that afford me' greater satisfaction than that of having faithfully adhered to the Liberal politics to which I attached myself in the earliest days of my existence, and unmoved by personal ambition or the existence of party purposes."

Mrs. Shaw, the American "Whistling lady," created much enthusiasm the other night in a large audience (which included the British Ambas- sador) at St. Petersburg. This (says our Corres- pondent) is a greater triumph since the Russians are extremists on the sinfulness of whistling, avid believe that he who whistles is communing with the Evil One. Bi..t Mrs. Shaw not only gratified her audience, but promises—since further concerts are announced—to become a favourite for a season in a society that is fond of novelties.

The Duke of Orleans may be a very smart young man; but he is not a succese as an amateur photo- grapher. During hi § recent tour with his father, he took a camera with him, and at every opportunity "took a picture." On his return to this country upwards of four hundred plates were sent to a well- known local photographer for development. Of these three hundred and fifty or so were absolute blanks, and the remainder hprdly recognisable as scenes of any kind. The Duke has had to realise that, at all events, there is no rpyal road to photo- graphy.

An American lady is about to emulate Mr.' Stanley's explorations in Africa. She will start in February for Zanzibar, thence going to Mozambique, and afterwards journeying into Central AfOca. Her idea is to study the home life of the savage tribes. She is to take with her a phonograph in order to bring back some African voices. Mrs. Sheldon, the lady in question, is to have a special passport from Secretary Blaine; e"WQIL jt IPttarsirnm Nfr„ Stanley. She is to be alone in the enterprise, her attendants being Arabs and black women, with, perhaps, a military escort.

Many Americans are indignant at what they term the assassination of Sitting Bull. He was not a warrior, but chief Medicine Man, otherwise high priest, of the Uncapapa tribe of the Sioux nation. A gentleman of Boston, who met him frequently, describes him as representing in person, character, and manner the highest type of a race that posses- sed many rare virtues before the white man took their land fronrthem and caused their deterioration. He was deliberate, suave, and low-voiced in coin- versation, a genial host, a pleasant guest, gentle, affectionate, and, even merry in his family circle.

Mr. F. Impey, the author of the famous phrase, I "Three Acres and a Cow," has the following refer- ences to the late Lord Tollemache in the current issue of "Land and People ":—" In Cheshire Lord Tollemache established nearly three hundred three acres and a cow' allotments. There is no other such sight in England as is presented by this unique illustration of what can be done by a pains- taking and kind-hearted landlord. For many years, ' as Lord Tollemache told me himself, in 1883, but little notice bad apparently been taken of this re- markable state of things en one estate in Cheshire.

“It was with great rejoicing that I was enabled to give a description of what Lord Tollemache had done for the labourers before the Royal Commission on the Rousing of the Poor, in 188-4 and in 188.5, after the passing of Mr. Gladstone's Household Suf- frage Bill for the Counties, the description I wrote of the Cheshire 'three acres and a cow' allotments made their existence still more widely known. At first, of course, the Tories ridiculed the whole matter, but they quickly found that this would be very bad bifsiness with the county voters, and now there is not a Tory county candidate who does not ground his appeal to the labourers for their votes on his own and his party's long and well-known affection for allotments !”

Mr. Charles S. Keene, " Punch's" talented carica- turist, we regret to record, died on Sunday. Mr. Keene has been ill for some time, and his facile pen has been missed from the pages of "Punch" His last drawing, representing 'Any on the Boulevards, appeared on the 15th August. Mr. Keene set him- self out to portray middle class and lower life. his favourite subjects were 'Arry and 'Arriet, the bank clerk, the old lady in the omnibus, cabby, porters, waiters, street arabs, and Scotch characters. He knew his subjects well, and delineated them with con'siderable power. His admirers looked upon him as Leech's successor and his equal. Mr. Keene was born in Hornsey in 1823, and was educated at the Grammar School at Ipswich.

Blenkin—Canon Blenkin—Vicar of Boston, says that pleasant Sunday afternoons are "devilish.": There is a" Pleasant Sunday Afternoon Society " in Boston, conducted by Mr. Josiah Beaulah, Mr. H. Casswell, and other local"gentlemen, who give short religious services, interspersed with the sing- ing of hymns and the reading of choice morsels of literature,such as Dickens's" Christmas Carol." The vicar believes that the devil is at the bottom of these Pleasant Sunday Afternoons, and has de- nounced them. This Blpnkin, who has lived very pleasantly and comfortably at Boston for forty years, drawing over £4OO a year, evidently does not want people to spend pleasant Sunday or other afternoons. Like a medimval religious tyrant, he has issued an edict against them, and declared that "1 will not give any young man a character who gdes to the Pleasant Afternoons."

The report that Mr. Blaine has consented to arbi- tration in the Behring Sea dispute on the lines suggested by Lord Salisbury is contradicted. bir E. Clarice, who spoke at Plymouth on Tuesday, referred at length to the Behring Sea question, and made much of the fact that Lord Salisbury has suggested arbitration. But that is only half the. truth. Mr. Blaine is as willing as Lord Salisbury to submit the matter to arbitration provided the terms of refer- ence cover all the questions in dispute. What he objects to is the limitation of the terms to the single question of jurisdiction. Sir Edward Clarke is, as we think, right in his contention that Lord Salisbury claims nothing that maritime law will not give him, but Mr. Blaine is equally right in urging that without supervision of some kind the seal will soon disappear from the Behring Sea, and that would not be to the advantage either of England Or the United States.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"By Sea and Land, a Tale of the Blue and the Scarlet " is the title of a new novel published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co., and is frpm the pen of that instructive and lively writer Dr._ Gordon Stables, R.N., author of "The Cruise of the Snow- bird," "From Pole to Pole," &c. This narrative of strange experiences on sea and on shore is, like all that Dr. Stable has written, cheerful and wholesome

and • exceedingly interesting. Young people of both sexes will read it with as much profit as pleasure, for there is no exaggeration, and a good deal of useful knowledge is imparted whilst telling the story. The character of Lord Kildoon is admir- ably sketched. It has the appearance of being drawn from life, and is the revelation of an alto-

gether bright and loveable nature. His career and adventures are well told, and constitute, as they are entitled to do, a large portion of the volume. The book, which is one of 350 pages, is admirably illus- trated by Mr. W. S. Stacey, and it is well printed and handsomely bound. lathe Camelot Series, published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have "Comedies byAlfred D. Mussett, translated and edited with an introduction by S. L. Gwynn." The introduction is really a brief biography of Mussett, who was born in 1810 and died in 1857. There are four oomedies in this volume. " Barberine," "Fantasio," "No Triffing with Love," and "A Door must be either open or shut." The gaiety and brilliance displayed in these comedies are characteristic of the author, and make charming reading. The fool in " Fantasio " is quite as fine in its way as some of Shakespeare's fools, which is the highest compliment we can pay. The volume ought to be in demand by all who enjoy a

literary treat. "The Life of Sheridan" is published by the same firm as one of the " Great Writers." It is written by Mr. Lloyd C. Sanders, who has made good use of other bio- graphies of Sheridan, and produced a life which is eminently readable. Sheridan's career was varied and eventful froth the time he eloped with the celebrated Miss Linley to the "The last dread scene of all "when he was overpowered by debt and besieged by duns. The story of his fame as a dramatist and orator is throughout well told. "The Magazine of Art "for January, has as its leading feature an article with illustrations on the portraits of Mr. John Ruskin. In the frontispiece there is a finished etching of Sir John Millais's celebrated portrait of the great art critic. Other illustrated papers are "The proper mode of study in drawing," by Mr. Holman Hunt ; "Mr. Brocklebank's Collection of Pictures at Childwall Hall "(near Liverpool) ; " Belvoir Castle and its History " ; and "Alfred Hunt," by Mr. Frederick Wedmore, &c. "The Cabinet Port%it Gallery" issued by Messrs. Cassell and Co.,continues to maintain its high reputation. The subjects of the photographs and biographical sketches this month are the Rev. Dr. Abbott, Miss Ada Rehan,and Mr. Bret Harte. The photographs are by Messrs. W. and D. Downey, and they may be said to be master- pieces in the art of which these photographers are masters. " Cassell's Magazine" has for frontispiece a charming picture of the "Queen of the Ice." Among the illus- trated miscellaneous papers are "Memories of Milan " ; "The Stranger " ; "The Garden in January " ; "My Mongrel " ; What to Wear in January ; " "The Gatherer"; &c. there are besides several serial and other stories all of the highest interest. "The Quiver" makes a capital start for the new year. Three serial stories are running, and amongst the papers for the current number we have "An Address to the Members of the Metropolitan Police Force by the Bishop of Rochester" ; "From Santa Claus " ; " Christ Wrapped in Swaddling Clothes " ; "Sunday with the Younci " • "Short Arrows"; Szc. "Little Folks" has for frontispiece a delight ful coloured plate of the children's game • known as "Oranges and lemons." The stories, sketches, and "odds and ends" in prose and verse are, as usual, brightly and cleverly written, and the illustrations are throughout first class. Messrs. Casstll have commenced several new serials of more than oVinary interest. We have to hand part first of " Figuier's Popular Scientific Works." It is being revised and corrected by eminent British authorities, and issued in monthly parts of 6d. each. The part to hand is crowded with highly finished illustrations, and the book will altogether contain no fewer than 2,500 illustrations. The first part deals with the "world before the deluge." A new edition of "Robinson Crusoe " is also being published, The story is old and yet it is ever new, for Defoe's work Will be read as long as the English langu- age endures. The present edition is rightly called a fine- art edition. The illustrations are the work of Mr. Wal- ter Paget, and they are being expressly executed for the work, and are really first class. " Cassell's Natural His- tory," edited by Dr. P. M. Duncan, F.R.S., is most pro- fusely illust eractid has reached part three. reationaFiArrrary- Messrs. Cassell in paper covers at 3d. ,pr in cloth at 61. The first volume consists of "The Haunted Manor," by Charles Dickens, and itis so well printed,and well bound as to be a sixpenny wonder. Next week Moore's " Utopia " will be published. TITE ROMAN CATHOLIC VIEW OF THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND.

_ Dr. Vaughan, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Sal- ford, has just issued a small pamphlet, in which he refers to the progress which the Roman Catholic Church is making in England, under the teaching of the Ritualistic clergy. Referring to" the change in the Establishment,' he says :—" Its bishops. minis- ters,and people,are busily engaged in ignoring or de- nouncing those very Articles which were drawn up to be their eternal protest against the Old Religion. The sacramental power of Orders, the need of juris- 'dictioti, the Real Presence, the daily sacrifice, auri- cular confession, prayers and offices for the dead, belief in purgatory, the invocation of the Blessed. Virgin and the Saints, religious vows, and the insti- tution of monks and nuns—the very doctrines , stamped in the Thirty-nine Articles as fond fables and blasphemous deceits—all these are now openly taught from a thousand pulpits within' the Estab- lishment, and as heartily embraced by as Many crowded congregations. Even the statue of the Blessed Virgin Mary has been set up with honour over the principal side entrance of Westminster Abbey, and she has been recently enthralled upon a majestic altar under the, great dome of St. Paul's." In view of these facts; Bishop Vaughan claims that England is already "half Catholic."—The Liberator.
THE "VICAR OF RUNCORN TO HIS PARISHIONERS.

The January issue of the "Runcorn Parish Magazine" contains a letter from the Vicar the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, MA., from which we wake the following extracts :—As I enter upon the fifth year of my ministry in Runcorn, and wish you earnestly the blessing of God for that coming year, I cannot but thank you at the same time for the many kind evidences of your support and sympathy during the past year. The last year has been eventful. The mission and the effort made for St. Michael's are of themselves sufficient to make the year remarkable. I am obliged to add to these things a three months' absence from home and a good deal of anxiety. May we all as our lives draw on find ourselves drawing nearer to the permanent home in the better land. My good wishes are very cordially with the effort to give a treat to the aged persons of the ,town, and I do not see why it should prevent our giving other help, if in consequence of the frost others should be required. There is a great advantage about efforts at feeding the hungry, that you need i not ask him what his religions or political views are before civina him something to eat. We all eat much in the sanie wa:st, and-it really is a comfort to find something in which every man with a kind heart and sixpence to give can unite with others like himself. We ,don't want un-denom- inational benevolence, but pan-denominational. Probably soon after this is in. _ your hands we shall know what the Cheshire County Council in- tend to do, but whatever they do, of this you may be sure, that a Public Secondary or Junior Tech- nical School would immensely benefit the town. It ought to be possible to give our boys a higher education than that of the elementary schools, good asthat education is, without haling to pay railway fare to Liverpool or Frodsham.• The Church Army wants more sympathy than it gets from our ordinary Church people.—Very faithfully yours,
A. MAITLAND WOOD."

Yo' see th' wood i' this case wer a han- kerin' for a young woman for his wife as hed a bit o' summat ov her own i' th' way o' property, an' like a lot o' fortune-hunters, he'd to wait a long time afoor he met her, an' then he geet jolly wee! sowd. OWD NICK'S THROT HIS CLUB O'ER ME.

div.head: OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
div.p: OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVANUS COBB, JR.
CHAPTER XII.
A CONFERENCE, AND HOW IT WAS INTERRUPTED.

Rosalind Valdai and Zenobie were together in their sitting-room, and the former had been weep- ing. She looked paler than 'when we saw her before, and her brow was heavy. Smiles no longer crept about the dimples of her cheeks, and her eyes had a sad, mournful look. Her face plainly showed that she had suffered much.

"My dear mistress," urged the faithful Zenobie, throwing her arms about Rosalind's neck, and draw- ing her head upon her bosom, "weep no more. Oh, there must be some hope. Surely God will not suffer suQh an unholy work to be done." " Ab, Zenobie," returned the fair maiden, in a fluttering r melancholy tone, "where can I look for hope." "I say, in God. You have told me we must look to Him, and,l believed you. Have you not always been good lb_ God ?"
"I -have been as good as I knew how, though I have sinned."
"How sinned? Oh, my, mistress, if you have sinned, then who is pure? Tell me:'

"We all sin, Zenaie. It is our nature." "So I have often heard, but I hardly think you have sinned. What have you done which you knew to be wrong ?" . "Nothing—nothing." "Then how have you sinned ?" Ah, Zenobie, we all do things which we ought not to do; but yet I mean to do as near right as I can." "Then leave the rest with God. Oh, when poor mortals do as near right as lies in their power, sure- ly they may leave the rest with God without fear. And now, if God is just, as you tell me, why should He allow the wicked dnke to triumph over you? What justice would there be in that—when you are all goodness, and he is sin itself?' Rosalind was puzzled. She had tried to teach her attendant to love and honor God, and she had

so far succeeded that Zenobie understood all the principles of Christianity, and embraced them gladly and joyfully; but now how should she make this point understood? How should she nconcile this apparent injustice with God's universal mercy and justice? _
" oan you not tell me?" the young girl asked again. *Why should God allow such a thing? You say He is all-powerful, and can do what He wills."

" Zencbie," returned the maiden, after pondering for awhile, "you do not look at the subject in a proper light. God does not operate by petty in- dividual decisions, as an emperor does. He sees that certain laws are necessary for the good of man- kind—and not a single law of all his code is there but is very good. Last night your head ached, and you suffered; and of course you had violated some natural law. It was your own fault. And so this suffering which is now come upon me is the result of a violation of one of God's laws." "Ah," cried Zenobie, eagerly, "but you are the one who sufers, while another violates the law. In my case I did both. and do not complain,." "But listen:" pursued Rosalind, with a brighten- ing countenance, for the true idea had come to her mind. "It would not be just for a person to enjoy all the good of a law and leave others to suffer all the evil. God has established in us a social nature, and through that part of our nature come the sweetest of our earthly enjoyments. Such a law— the law of sociality-i-must be universal, and if men break that law they must suffer, and the only way in which God could shield me from suffering would be to release me from the effects of the law. Then I should be a poor, lonesome outcast; forced to live all my days alone like a barren rook upon the top of some bleak mountain. But I would rather live among people, and enjoy the companionship of my fellows. I have freely accepted the boon; and now, when its, evils come, I must suffer. Had God's in- tent been followeci-0..- tharmwulil ,ha.vo ,been no suffering. It is not His fault that the othice sins. Do you understand me ?" • "I don't know," murmured the young girl dubi-

ously. "But see," resumed Rosalind; "you choose to ex- ercise your social nature, and of your own accord you mingle among your fellows. Do you not see that thus you are enjoying one of God's richest blessings—the blessings of sociality, friendship,and love ?" " Yes—l see." "Well, so far God is good in having given you that power for such enjoyment ? " "Yes—l see." "Well, now; under that law, when my father and mother died, I found a friend in the duke, and here have found a home. But circumstances have changed. The duke has become wicked in thought —he wants more money—and he will prostitute a power which, in obedience to God's law would be good, to my ruin. Now God can not save me with- out rending to pieces on of His most powerful laws, and one which is meant for a universal good The Moment He does that He destroys that princi-. ple of human dependence whence flow those most holy virtues of love, friendship, and charity. He must act by universal laws, and not by partial rules and individual exceptions. So as long as I can en- joy the blessings of social life, 1 must be subject to the evils of treachery and social wickedness. Do you not understand now ?" "I see—l see," the girl murmured thoughtfully. 1 "Aye, Zenobie," the mistress added, while a holy light shone upon her countenance,"God has made us subject to ills here; but look beyond the grave, and how bright it is with hope! I , have a father and a mother there, Oh, in all my misery—even in the worst state to which the bad duke can re- duce me, I would not change places with him. You seemed to intimate that God would see me suffer, and yet let the duke triumph. Triumph? Oh, Zenobie, for what would you have that man's heart in your bosom, and his soul in your keeping ?" '1 would rather die!" the girl cried, while a cold shudder ran through her frame. "Then you see he does not go clear. Oh, how blind and simple are those who imagine there can be pleasure in sin!" This opened a new theme to.Zenobie's mind, and she Pondered upon-it a long while. But by and by she came back to the theme from whence they had started; and in pursuance thereof she said : "My mistress, are you sure the duke will persist in this ?" "Aye, Zenobie; I know he will," Rosalind an- swered, while the old shudder came back to her frame, and the old grief to her soul. "And have you no hope?" "Only one—in Ruric. He may help me? "Oh, I hope he can. He is a noble man." Rosalind answered with a look of gratitude, and Zenobie proceeded; " Where is the titled lord more noble than he? Oh, were I to choose a husband now, and he was free, and I was in your position, I'd choose Rune Novel before all the emperors of earth." "So would I," returned the fair maiden. "If I were a countess, as you are, how I should love to make such a man a count." "But my marrying him would not make him a count. Were he a count, and I like what he is now in station his marrying me would give me the title; but we poor women do not have that power." "Well then, we should so much more have the right to choose our own husbands." Rosalind made no oral answer, but her look showed that she sympathised with the sentiment. "My mistress," at length spoke Zenobie again, this time in a low whisper," why may we not leave this place ? " Rosalind started as though she had heard the speech of a spirit, and for a moment a lo.ok of hope gleamed upon her face .; but it quickly Passed away. " Alas ! where should we go ! " j This was a part of the plan which Zenobie had not thought of; and ere she could make any reply one of the female domestics entered the apartment, and announced that a woman wished to see her young mistress. Rosalind asked who it was, but the girl could only tell her that it was a middle-aged woman and very good-looking. The young countess bade Zenobie go down and conduct her up. Ere long afterwards the attendant returned, and with her came Claudia Nevel. Rosalind had not seen the good woman for over a year, but she knew her at once, and starting up from her seat she bounded forward and embraced her warmly. " Ah, Aunt _Claudia, I am glad you have come. You will let me call you aunt, as I did in those happy times long gone by." Aye, sweet Rosalind," returned the widow, im- printing a warm kiss on the fair white brow. The countess noticed the strange sadness of the woman's tone, and then, for the first time, also, she noticed the sadness of her look. . " Aunt Claudia, you look sad," she said, while a chill dread struck o her own heart. "Aye," the widow uttered, as though she were

afraid to venture the question she wished to ask. I have been very sad because I have had a terrible fear. has—has—not Ruric been here ? " " When ? " uttered the maiden, catching the whole fear now. " Within these three days ? " "Just then. Day before yesterday he was here— in the forenoon."
"And I have not seen him since!" the poor woman groaned.
"Not seen him ?—Ruric gone? Oh, where? where ?"

"He said he was going to see the Count Damonoff when he left here," interposed Zenobie, who joined in the grief. "Aye—so he told me," returned the mother. "I have been there, and they have not seen him since that evening. The surgeon who attends the 'count went out to the inn where Runic put up his horse and the animal was still there, his owner having not called for him." _ _

"Oh, God, have mercy !" ejaculated the young countess, in a paroxysm of grief. At this moment there came a rap upon the door, and Zenobie went to answer the summons. It, was the black monk, Valdimir, who thus demanded ad- mittance. At any other timb both Rosalind and Claudia might have been startled by the strange visit, but now they instinctively hailed his coming as a source of hope. "Ladies," spoke the fat monk, approaching the ' spot where they stood, and bowing very low, " you will pardon this unseemly method of gaining admis- sion here, but I had no other choice, for I feared the duke would refuse me did I apply to him. I have come to learn, if possible, where Ruric Nevel may be." The widow tried to answer, but instead of speak- ing she burst into tears. Rosalind struggled a moment with the deep emotions that stirred within her, and she, too, fell to weeping. Zenobie was obliged to answer. •

" Good father," said she, "we here are after the same knowledge. IBS poor mother has come here to try if she might finß some clue to the noble youth; and thus did my mistress gain the first in- telligence that he was one. Pray, good sir, do you know anything about him? What have you heard ?" Both Claudia and the young countess now raised their heads, for they would hear what reply the monk could make. "I only know that he is missing," Valdimir re- plied. "A little while ago I called upon the sick count, and there I learned that Ruric Nevel had mysteriously disappeared. And I learned, also, of the noble purpose for which he visited the count. "Aye," interposed Claudia, with sudden energy, "he went to try and gain the count's forgiveness. I don't think they spoke falsely there. I don't think any them would wish him harm from any lingering revenge." "No, no," returned the monk; his mission thither was most nobly fulfilled. So far from cherishing any spirit of revenge in the count, that he will ever bear for Ruric the •holiest gratitude of his soul?! "Do you think so ? " the widow asked hope-, fully. "I know it," was the monk's assured reply. "But," he continued, relapsing into perplexity, "I can not imagine what has become of him. But hold. My dear child, is there not a humpbacked, ungainly priest who sometimes visits your guardian?" This was addressed to Rosalind, and a fearful tremor shook her frame as she heard it, for its im- port was at once apparent. "Do you suspect—" She had started forward and grasped the monk's arm/ as she thus commenced, but she could not continue. The thought she would have uttered was terrible. "Go on," whispered Valdimir, bending his head low down so as to catch her very thoughts if they left her lips. "What would you say ? ' "Oh, I ought not—and yet I know his soul is cap- able even of that." Thus much the fair countess murmured to herself and then she gazed up and spoke to the strange manbefore her: "Do you suspect my guardian?" "Do you suspect him?" the monk returned. "Oh. I know not what to think ! " Valdimir, earnestly. " would know all that ean assist you. Fear not, for as true as God lives. mean to save Ruric if I can; and if I can but gain a clue to him now, I can surely save you both. Trust me, for I possess a wondrous power for the good of those who trust me. Now, what end could the duke have in view in wishing for Ruric's removal. I know what he had in view in concocting the duel: it was the death of Damonoff, and the undivided posses- sion of Drotzen. Now, answer me. What do,is he aim at now?" In spite of all doubts Rosalind found herself trusting the monk. There was an air of conscious truth and power in his look and tone that won upon her.

....... , 'Good father," she returned,after a few mr,ments' thought, "the duke has sworn by a most fearful oath that he will have me for his wife ! " " Ha! uttered the monk, starting back a pace and clenching his hands, "Does he mean that?" "Oh, most truly he does!" the young countess replied; and she spoke more firmly now, for there was something in the sudden energy of tt e monk's exclamation that gave her hope. "Then he wants your estates, too. By my soul, he is aiming for wealth with a high hand. And do you suppose he fears Ruric Nevel in connection with this scheme?' "Yes father—l will speak plainly,for I trust you. I do not think you would betray one who never harmed you." . . "Let the end of these things tell you that. But now finish what. you had begun—about your thoughts of the duke." "He knows, holy father,that I love Ruric, and he knows too, that Earle loves me. May he not, un- der such circumstances, fear that the noble youth will try to thwart him?' "Very likely," returned Valdiniir thoughtfully: "I will profit by this, and I am much mistaken if you do not also profit by it. I have those in Mos- cow who will work for me. I cannot, of course, directly assure you of salvation, for Runic may never be found !' A quick groan escaped from Claudia's lips as the monk thus spoke; but before Rosalind could speak , the door of the apartment was opened, and the Duke of Tula strode in! He stopped as he came nigh to where the company stood, and his eyes flashed, and his framo.trembled with passion. "How now ?" he cried, as soon as he could com- mand speech. "What means this gathering here in my own palace? Meddling mink, how dare you drag your detestable form hither? Out, reptile! Out! And let me catch you here again and my dogs shall tear you up as they do carrion !" Without a word the monk turned away. His face was pale as death, and his hands were clenched till the fingers' ends seemed to settle themselves into the palms. "Remember," the duke exclaimed, as Valdimir reached the door, "if you dare to cross my door- step again—" ' Hold !" gasped the monk, in a hoarse, startling tone. "Offer no more threats. But mark•me,proud , duke,—you shall see the day on which you'll wish God had made you a dog ere he( gave you speech to arouae the just vengeance of Valdimir !" ' And thus speaking the black monk disappeared. Olga started to pursue him, but he did not follow out the impulse. Ere he reached the door he stopped and turned back. "And you, woman—who art thou ?" he uttered, • turning an angry look upon Claudia. ' "I am a mourning mother in search of her lost , son,' the woman sadly replied. ) "Ha ! I see the likeness now. You are the woman Nevel—mother of the young villain who ; bears that name! Leave my palace at once; and , don't you dare to enter it again !" I The poor woman tried tospeak,but she could not. With a deep sob she turned away,and slowly walked from the room. ; "Now," resumed the duke, turning towards Rosa- had, what means this secret coulacil ?" I "My' lord," returned the countess, struggling .r hard to overcome her powerful einotions, "they I were here—to—to—" L But she could not finish the sentence. Her soul ; vas too deeply moved. She, only gave the foul : wretch one look of horror and disgust, and , then covering her face with her hands, she sobbed sloud. ; If the bad man had anything further to say, he . reserved it for some future time. (To be continued.)

THE ROMANCE OF THE NEEDLE.

The sun, setting in the glory of golden amber, flung its beams in a parting caress over the rip- pling blue waves of the Bay of Naples. Near the water's edge, all embowered in vines, was a tiny cottage, and on its low porch, before her spinning wheel, sat Rosolyte, the daughter of Flavio the vine-dresser. As she turned her wheel she sang in a low voice dreamily to herself. Suddenly' her song ceased, as from the cottage door issued the figure of her father. He was a very old man, and his features betokened thought and intelligence beyond his humble station. Just now he seemed greatly excited; for, as he came to his daughter's side his eyes flashed and his face worked convul- sively. "Father! what is it? what Ilas happened?" she cried, in evident alarm. To her question the old man answered nothing, but held out to her his hand, in which rested a small, round object. But the circular disk with what seemed to be a needle tremulously vibrating beneath its glass cover conveyed no meaning to Rosolyte's mind. "Father, speak, and tell me the reason of your excitement. I do not see aught in this you show me to cause it." The old man seated himself by his daughter's side, and began a long and earnest explanation; . and as she listend the girl's mobile features lighted up with a fervour equal to his own. For then and there, in the humble vine-dresser's cottage, was ex- plained for the first time the properties of that wonderful magnetic needle which has since been the guide of every mariner on the great deep. • "My daughter," said the old man at length, "I have laboured and thought long,, and now success is near at hand; but my work is not done .until some one high and powerful sees and understands its importance." "Father !" exclaimed Rosolyte, "in three more weeks will be a fête day, and the king and queen will be in the city. Shall we not go and lay your discovery at their feet? I have heard that they delight to honour all who like themselves, love learning." His daughter's proposition found favour with Flavio; and the time passed slowly on until the impatiently looked-for morning dawned. "Make yourself fair, my child," said Flavio' lay- ing his aged hand proudly upon his daughter's head. "For who knows but that to-day may be the turn- ing-point in your destiny? Some noble lord may see and love my Rosolyte." The girl grew very pale as she said: "Father, you know that neither loving nor marry- ing are any more in my thoughts. You refused your consent to Paulo, and drove him from my side by your stern decision • and now I shall never see any one else who will have the power to touch my heart." As Rosolyte had said, it was fête day. Down the street, beneath the myriad waving banners, came the royal cavalcade. Foremost rode Bing Ferdinand, and by his side, on her snow-white palfrey, his lovely wife, Queen Jeanne. Then followed the nobles, who had been honoured by being allowed to form the immediate escort of their sovereigns. Conspicuous among the glittering throng was one youth, taller and nobler than the others. As he passed the porch from beneath which Flavio, and his daughter were gazing out upon the, to them, novel spectacle, his eyes suddenly rested upon Rosolyte. A crimson flush sprang to his very brow. In another moment he had passed, and Rosolyte had not seen him. It was late in the day, and the time had arrived when the king received the Petitions of his subjects. In the line awaiting their turn was Flavio, one trembling hand holding the case which contained his precious discovery, and the other resting iipon his daughter's shoulder. Suddenly a page, clad in royal colours. ap• proached. "Is your name Flavio ?" he said. "If so, you T and this maiden are to come with me." Wonderingly, Flavio and Rosolyte followed their

Quickly be--aT-the_heszt of the Tillage girl Eta she found herself in the-presence of royalty; and, with her eyes timidly veiled within thcar..aarit fringes, she stood while her father, in few but clearly expressed words, laid before his sovereign his invention. As King 1 erdinand listened interestedly, Queen Jeanne rose and beckoned to Rosolyte to come forward. Tremblingly she advanced, looking, in her simple robe in that gorgeous assemblage, like a pure white rosebud amid a setting of dazzling tropical exotics. Queen Jeanne noticed her agitation, and, gently' laying her hand upon her arm, she drew her close to her side and looked penetratingly into her face. "Truly, our nephew has a good taste," she mur- mured softly to herself. By this time Flavio had finished his ea-planatiop, and, with eyes whose light age had no power to‘ dim, he was receiving his king's commendations and congratulations. It was a proud moment. The success he had dreamed of was his. Suddenly Queen Jeanne's soft voice interrupted her husband's words. • "My liege," she said, "have I your permission to carry out at this present and most opportune moment the intention of which I told you some time back?" Then, as her husband signified his consent, she turned to Rosolyte. "Sweet one," she cried, "I have long known of you—of your beauty and great goodness—and had intended ere now to have summoned you to our presence; but hearing of your father's discovery, and that he intended to lay it before the king, have waited until now. • "Some time ago, while passing through the village in which you live, a young and favourite kinsman of ours saw and lost his heart to you. He told in of his passion and besought my help, which (for I love him as a mother) I promised.

"I now ask you, in the presence of ourselveg and these witnesses, will you consent to be united in holy matrimony to our nephew, the young Lord D'Aubigny ?" Rosolyte had listened, almo.st uncomprehend- ingly, to the above startling words. - New she drew' back, and the delicate colour excitement had brought faded from her face, as, in low, but resolute tnneS, she replied: "Pardon me, most gracious Queen, but I shall never marry!" As he heard, Flavio started to her side, and low' in her ear, whispered: "My daughter, did I not promise you that this day would be the turning point in our lives? D° not now ruin all by your foolish clinging to the past. Accept this great good fortune which is loia before you.' But the maiden was firm. "Your Majesty," she said, "I know of no noble lord whom I have ever seen; but there is one. and only one—a humble artist—who has my heart, even though I shall never meet him more; for he left me in anger, deeming me cold, because I re- fused to disobey my father's commands." With an arch smile curving her lovely mouth, Queen Jeanne turned. to.a group of courtiers who stood in a distant corner of the audience-chamber' "My Lord D'Aubigny, came near," she said. Suddenly Rosolyte felt her hand clasped, and ber eyes rested upon a handsome, pleading face Oa well knew.

"Paulo!" she ejaculated. "Yes, Rosolyte ; can you forgive me my deceP, tion ? I wished to win my wife for love of myseP alone, and I, the Lord D'Aubigny, am that Paulo": the humble artist—whom you sent away so coldli and cruelly. I was deeply: angered at first; but,' soon learned that it was only filial obedience whicii had caused your actions, and then I laid la desperate case before my aunt—our gracious quee...„l/ —and in this romantic manner it has pleased to fulfil her promi6 of assistance:" Thus, with the marriage in the full blaze of CO glory, of the Lord D'Aubigny and Rosolyte, tb.„e daughter a Flavio, the discoverer of the magnet!, needle, Was completed a romance whiah, wherec, the liquid Italian tongue is known, has been SI" in ballads and told in prose and verse.

div.head: TECHNICAL SCHOOLS.
div.p: TECHNICAL SCHOOLS.

The Library and Museum Committee gave the follow log return for the month of November i—Visitor s te the Museum 2,Z13, increase 4 per cent. compared with November, '1889; books issued in the reading-room, 1,458, decrease 22 per cent.; books issued in lending de- partment, 2,7103, increase 14 per cent. Report of the following gifts, for which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors-:—Bearded Vul- ture, from Col.-Sergeant Shaw, Pashawur ; "The Heretic," 18E6, from Captain Tucker; Priestley's " Hiss tory of the Church," and other of his works (16 v 015.),: from Mr. James Parlane ; "Warrington Friary," by William Owen, F.R.1.8.A., from the author ; " Trial ;, Attorney General v.. Mersey and IrwellFavigation Com- pany, 1826," from Mr. R. Davies; Push Plough, from Thelwall, from Mr. T. Tunstall. The Committee also submitted a -copy of the report of a -sub-committee, giving the scheme for the establishment of a technical school, which has previously been given in full in the columns of this paper. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS, in moving the adoption of the minutes, referred to the proposals.of the Museum Committee with regard to technical education. It was, he said, a matter of considerable pride to all Englishmen that this country had for so long a time maintained a position of absolute supremacy as a commercial and manufacturing nation ; but that position of supremacy had at last become somewhat threatened owing to the great discovery of metals which had taken place in other countries, and to the fact that the people of those coun- tries were educated, intelligent people, and were apply- ing themselves to the development of their ovrn properties to the fullest possible extent; and they were now running Englishmen a verycloseraoe in some of the open fields of the world's commerce. Englishmen could not therefore rely, as they had been able to do for many generations, upon the mere fact of the country's rich- ness in metals, and the long acquaintance of the people with the manufacture and development of those metals. Seeing that the question of technical instruction had re- ceived onthe continent such a large impetus during the past generation, it would be a great misfortune if Eng- lishmen were to fall behind in the race, owing to the want of application on their part and the use of the talents with which they were endowed and the opportu- nities which were at their hands. (Hear, hear.) If, therefore, it was the duty of the nation to apply itself in that direction, It was none the less the duty of little constituencies, like the one that Council represented, to apply itself, as far as it had the opportunity, in the fame direction. There were in Warrington a multiplicity of trades, but he ventured to say that there was no town in Lancashireor Cheshire which was so poverty-stricken in the matter of superior education as this borough was. At the present time there was no method by which, unless a young man went to Literpool or Manchester, he might cultivate himself in the higher branches of knowledge required for the development of some of the [ principal industries carried on so successfully in the Itown. It was rather a discredit to the public spirit of the town for such a state of things to last so long. The time had come for taking action, and in the minutes submitted that evening would be found the details of a scheme the most important item of which was the proposed taking over of the School of Art. It might naturally be asked, "Will the Corporation be taking over any debt or liability? He was very glad to be able to state that so far as the income and expendi- ture account was concerned, the School of Art was now a self-supporting institution. (Hear, her.) There was a small debt on the building which, he had good authority for saying, would be cleared off in the event of the institution becoming Corporation property. In any case, the Corporation would get a very handsome return if they took the institution as it stood. The Council were not asked to commit themselves to any of the details of the scheme; the whole matter would have to be sub- .mitted in detail for approval a little further on. In regard to the estimated income which appeared on the minutes, he might say a few words. He thought it was pretty well understood that, under the Beer Tax levied last year, the County Council would have, after the pay- ments had been made to the county boroughs, a sum of something like £40,000 to distribute. The County Council were not of necessity bound to apply that sum to the purposes of technical education, but they had received a strong recommendation from the Government to do so, and it might be taken for granted that the money would be so applied. (Hear, hear.) But the question arose—would the County Council do the work themselves, or would they transfer to the Local Authorities the responsibility of carrying out the Act, apportioning to them their shares of the £40,000? If the County Council did what was being asked of them— distributed the money upon what, was considered to be a fair and right basis, the rateable value of each authority —Warrington would receive £700; and-that grant would certainly be continued if once made. In regard to the estimated grants from the Science and Art Department— £soo—the School of Art already earned £2OO a year, and the Committee did not think it too much to estimate that a further sum of £3OO would be earned from the multiplicity of subjects it was proposed to teach. The same remark applied to the question of fees. At pre- sent a sum of £3OO was received in fees, at the School of Art, and it was anticipated that that amount would be at least doubled. The expenditure would be limited to the income. The Council would not be asked for any subsidy in the way of aid from rates until thelquestion of suitable buildings came before them. For th, pressnt

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1891.

and for some time they would be able to avail them- selves of buildings which were ready to hand,and which would not requireany capital expenditure. n was very desirable that the question be decided in favour a the Committee that 'evening, because the County Council met next week to receive the recommendation of their Technical Instruction Committee, and if the Warrington Council did not put themselves in a position—by having some scheme in existence not necessarily committed as to the details but as to the principle—to go to the County Councileand ask for their share of the money—if that opportunity were allowed to pass, it would be a matter of very great difficulty to get a grant in future. A number of other towns in Lancashire had already done considerably anom than it was now proposed to do in Warrington so that he hoped the Town Council would notbe behindhand in taking action .on so important -a sUtiject. (Applause.) Councillor VOISEtE seconded the ,confirmation of the minutes. He saidke thought no member of the Council could have any ,deubt that on a 'question of that kind it really concerned :the Council very much to see that some steps were taken'to carryout a scheme as was suggested. 'ln 30 or 40 other districts the matter was being actively taken up, and Warrington ought certainly not to be left behind. A very good basis was to hand in the School, of Art, and that and the Museum formed a capita?, set of buildings to 'work upon. Counepor'Dixoel supported the proposal of the Com- mittee, observing that itdeserved the assistance of all persons interested in the trades of Warrington. Alderman Surron thoughtthey would all be averse to any increase of the rates, but relying on the .assurance that no immediate call would be made upon the rate- payers he gave his support to the scheme. Councillor FLEMING said that as one who 'took a deep interestin the education df the people of this town, he heartily 'approved of the Committee's proposals. Cogneillor J. Suale-Gnssas expressed a hope that the scheme would receive the unanimous support of the CoonCii. The Chairman tif the. Museum Committee (Mr. F. Monks) had been atinfinite pains in regard to the matter. As for the figures, the estimated returns were rather 'below what inighebe expected. Councillor Mum also supported the proposition. Councillor F. A.. RONERTS said he happened to be a meniber of the Technical Education Committee of the Comity Council, who were considering t'the subject, and wank' lay a report Wore the February meeting of the County Council. What he said that evening was only an tindividual 017iMied formed from the opportunities he had had of discussing the question Df ,the distribution of thc"240.000. TheOaromittee had power only to formu- late a scheme to be submitted to the County Council. He did not thinkthe .matter of figures would be con- sidered by the County Council at the meeting in February. They would simply-require from the' Committee a state- ment as to the drift of that question. There were cer- tain membersOfthd "County Council Who were very much 'opposed to the Whole of the money going to Technical Education. Alew of them felt thate some of it should go 'towards the main roads, because the money was given I,to the County 'Council as a sop for the Van and Wheel "*Tax, which was withdrawn. He did not think that the 'County Council as 'a whole would 'listen to that plea. ,`After what had lately fallen from the members of the Government, the County Councilavould probably devote the whole of themoney to technical education; especially as they had reason-to believe from Mr. Goschen that• if such were done' the grant would be an annual one. Fail- ing its being distributed in that way, the Chancellor of the Exchequor practically threatened that the payment would not be renewed. Whatwas the best way in which to develop technical education in the country? That was a question Which would, he believed, influence 'the County Connell in the distribution of the money. He thought the County Council would be actuated by the feelings of Which Councillor Henry Roberts had speke,n, by the feeling that technical education in this country had been neglected, and that it was necessary that it' should be spurred on in order that English people might take their properposition among the nations of theeerth. Already the knowledge that the County Councirhad £40,000 to distribute had in Lancashire given an impetus to the development of technical education. On all hands new schools, arid'fresh developments were heard of. He felt very strongly that Warrington was very much in 'the background in net having approached the County Coun- cil before,liyanaking some claim on the amount Which it was supposed:they would have for distribution. 'The applications had been many, but up to the present time Warrington had put in no claim. He saw now the reason for the delay. Trite Sub-Committee had been considering the matter, alid endeavouring to formulate a schemefor presentation tothe Council. He had no desire to throw cold water on the scheme ; he only wished that further developmentaliad been suggest,ed, but he did not think for his own observation among the members of the County Council that Warrington would receive a sum of £7OO. He believed the course taken by the Committee and the County Council would be to help those 'who helped themselves; and until 'Warrington showed that it was prepared to do something for itself in the direction of technical education, he doubted whether the County Council would-render much assistance. Of course if the i principle Of assessment were 'accepted Warrington was ' entitled to 2700. He claimed that Warrington was entitled to morethan that assessment, because it had toad very large breweries, and as thetax came from the beer duties the town should have had more of the money— (laughter and hear, hear)--but as the non-county boroughs were in such a small ;minority in the County Council, he was afraid that the principle of assesemefft: would not be adopted. 'The County Council would in &11 probability first assist those who were assisting them-! selves, and any -worthy institution which was developing technical education according toproper and systematic `einethods. Very likely before 'Anything could be done a

new Standing Committee of the County Council would have to be appointed to deal with the question, and he presumed that in their hands the money would be placed for distribution. Those institutions which were obtaining results would receive the largest grants. He cordially supported the proposals submitted that even- ing, and only wished the Committee had seen their way to gostill further. He should be glad to see technical instruction developed in Warrington if they were able to do ittvith a -Id. rate, and he wished that had been a penny - rate instead. Warrington had been in the background in the past, and it ought to take up its proper position. ,energy were shown in the direction of technical edu- Cation, the town would receive a very much larger grant f,rom the County Council. (Applause.) Alderman BURGESS said the Council would do well to consider what had fallen from the lips of Councillor F. A. Roberts, one of the members for Warrington on the County Council. He (the speaker) did not intend to raise any objection to the provision of a technical school, but Councillor F. A. Roberts had made it clear thatinas- much as Warrington had only a scheme on paper, it had a small chance ei getting from the County Council what had been suggested it would have. A suggestion had been made by the same gentleman to the effect that nothing had been decided upon. It was a reflection on the Committee, which had been in existence for 40 years, that they were so much behind neighbouring towns. It was a reflection on the Committee that they had allowed the matter of technical instruction to remain in the posi- tion it was in up to the present time. If the Committee could commence operations at once, they would have a greater claim upon the County Council than they ap- peared to have at the present time. He should like to know the constitution of the Committee which would have the disposition of the money. Would it be com- posed of members of the Council and non-members? Councillor SHAW-GREEN: Certainly. •The MAYOR : It will be the Museum Committee. Alderman BURGESS: Members and non-members of the , Council? The MAYon : That is so. Alderman BURGESS contended that gentlemen who held no responsibility in the Council were not the people to spend the money of the ratepayers. If gentlemen did notchoose to come into that Council and accept positions of trust he• (the Alderman) did not feel disposed to sup- port them if they wanted to have the expenditure of public money. He did not object to any particular in- dividual. 'Allthose to whom he referred were gentlemen, but he thought a position of responsibility should beheld by them. Alderman HARRISON did not rise even to throw out an insinuation or a doubt with reference to the desirability of establishing technical education schools. It was very • desirable that they should have education in its most •ample force. They could not educate too highly, and he believed that the more education was disseminated amongst the people the better, the more enlightened,and the more intelligent they would become. At the same time„he did not like to hear first one gentleman and then another getup and say that Warrington had not done its • duty,and that it was so far behind other towns. He • should like t 4 be allowed to put to certain gentlemen rather a posifig question, which would be difficult to solve. If he were to ask them "In what zespect has Warrington fallen behind other towns of a similar size?" he did not believe for a moment they would be able to answer the question. As good work was turned out of .-Warrington as out of' ' any other town in England, and the people of Warrington weroquite as capable of appre- ciating good work. (He,ar,hear.) He was rather struck With what Councillor Henry Roberts said as to the desira- bility of cultivating technical schools, because he said •'we were getting behind other nations, that was, from a national point of view. 'Councillor Ronizirrs : No. 'I said we were now feeling 'competition in a more severelorm than before; I would not like to admit we had fallen behind. Alderman HARRISON: It is pretty nearly equivalent. (Cries of "No, no.") Ido not think that' technical edu- cation has anything to do with that,and all the technical education in the world will ,not alter the state of things as long as you find Germanswilling to work for one-third less wages than Englishmen, and one-third longer. 'Under those circumstances,,we are bound to comehe- hind, and I want to know how technical education is to alter that unhappy state of things? In addition to that look at the excessive, unjustnnd monstrous tariffs with which we are assailed on every hand. We are the only free trade nation in the world. That is a point you should I look at and consider. Technical education is all very well, but even when it is on the most approved plan it will not I do everything and will not remove those misfortunes which apparently at present appear to be assailing us. What better schools for technical education can you have than the various workshops ? If you send a lad to an archi- tect,does he not receive a certain technical education'? If you send him to a smith's shop, does he not learn how-to become a fitter? Does he not undergo a process of tech- nical education? We have an education given inWarring- ton equal to that given in almost any town of England of the same site; and I dislike to hear these accusations constantly made. Warringtorelaas done well, and is still doing well, and I don't see why we should not aid the present technical schoel. I mean the School of Art. Science is taught there, and 'Why cannot we apply a penny rate, or a portion of it, to aid the technical arid scientific instruction given in that building without en- cumbering ourselves with an al:hailer:tat building, with all the responsibilities connected with it? That would - put us in a position to ask the County Council to award us a portion of the money they haveat their disposal. Alderman Pr.arr said that they had to take the report, and what the Museum Committee proposed to do, to a 'large extent upon trust ;in fact, the Committee them- -selves had to take it upon trust. No ,one could lay be- (fore the Council a scheme of that description without the
