result being to some extent of a speculative character; in fact, no one could tell how the matter would work out. At the same time, he thought the Committee deserved very great credit for the report they had prepared. He thought they were on the right track, and that they they might be safely left to work the matter out to a pro- per issue. (Hear' hear.) He had been rather disappointed with the remarks which had been made by Alderman Harrison with reference to the position of England and .other nations. He held that we had not fallen back. That might be so; but they must nO forget that on the other hand other nations had been coming up more rapidly, and that was the true solution of the matter. It was not that Englishmen as Englishmen had fallen back from what they had done in former times. They might have advanced, and had advanced, but other nations—and the Germans had been mentioned—had been advancing more rapidly than England,and that to a great extent had been the cause of our losing, not altogether losing our trade, but not securing the proportion we used to have. Let them, for instance, take the Christmas cards and books which had been circulated throughout the country dur- ing the past few days. It was a lamentable fact, if they examined them, that although the cards had been de- signed in England, they had been printed abroad. One after another had been designed in England, but printed in Bavaria or Germany. It a lamentable fact that we could not do all that work at home. (Hear, hear.) He did not intend to talk about-free trade. That was beside the question' but they had to see that they could do the work better than anybody else. Unless they could do so they would not be able to maintain their position at the head of affairs. He cordially supported the attempt now being made to provide technical education. Whether they got the contribution from the County Council or not some scheme of education should be adopted and carried through. He could not agree with what Alderman Burgess had said about the constitution of the Committee. They must not forget that if the Committee were not entirely composed of members of the Council, it could do' nothing without the sanction of the Council, so that he thought they were in no great danger in accepting recommendations from gentlemen outside the Council. (Hear, hear.) On the contrary, he thought it was greatly to the credit of those who were not members of the Coun- cil that they should spend their time and energy in pre- paring a reporb of the nature which had been submitted that evening. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BEAMAN said reference had been made to workshops and factories being made technical schools. Alderman HARRISON: In a sense. _ _

Councillor BEAMAN : The main object of a workshop or factory is to make machines. The workpeople do certain things and leave certain things undone, but they cannot give an intelligent reason for doing so. Alderman HARRISON: That may be. Councillor BEAMAN : We want men to know why they do certain things, and why they leave others undone. We want them to give a reason for everything they do, and when they can do so we shall find fewer failures and much more success. (Hear, hear.) Councillor FAIRCLOUGH would support the scheme, as he thought that after boys had left school a chance should be afforded them of centinuing their education. There was nowhere for them to go in Warrington except to the School of Art. He instanced the case of his son, who had to go to Manchester when he had finished his duties in Warrington, and it was a hardship that, to enable him to continue his education, he should have to make such long hours. Alderman HARRISON Does he go to Manchester for his technical instruction?

Councillor FAIRCLOUGH : Yes; which under the scheme he would get in Warrington. Councillor BEAMAN : I have a son who is in exactly the same position. Councillor H. ROBERTS, in reply, said the Committee were exceedingly gratified at the favourable manner in which the report had been received. He was surprised at the remarks which had been made by Alderman Har- rison. He knew he had a vast amount of experience of commercial matters, and that he knew a great deal about the subject, but he was considerably surprised at the tenor of his remarks nevertheless. He thought that if ever a Daniel had come to judgment, Alderman Harri- son had come that night, but where he had been before he came to judgment he could not say. To tell them calmly and quietly that technical education had had nothing whatever to do with the present position of Germany as a mannfacturing nation was a little too---

Alderman HARRISON: I aver said sn in this world: I never said anything of the kind. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS: By inference. Councillor H. ROBERTS: Alderman Harrison, I said, did not think technical education had anything to do with the severe competition we were receiving at the present moment from continental nations. Alderman HARRISON: Allow me. I said the teChnical education we might introduce would not cure that. That is what I said. Councillor H. ROBBRTS : I took the words dewn and- Alderman HARRISON: I repudiate the assertion most completely_ CouncillorlF. A. ROBERTS: He withdraws. (Laughter.) Councillor H. ROBERTS: I accept the worthy Alder- man's disclaimer, because he told us afterwards that the real secret °fell the trouble was not technical education but free trade.
Alderman &ma'am: never mentioned free trade.
The MAYOR (to Alderman Harrison) : I am afraid you 'have forgotten•that. Alderman HARRISON: I am open to correction, if I did use those words, but I am unconscious of having done so.
_ Councillor H. RatIERTS : This is neither the place nor the time to discuss that matter; if it were I should be .quite ready to discuss the question with Alderman ilarrison.
Alderman PLArr : Have a special night. Councillor H. ROBERTS also referred to other points that had been raised, after which the minutes were adopted unanimously.
'rHE COMPLAINTS AS TO THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS.

Councillor Dixos moved "That immediate steps be taken for closing the Intercepting Depots either by the Sanitary Committee, or by a special Committee ap- pointed by the Council." Councillor DIXON contended that the quantity of air passed into the manure at the depots was most detrimental to its quality, and said there was not _another Corporation except that of Staf- ford that had adopted the ejecting process for dealing with excreta. An engineer had told him a few weeks ago that the utmost precautions were used to exclude air, and that a force pump was used to lift it from the cistern into which the manure was emptied when it was required to pass it Into other vessels. But he was quite sure that in summer a very large amount of air must pass out of the building, and be so tainted that it would be most disagreeable for every person coming in contact with it. Last year Councillor Garner had a letter sent by a resident somewhere near the works, stating that the air in the back part of the town was se tainted that there was not a room in the house that was not tilled with bad atmosphere. There was no way, Councillor Dixon maintained, of doing away with tainted air without passing it through fire. The manure, he said, only contained 6 per cent, of ammonia, and it ought never to have less than 9 to 12 per cent. Councillor Dixon held that the depOts so far from being a saving, as had been argued, were an expense to the town on account of the deterioration of the manure. He hoped the Corporation, for the sake of themselves and the poorer inhAbitants, especially the children—for it was a shame That they should have to eat bread and butter tainted with the gasses arising from the intercep- tor—would accept his resolution. 0 Councillor CANNELL seconded the motion,and advocated the appointment of an independent committee to dial with the question. He had experienced the nuisance. He had been out at night and had a good emetic from it, enough to occupy him for half a mile. The Sanitary Committee had promised to do something, and the time had come for something to be done. He had been requested by a very influential portion of the Howley Ward people who felt this nuisance every day to bring. forward the matter. If closing these depots would involve4hrowing away £20,000 to £30,000, were the inhabitants on this account to be• poisoned in the summer ? He cared not for medical officers of health or anybody else, he had cases of diarrhcea, and enteric and typhoid fever which he put down to the emanations from the intercepting depots. Councillor JENKINS maintained the necessity of some- thing being done,but said he could not accept the drastic resolution of Councillor Dixon, and desired to propose an amendment, but was informed by the Mayor and Alderman Sutton that he could not do so.

Councillor HILL supported the motion. He Said he had experienced the smell at home many a time night and day, and it was enough to sicken everybody in the house. His neighbours also complained, property was depreciated and If that nuisance could not be abated in some other way the depots ought to be done away with.

_ Alderman SurToN said he was of opinion that the motion was a very foolish one, but Councillor Dixon was in the habit of making extraordinary proposals and statements in that Council Chamber, without the slightest regard to their justice or injustice. If Coun- cillor Dixon considered himself a true friend of the rate- payers, he had a very queer way of showing this, for at one fell swoop he would throw over property which had cost thousands of pounds and years of labour. If Coun- cillor Dixon thought he had the support of the rate- payers to his proposal, he (Alderman Sutton) would remind him that he had been rejected hy them in nearly every ward of the town time after time during the last two or three years, (" no, no,") though he had made this depots question his war cry. He was elected to that Council by a majority of five only, and that was obtained, he (Alderman Sutton) believed by an accident. Therefore he could not ,come there and say he was re- presenting the ratepayers in continually bringing this question forward. He could only tell the Council what somebody else had told him about this nuisance: he knew nothing of his own knowledge. Councillor BEAMAN opposed the resolution. He admitted that under exceptional circumstances and abnormal conditions, an effluvia might arise from works that some persons with very sensitive olfactory nerves might deem a nuisance. From enquiries in the immediate neighbourhood of the depots,he found opinions varied very considerably, but in no case did he find that the nuisance was continuous, Councillor Beaman chal- lenged .investigation into the matter, and deprecated bold and senseless denial of the good belonging to the system adopted at the depots, and crude and unscientific theories.

Councillor GREEN maintained that a nuisance existed' and demanded a remedy,though objecting to the form of the resolution. The people of Battersby-lane, had he said, complained to him of the nuisance. _

Councillor FLEMING thought something ought to be done to remedy it; failing that let the depots be abol- ished. Councillor H. ROBERTS submitted that there had not been a word said against the depots that night, which was capable of proof. There had, he said, been erected a plant for the special purpose of dealing with the vicious atmosphere so much complained of, and th9re were independent reports on this plant up to date which were most satisfactory. He maintained that the agitation •of the question was merely for the purpose of manufac- turing electioneering capital. Cotncillor VOISEY expressed the conviction that the Sanitary Committee had but one object in view, to re- duce the cause of complaint as much as possible. He unfavourably, contrasted the system of conveyance in pails which formerly prevailed in the town, with the present treatment of the manure. Alierman BURGESS said he should have supposed Councillor Dixon would have backed his motion with an allegation of some serious nuisance -but he had not done sp. What had been done had been done with the full concurrence of the Council, and their action he believed was supported by the vast majority of the community. Alderman Burgess said hequite agreed that the elections had something to do with the complaints made, and quoted an election address of Councillor Dixon pledging himself to support any resolution for abating the nuisance and to vote if possible for the abolition of the depots. Alderman Burgess said he lived a great deal nearer the works than Mr. Dixon or Mr. Fleming, and on no occasion had he detected the faintest smell from them, or heard a syllable from anyone in the neighbourhood or across the river about any unpleasant- ness arising from them. The doctors,in his opinion,were very much more responsible for deaths in Warrington than the depots were. (Laughter). He was satisfied that the arrangements which had been made were such that there would be no nuisance in the summer time. The system was, t e considered,the greatest success that the Corporation had achieved. The death rate in War- rington at present was one they could turn to with very great satisfaction; having been reduced by cne-third compared with what it was before this work was com- snenced. S - ,

Alderman PLArr did not approve of the terms of the resolution, but considered there had been, was, and would be, a nuisance. He had, personally, on many oc- casions been a victim to it,and hundreds of people had had a like experience. The Chairman of the Sanitary ' Committee said there never had been a nuisance, and , that in spite of a memorial signed by I,ooohouseholders, desiring it to be at °nee suppressed. What hope of re- medy by the Sanitary Committee was there, under such circumstances? He did not think the Chairman of that Committee ever did smell it or ever intended to smell it. —(a laugh)—having that peculiar constitution which enabled him not to smell. As to the assertion that the complaints were merely a matter of electioneer- inp Alderman Platt said the, first time kr. Dixon was returned it was In the North-east Ward, and the very reason he was elected by so small a majority was because he said nothing about the depots, and Mr. Jenkins who was returned by a larger pledged himself to deal with the depots ques- tion. Mr. Beaman said the nuisance was not continu- ous, but not being a member of the Sanitary Committee I he possiOly did not know that the working for half the , time at the depots was not continuous. Alderman Platt ' advocated the conveyance of the manure to Longford rather than that the depots should remain in a neigh- bourhood where they were not wanted. Had they, he said, been placed in Palmyra Square there would have been such an uproar that the Corporation dared not have allowed them to continue there. But they were placed amongst poor cottages, the inhabitants of which had as much right to pure air as any persons round that table. Dr. Cannell was not the only medical 1113,12 in the borough who held the opinion he di sa on the matter. And now after waiting year after year for the remedying of this nuisance they were met with the assertion that there never had been any.

Alderman BURGESS emphatically denied ever having said this. Alderman PLATT contended that Alderman Burgess had distinctly said "There never has been a nuisance: I never smelt it." This subject had been unfortunately brought forward at an inopportune time for his (Alder- man Platt's) argument, but in the summer time it would be found that there was a nuisance, and nobody but Alderman Burgess would say there was not. After the impracticable stand taken by him he (Alderman Platt) felt compelled to vote for the motion. Councillor Duce; having made a few further remarks, a division was taken, when Alderman Platt, Councillors Cannell, Dixon, and Hill voted for the motion; and against it there were Aldermen Sutton, Holmes, Burgess, and Wright, and Councillors H. Roberts, Hepherd, Walker, Beaman, Green, Voisey, Greening, Monks, Ashton, Fleming, and Fairclough. There were thus four , for the motion and 15 against, including all present, ex- cept the Mayor, who did not vote. Several members had left before the division took place. The meeting then concluded.

Day by day blood spitting from the lungs diminished, Bronchitis disappeared, like magic, to the four winds of the heavens, and in a few weeks, by the Continual use of Tudor Williams' Balsam of Honey, I was restored to my usual good health. The Distress 'The official mind is slow to Per' in ceive or to learn anything 35 14,1 Ireland. Ireland; but it has at last dawD° upon the LORD LIEUTENANT and the Iniss SEe°,l TART that there is distress in the West of Irelazir of such a character as to necessitate an appeal f°o charitable aid. An appeal has accordingly beed issued which is signed by the Earl of ZeTLAND ' il Mr. BALFOUR ; and it is to be hoped that it be cordially responded to irrespective of religio'
( a arf) fot
weal! id 11,tiOx!,ti Pee° iclud° )r

or political creed. As "Christopher North" once nobly said—" The animosities are mortal, but the humanities are eternal." After describing the circumstances of the poor people who are suffering , from a potato famine, the official letter proceeds: " Here, then, is a state ot things which may well appeal to the charitable. Here is poverty; here la helplessness; here, in a word, is a social or- ganism, sickly at all times, stricken now with a disease from which without extraneous help .it • has no power to rally." This is a far .different view of the situation from what was taken in September last, when the Tory Papers were ridiculing the statements of the
Isla-tionalists, and broadly hinting that the distress 'cry was merely a cry, got. up with the object of

stimulating interest in the advocates of Home Rule. Mr. BALFOUR had not then taken the trouble to make inquiry on the. spot; and he had the hardihood to declare that the distress from the Partial failure of the potato crop was not too serious to be left to the ordinary operations of the Poor-law. He harps on another string now, for it seems that it is so serious that not even the poor- law—plus the wages to be paid for the making of light railways—is sufficient to meet it. The appeal is therefore a confession of failure—of failure, alas, too common in our dealings with the people of Ireland. We ignore their complaints, their claims, and their aspirations until too late, and then, in a tinkering way, we seek to repair that which can-, not be repaired by tinkering. It is Mr. BAL-' Fouß's weakness as Irish Secretary that he is ready to swallow official statements without due inspection. When he treated the approaching distress as nothing of moment, it is to be supposed that, he had made :inquiry from the •officials resident in the West. If he had not, he deserves to be punished for culpable negligence. But, on the other hand, what are we to think of that official information which is now found to be unreliable? Is not the whole situation—deplor- able though it be—another argument for letting the people df Ireland have an. opportunity of man- aging their own affairs in their own way? If Mr. Balfour had gone to the West of Ireland some months earlier—beforein fact he was shamed into going—it is just possible that steps might have been taken, whilst Parliament was sitting, to ob- viate the need of this appeal to the charitable. But the distress is in existence and it must be relieved. "The conclusions at which we have arrived (say the Lord Lieutenant and Secretary), as to the form which charitable aid may most safely take are three. It should be confined—(l) To aiding families in serious want who, from having no able- bodied persons among them, cannot derive any direct benefit from pubic works; (2) to providing meals at schools for children who ought to be in attendance there; (3) to providing clothes for Children who are unable to procure them, and Who at present are prevented by the want of them from going to school at all." We do not suppose that anyone will quarrel with these conclusions, for they are definite and practical. What is re- quired now is that they shall be efficiently carried out. There is plenty of money in the United Kingdom, and there will be no lack of funds, if Pressing and immediate Stal)o-be taiiiin to obtain them. This is a case in which the adage may be said to apply: "He gives twice who gives quickly."

Facts and THE Financial Reform Associa- Figures tion which has its headquarters? at Liverpool, and of which Mr. E. K. MIISPRATT is president, doesn't make much noise in the world, but it does a large amount of useful work. Its annual Almanac has been issued for twenty-seven years, and it is not too much to say that no other publication has been of such service to politicians, lecturers, and newspaper writers. There was a time when its editors toiled almost alone in the hard field of national statistics; but of late years there have been others to work on somewhat similar lines; and as the result shows thero is plenty of room for all gleaners. The Almanac for 1891, while retaining and bringing up to date all facts and figures of first importance, Contains additions which are especially valuable as -hearing directly upon current questions. Several Pages are devoted to giving the numbers of per- sons employed in coal and other mines, and the number of hours worked by miners in various Parts of the country. In view of the growing agitation for Parliamentary enactment of an eight hours day for this class of workers, it is a matter IA course to say that these statistics are of the highest importance. They show that the hours 'vary considerably, some counties working much longer hours than others. In Durham, Northum- berland, South Staffordshire, and Worces- tershire the hours at present worked in coal inines are just under eight per day, while in Xorth-east Lancashire, and in Ireland, they run Irom 9/ to 91 per day. Why should there be this difference? It is certainly not to be ascribed to variety in the nature of the material, or of the Means employed. It may be said that if the miners of Staffordshire and Durham can secure an eight hours day without legislation it ought to be Possible for the rest to secure a. similar boon. But this does not by any means follow, especially when the smaller mines are taken into .account. Scat- tered bodies of men have just as much title to consideration as the rest, but being scattered, and therefore lacking an organisation, they cannot en- force their pleas. They are relatively weak, and it is because they are weak that it becomes the business of the State to afford them protec- tion, when it can be • usefully and legitimately given. This particularly applies to metalliferous nines where as a rule comparatively small bodies men are employed. It is the practice already in these mines in the Isle of Man, in Shropshire, and in some other places, to keep to a day of eight hours. while the custom in North and East Lan- cashire is nine hours per day. We have not yet Ina anyone who. asserts that eight hours is not long enough to work under-ground; and having regard to the fact that the eight hours plan has Proved successful in so many places, we do not see .11j113' it should not be made uniform by Act of Par- rnient. For those who want further details on ;his important question, we must refer them to the lmanac itself. It is to be had for a shilling, and It contains, it is hardly necessary to add, special Information on scores of other matters relating to trade, finance, taxation, land, licensing, and local nd national government.

div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

"Mill Place."—The factory you inquire about was burned down on October 22nd, ISSO. We have no means of ascertaining the other informa- tion you ask for. We hold over, under pressure upon our space, a letter on the distress in Warrington ; and a sketch by Mr. Percy Silcoek on hot-water systems in dwellings, and their relation to frost.

"After long years 1" The Warrington Town Council decided, on Tuesday, that when the next rate is laid an extra halfpenny shall be levied for the Library and Museum. This means that the Library is at last to be made absOlutely free.

4ould seem as if the Warrington Town Coun- cil will talk, and talk, and talk for ever about the nuisance of the Intercepting Depots; but they get nothing done. As some of the members want evi- dence before taking action, why not appoint a Special Committee to inquire and take evidence? We venture to predict that if this be done, the result will stagger those who are sceptical on the subject.

There is an American Archbishop who has sus- pended a priest for having permitted a bazaar and fancy fair. Let raffling at bazaars be prohibited by all means ; it is demoralising, and it is illegal; but to put a veto on bazaars themselves is to push purity too far. It is like, to quote a well-known couplet— Dissecting the whole inside of a question, And with it, too, the process of digestion.

The severe weather is having an effect upon the attendance at the Warrington Ragged School. Some of the children are staying away for want of shoes and stockings, but the officials are doing all their very limited means will permit, to remedy the evil. It is to be hoped they will be more successful than they have hitherto been in obtain- ing contributions. They are doing admirable work, and doing it in.an admirable way.

Another slave dhow has been captured off the North-east coast of Africa; but it is not pleasant to think that there are slave dhows still to capture. The combined eflorts of European Powers ought to render the slave trade impossible. Slavery is a crime against humanity; it is the sum of all villanies, and the slave dealer, once caught red- handed, ought to suffer long, and bear ever after the brand of his iniquity.

, -- Dr. Crispie has been detailing his experience of the treatment of drunkards to the Society for the Study of Inebriety. He recommends compulsory control of confirmed drunkards; such people suffer from disease—even as insanity is a disease. What a blessing it would be to thousands of families if a law to attain this end were placed upon the sta- tute book! It would be home rule of the very best kind.

Another rumour as to Mr. Gladstone's. retire- ment. This sort of thing comes, like Christmas, once a year. It is "a weak -invention of the enemy" as a rule, when the, wish is father to the thought. This time the rumour is suggestive of "the lie circumstantial," for it is actually stated that he is "preparing his valedictory, address:' As a matter of fact Mr. Gladstone has made arrange- ments, as usual, for living in London during the approaching session.

Sir W. Hart-Dyke has caused no little stir, as one of the "whips" of the Conservative party, through advising the National Conservative League that "they may expect a dissolution in a few weeks." His statement is now being minimised as much as possible by the Tories; but there is no gainsaying the fact as to his opinion of the likeli- hood of such a step being taken. Liberals should take the.hint as well as Tories, and make ready for the fray.

"It's a mad world, my masters." How slow it is in learning the doctrine of peace and good-will to all mankind! Here is Russia, a Christian coun- try, revealing her idol, of Christianity by expelling people who happen to be Jews!. And this is not the ninth, but the nineteenth century. These Jew- baiters ought to give themselves time to reflect that Christ himself was a Jew. But reflection is not one of their traits; the barbarian would expel Christ himself in enforcing a barbarous edict.

There have been complaints both at Warrington and at Earlestown of the neglect of the authorities to see to streets and footpaths being cleared of snow; and if there haven't been complaints in many other places it is not because there has been no need to compl&n. Proceedings were taken, the °Vier day, against the Paddington Vestry, and though, through an error sin proceeding, the case collapsed, the adtion had the effect of awaking the Vestry to a sense of their duty. How would it be to indict somebody nearer home?

Fishing is usually associated with ideas of peace ; but now the talk is of war, if certain ques- tions of fishing rights in northern seas are not settled. Lord Salisbury is beset on two sides; there is a difficulty with France as to what should or should not be done off the coast of Newfound- land; and there is difficulty with the United States as to the Bi3hring Sea fisheries. It is hard to be- lieve that the tall talk will end in blows in either case; but rations display no more sense than fish- wives now and again.

Particulars have been furnished us of two cases in which persons have "got themselves into trouble" through, as it is alleged, giving informa- tion to the Warrington authorities of actual or apprehended wrong-doing. In one instance legal proceedings have been taken against the informant, and in the other proceedings are threatened. It is not for us to prejudge cases which are as yet to be decided upon; but we must say that occasionally the way seems to be made hard not for transgres- sors but for those who venture to call attention to transgression.. Let the Watch Committee mind what they are about; it is their duty not to harrass but to protect law-abiding citizens.

SpeaKing in Birmingham, at a Provident Society on Monday night, Mr. Chamberlain said of 6,567 Friendly Societies as to which quinquennial returns had been made, that "5,030 were in a more or less insolvent state." This is a very hard saying on the face of it, and yet it is a very vague one. What does "more or less insolvent" mean? Mr. Cham- berlain should either have said more •or said no- thing at all. His remarks as they stand cast a reflection upon the majority of the Friendly Socie- ties of the country and may do great harm. Having gone so far, the matter should be further pursued. It would be a national calamity if hun- dreds not to say thousands of Friendly Societies should become insolvent.

Ambassadors have been described as men who "lie abroad " for the benefit of their countrymen at home ; but without going so far we may at least say they belong, like the members of the House ef Lords, to the class of people who do nothing in particular, and do it very well. Having nothing to do at Washington, the ambassadors of England, Germany, and Austria, have been having a little quarrel as to who should go in first at the recep- tion of the President of the United States. The great question has happily been settled without a declaration of war. The conclusion come to is that seniority decides precedence; and this means that the man who represents John Bull must not precede, as he has been doing, but follow the other two.

MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AND TIED HOUSES. Mr. J. T. Brunner has given notice that at the April Quarter Sessions for the County of Chester he will move for the appointment of a committee of justices to examine into and report upon some questions of law relating to the licensing of houses for the sale of intoxicating drinks. Mr. Brunner complains that the system of putting managers in tied houses takes away from the magistrates nearly the whole of their power. BAIGRATIEM—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Onion, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, " Examiner " Office, Bewsey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.p: SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN MUSICIAN.

Mr. John Holford, conductor to the Runcorn Tonic Sol-Fa Choir, and musical instructor to the Widnes School Board, has just succeeded in passing the final examina- tion for the diploma of Graduate of the Tonic Sol-Fa College. ANNUAL ELLE now on, at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. FATAL FALL AT WIDNES.

On Monday morning, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held-an inquest at Widnes Accident Hospital,on the body of Ellen Moan, 44 years of age, who lived with her husband at 3, Farrant-st. Ore the 26th December the deceased fell down on the pavement, which was slippery, owing to frost and snow, and broke her leg. She was taken to the hospital, where she died on Friday. A Verdict of accidental death was returned.
• ANNUAL SALE now on, at J. Sc W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. SUNDAY LABOUR AT WIDNES.

The Rev. G. A. Le Bert of St. Ambrose Church,Widnes, who has recently agitated for reduction of Sunday labour in Widnes has received a letter from Mr. Carey, secretary, to the United Alkali Company, stating that as soon as the directors can get installed in the new offices they will be prepared to receive a deputation of Widnes ministers of religion, and the petition lately signed by them. He adds that" it is the desiVe of the directors to diminish Sunday labour as far as possible."

div.head: POACHING AT NORTON ESTATE.
div.p: POACHING AT NORTON ESTATE.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Isaac Johnson of Halton, and Henry Wych, of Norton, were charged with having on the 22nd December trespassed in fmrsuit of game on land at Norton, in the occupation of Sir Richard Marcus Brooke.—Gamekeeper Hargraves stated that on the day in question he found the defendants at Weirs Gorse, attempting to catch rabbits by Means of a ferret and a net. Johnson pleaded guilty and was fined 10s. and costs. A warrant was issued against Wych,whe did not appear.

ACME DOOll CHECKS AND SPRINGS.—Garland, Ironmonger, Earlestown and Warrington.—.Advt. FOOTBALL MATCH FOR THE WIDNES ACCIDENT HOSPITAL. On Thursday afternoon, a football match was played on the Widnes ground in aid of the Widnes 'Accident Hospital. The contestants were Mr. Levey's theatrical company, now engaged at the Alexandra theatre in the production of the pantomime "Dick Whittington and his Cat," and a team of the Widnes club. The fun was fast and furious, and the 300 spectators who assembled were repaid for braving the intense cold wind that blew across the ground. The score at the finish was Theatri- cals 2-2.0; Widnes 2-1-0.
A BOATMAN FOUND DEAD AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday morning, a boatman, named John Den- ton, alias Basford, who is said to be related to a well- known London preacher, was found dead on the canal bank at Runcorn. He was employed on the narrow boats George and Alice, belonging to Messrs. Rathbone and Co., and on Wednesday night he complained of a pain in his side and of feeling generally unwell. He got up early on Thursday and later was found dead on the bank by Peter Bradbury. An inquest was held yesterday and a verdict of death from natural causes was returned.

div.head: DESTRUCTIVE THIEF AT WIDNES.
div.p: A DESTRUCTIVE THIEF AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, yesterday, Julia O'Brien, an old offender, was charged with having maliciously smashed a pane of glass worth £l2, in the shop of Messrs. Freeman, Hardy, and Willis, boot dealer, Victoria-road, and also with having stolen a pair of boots worth 6s. 7d. on the previous evening at half-past six. Mr. Machin of the Arch Hotel, saw the woman smash the window with a stone, and seized her just as she was taking a pair of boots. He handed her over to P.C. Evans. The pri- soner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. AnruilL SALE now on, at J. I W. DUTTON'S Sankey-A., Warrington.—Ar4l.

div.head: MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN.
div.p: MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN.

The annual tea party and concert in connection with the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen was held in the Mission Room, at Bottom Locks, which had been decorated for the occasion. A Christmas tree, on whose branches were hung various articles, was sus- pended from the ceiling. The tea was dispensed by the following ladies who presided at the tales :—Mesdames Woosnam, Meadowcroft, Abel, Crosby, Howitt, Read, Digges, and Misses Taylor and Newman. At the subse- qnent entertainment Mr. J. J. Howitt presided, and de- livered an appropriate speech; and during an interval in the programme the Rev. C. M. Woosnam proposed a vote of thanks to the kind friends who had contributed to the tea and Christmas tree.' He remarked that he had been struck with the generosity and kindness of the people on both sides of the Mersey. During Christ- mas time no fewer than 1,500 seamen bad been enter- tained at the Mersey Missions and he wished they could have entertained more. (Applause.) Next year he hoped they would have a new institute in Runcorn. Liverpool had done its share and had contributed be- tween £2OO and £3OO, and he trusted that they would soon see the erection of the institute commenced. (Ap- plause.)—The Rev. J. Fell seconded the proposition Which was carried by acclamation.—Mr. W. Shaw (the missionary), proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies who had presided at the tea tables, and also to Mr. Fox for arranging the musical programme. The motion was seconded by Captain Crowther, and carried unanimously. —The entertainment was carried out by the following local vocalists, who acquitted themselves in a manner which gained the hearty plaudits of the audience : Messrs. Pennington, Fox, Pilgrim, R. Edwards, Fitton, .1. Nickson, Grounds, Morris, and Temperlev, Misses Temperley and Stubbs, and Mrs. W. Grounds.—A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceeding.

div.head: ASSAULT IN A RAILWAY @ARRIAGE.
div.p: ASSAULT IN A RAILWAY @ARRIAGE.

Henry Shard, labourer. was indicted on Wednes- day at the Cheshire quarter sessions, held at linuts- ford, for assaulting in a railway carriage near Stock- port a young woman named Elizabeth' Abbotts. The girl, to escape his violence, got on the foot-. board, and thence fell on the line, with the result that one of her feet was so injured by a passing train that it had to be amputated. The prisoner was found guilty and sentenced to twelve months imprisonment, with hard labour.

Now OPEN FOR THE BEASON.—Smart and Co.'s private Writing and Commercial Academy for ladies and gentlemen, at Mr. Chantry's, 13 Sankey-st., Warrington. Open every Tuesday from 3to 9 p.m. Writing: Gentlemen are taught a fine bold, rapid business hand, and ladies an elegant and fow- ing style. Terms for the complete course, One Guinea. Book- keeping: Pupils are taught how to open, keep, Valance, and close a complete set of books by double entry; and our certifi- cate for proficiency is given to each pupil. Arithmetic and mental calculation taught practically. Shorthand. Pitman's system. Pupils will be received on Tuesday next, at any hour from 3to 9 p.m. No classes, the *instruction is individual. Card of terms and full particulars may be had at Mr. Chantry's 13, Sankey-st., Warrington, or post free from our Head Academy, 2, Brown-st., thee Market, Manchester.— Advt.
ST. HELENS INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.-
PROPOSAL TO FREE THE INSTITUTION.

The St. Helens Town Council, had under Consi- deration at the monthly meeting on Wednesday a motion by Councillor Martin that, having regard to the many cases .in which payment of fees for mainV:nance in .the Infectious Diseases Hospital had been remitted, and for the purpose of the more effectual prevention of the spread of infectious dis- ease, no charge for such maintenance be made as from the Ist mat., except for pauper cases. The hospital was opened in 1881, at a cost of over £2,000, and the corporation had made a charge of is. per day for each adult, and 6d. per day for each child under fourteen years of age, admitted to the institution. These charges were made since the opening of the hospital, and in many cases had pressed very heavily upon some of the poor families in the town. The accounts of the borough treasurer show that during the last financial year the total expenditure on the hospital account was £837 10s. 2d., and the receipts (including £37 11s. rc- ceived as fees from patients) £ll9 Os. sd. After some discussion, it was decided by the Coancil that the matter should be brought before the Health Committee at their next meeting. HOT WATYR HEATING.—Garland sends estirnates free?. PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.

_ The Committee having the consideration of this subject in hand, are prepared to recommend the Board at their meeting on Tuesday next, to divizle the town int& six wards, each ward to return four members to the Council. On Thursday a deputa- tion of the Board Waited upon Lord Cross at Liver- pool, to ask him to use his influence in obtaining the charter of incorporation as soon as possible.
SEVERE WEA.THER.-THE MERSEY FROZEN OVER.

The Mersey at Eastham was on Wednesday morn- ing found to be frozen over—a phenomenon which has not occurred for many years. During the day the coating of ice disappeared. A dense fog pre- vailed in Belfast Lough, on Wednesday, and in the English Channel there was a considerable snowfall, with a strong north-easterly gale. Further deaths from exposure are reported. ANNUAL SATE now on, at J. SG W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

SAD DEATH OF A WIDNES FLIT MATE. Whilst the flat Pennington, on a voyage from Liverpool to Fleetwood, was off Blackpool Pier on Thursday morning, about half-past three, the cap- tain discovered that his mate had accidentally been carried overboard and drowned. The deceased was a young man belonging to Widnes. There were only tbe captain and mate on board, and the captain was obliged to bring the flat in himself. The occurrence was reported at Fleetwood on the arrival of the flat. SOIT-WtSTER Boor PLATES.—J. S. Garland, Builders' Iron- monger, 51, Bridge-st.,Warrington.—Advt.
SHAKESPEARE THEATRE PANTOMIME, LIVERPOOL.

" Humpty Dumptv," from the old time-honoured rhyme upon the egg falling from the wall, is the subject of the pantomime at the Shakespeare Theatre, Liverpool, as will be seen from our adver- tising columns. The scenery is of a magnificent description, and the charming dresses add to the effect of the production. Full of wit and humour, and with an exceptionally strong caste, Humpty Dumpty is attracting large houses, and it is sure of the success which it deserves.—On Wednesday afternoon the children of the Liverpool Bluecoat Hospital, numbering 350, attended the performance of the pantomime,' Humpty Dumpty," Their Cheers at the close testified to their thorough enjoyment of the play, and their appreciation of Mr. Harris's kind invitation.
ANNUAL BALE now on, at J. & W. DuTToN's Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt.

LORD CROSS AT WIDNES.

lUnder the auspices of the Widnes Division Con- servative Association a public meeting was held in Widnes Drill Hall, on Thursday night. The room was well filled, and was decorated *ith streamers and mottoes. Major Cross presided, and on the platform were Viscount Cross, Messrs. T. C. Edwards Moss, M.P., T. B. Roythin, M.P., J. E. Sheppard, C.C., Major Larmer, Colonel Strongitharm, Lieutenant. Colonel Williams, Major Royden, Captain Lewis, Lieutenant G. E. Sayce, Messrs. Graves, C. Neilson, F. H. Mort, F. Liddell, James White, C. E. Barlow, Mackenzie Smith, G. Pryde, W. T. Husband, W. 11. Evans, W. H. Strongitharm, G. Hughes, J. C. Craw- ford, and W. S. Callender. Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss,. M.P. for the Widnes division,speaking after a few introductory remarks had been given by the chairman, said that since the Conservatives of the division last met in that hall they had lost some supporters of the cause in the division, yet he ventured to think that the great Unionist cause was as flourishing, and more flourish- ing than ever. They Unionists must vote for sound policy and for sound principles; for measures, and not for men. (Applause.) Lord Cross, who wascordially received, contended that after Mr. Gladstone's association with Mr. Parnell and his party his judgment of men was not to be trusted. Mr. Gladstone's judgment as regarded men had bitterly failed. Mr. Gladstone had had a very fair field to work upon in Ireland. He had had a long series of years to think over what should be done, and they would, he was sure, agree with him that no one could adopt such a question as the Home Rule qustion without having fully deliberated on everything connected with it, and could not have bronght it forward without being satisfied that the measures proposed were right. The measure Mr. Gladstone brought forward was rejected by Parliament, a dissolution followed soon afterwards, and the measure was absolutely rejected by the nation. Therefore they had a man coming before them who, so far as measures are concerifed, was a man who had signally failed not only in Parliament, but before the con- stituents,who gave their verdict with an unqualified voice against him. (Applause.) A section of the Irish people had shown themselves absolutely incapable of self-control. Did they mean to tell him that Englishmen were goitigto give over to them the life and property, not simply of their own followers' but of that great Protestant portion of the north, who had nothing to do with them? There were also, thank God, hundreds and thousands of the most loyal Roman Catholics in the south who were equally entitled to protection, and he ventured to say that if the policy of the present Government was pursued for a few years more they would find hundreds and thousands more in Ireland who would hold out their' hands and ask to be saved from these agitators They knew exactly what these Irish agitators wanted; it was complete separation. They wanted Ireland to be an independe,ut nation, and ti's a first step they wanted to get the control of the land and of the constabulary. (Applause.) Mr. Geo. Pryde, moved a resolution expressing confidence in Mr. Moss, M.P., and in the Govern- ment, Captain Lewis seconded the motion, Mr. Royden, M.P., supported it, and it was carried unanimously.
DARESBURY HIGIIWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held in the Sessions Room, Daresbury, on Thursday. Mr. J. C. Parr presided, the other members present being Messrs. J. Darbyshire, W. Bradford, T. Hall. J. L. Jones, James Parr, W. Beswick,G. W. Phillips, W. Long, J. Cooper, E. Clarke, W. Tickle. and P. Darbyshire ; 11. G. Linaker (assistant clerk), aud Swinton (surveyor.) THE AUDITING OF THE ACCOUNTS.—The ASSISTANT CLERK stated that the auditor had audited the accounts of the Board for the year ending March 25th, 1890, and his certificate stated ' that the accounts appeared to be correct. —Mr. J. DARBYSEIRE said the accounts had not been audited till November aithongh the financial year ended on March 25th. The audit seemed to be very I considerably out of data, and the officers in connection with the Board could not remember the many details in connection with the accounts. He thought it would be better if the accounts were Zudited a littt nearer the ; end of the financial year.—The ASSISTANT CLERK said it generally got• towards the end of the year before the auditor gpt to the Highway Board's accounts.—A MEMBER said there had been the same complaint with regardto late audits at Northwich Board of Guardians.—The CHAIRMAN said he supposed it arose from the fact that the auditors had more than they could do. A SUGGESTED ROAD IMPROYEMENT.—Mr. H. Milling, of Warrington, accompanied by Mr. W. Owen, architect, attended the Board meeting and made an application with regard to rebuilding a wall at the corner of the road leading from Grappenhall and Latchford station near to the house owned and occupied by Mr. Milling. Before rebuilding, Mr. Milling wished to make an arrangement whereby he would give a piece of land and two trees to the Board to improve the highway, on condition that the Board make a footpath 4 feet wide alongside the wall.— After some conversation it was decided, on the proposi- tion of Mr. JN. DARBYSHIRE, that the matter be left to a committee consisting of the Chairman, and Messrs. W. Long, W. Bradford, W. Pierpoint, and T. Hall. THE Sam CANAL ENGINES.—There having been com- plaints as to the danger paused by engines on the Ship Canal Works running close to the highway at Morris Brook, the Ship Canal Committee had met some repre- sentatives of the Canal Company and the latter pro- mised that their overland route would soon be completed and the nuisance would be, then abated. The rest of the business was formal.
THE NEW REGISTER OF NORTILWICH PA RLIA.MENTART•DI VISION.

The register of the Parliamentary Divisions of Cheshire for the year 1891 have just been issued, and the following particulars collected from that of the Northwich Division may reveal some features of interest to the electors of that part of the county. The register contains a total of 12,328 names ; the regis- ter for 1890 contained 12,284, showing a net increase of 44, which is a very much smaller increase than in 1889- 90, when the augmentation was 233. It thus appears that the increase in the register is only in those districts which come under the description of "Chemical," and however we may account for the fore- going facts,the comparisons are certainly suggestive. For the first time several of the urban districts, as distinct from the municipal boroughs,have their register in alpha- betical street orderinstead of alphabetical name order as formerly, the progressive number of the houses in each street determining the order in which the names of the electors appear. This however, is only the case in which an urban district is also a complete or self-con- tained county electoral division, and in the Northwich division, Runcorn is the only town possessing a street register, although the urban districts of Northwich, Winsford, and Middlewich are capable of beiag simi- larly treated. We cannot help expressing the hope that the County Council may see their way at their next meeting, to order that all urban districts in the county shall in future have their registers prepared in street order, especially so as the neighbouring county of Lanca- shire so determined twelve months ago, and the regis- ters of all urban districts in that county for the current year are so made out. div.head: FROST AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE FROST AT RUNCORN.
RELIEF OF THE DISTRESSED

During the past week a severe frost has prevailed in Runcorn neighbourhood and outdoor labourers are suffering in consequence. Quarry workers have been out of employment for many weeks past. The thaw at the latter end of last week enabled the traffic on the Bridgewater Canal to be carried on with fairly good despatch, but the recurrence of the frost renewed the difficulties under which the Company had been working the traffic for the pre- vious ten days. On Thursday ice had accumulated to such an extent that the attempt to send flats atid tugs along was altogether abandoned. The banks of the canal are lined with "tied up" flats and narrow boats, and many hundreds of boatmen are thrown idle. There is considerable distress in the town amongst the poorer classes, and in order to relieve it to some extent a soup kitchen Was established at the Town Hall on Wednesday, Mr. R. Abel and Mr. J. Percival were the originators of the subscription raised, and Mrs. Jackson the caretaker of the Hall has done much work in connection with the affair. About 300 hundred persons, chiefly children have been fed each day. Mr. Percival dispensing the soup and bread. At the Mersey Missions on Thurs- day Mr. W. Shaw fed about 200 persons. Last night a meeting of the Committee was held to organise a plan to relieve the necessities of the poor in a sys- tematic manner and to-night (Saturday) a public meeting is to be held to consider the subject.

div.head: SHOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: SHOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Thurs- day, held an inquest at the Widnes Accident Hospi- tal, on the body of Thomas Flannigan, a chemical labourer, who was killed at Messrs. Muspratt's works, on Monday.—Mary Flannigan, of 60, Cromwell-st., the widow, deposed that the deceased was 40 years of age and had worked at Muspratt's since a boy.—James Dillon, labourer, said on Mon- day about 1.15, he and the deceased and two other men named Croghan and Quirke carried a big car- boy of nitric acid to the floor of a tower, in order to empty it into a cistern. Whilst engaged about this work, the flooring gave way and the deceased and the bottle fell to the ground. Witness caaght hold of a pipe with his left hand, and prevented him- self falling. The other men were going down a short ladder at the time and so escaped. The depth of the fall was about 33 feet. The deceased was rendered unconscious by the fall and he was much burnt by the acid. He was immediately conveyed to the Hospital.—James Croghan, labourer, corroborated the evidence, and said just before the platform gave way they had all four been standing upon it.—Mary Warburton,marron of the Hospital,said the deceased suffered from severe burns by nitric acid and from concussion of the brain. He was conscious partly. He died on Tuesday morning. Dr. O'Keefe attended him.—Mr. John Hedley, Manager of the'works, pro- vided plans of the tower, and a foreman produced a portion of the wood which had given way for the inspection of the jury. Before returning a verdict, the jury determined to inspect the spot and the in- quest was adjourned until Friday morning. The inquest was resumed at ten o'clock yesterday morning, and the jury immediately retired to con-, sider their verdict. The Coroner (Mr. Husband) was several times called in to consult with them- and at tWelve o'clock he left them, and swore Serr geant McGregor to keep them without food or drink until they had arrived at a verdict. At a quarter to two the jury asked to see the Coroner' who warned the jury that unless they arrived at a verdict in a reasonable time,- he should bind them over to appear at the Assizes, as lie had no power to discharge them without arriving at a verdict, The foreman (Mr. Hemingway) said the jury were agreed with one exception, and five minutes Would suffice. In a few minutes the foreman handed in the followinverdict :—"That the deceased died at the Accident Hospital on Tuesday, from injuries re- ceived on the previous day, by the giving way of a platform, owing to a defect therein, and to faulty construction.—The Coroner said the jury wished him to impress upon Mr. Hedley, manager of the works that the platforms of towers ought to be periodically and thoroughly examined, and ex- pressed the opinion that this accident could not have happened if the examination had been a little more perfect. The Coroner excused the jury from iurther attendance for three months in consequence of the care and time they had spent upon this in- quiry. •

div.head: FRODSHAII.
div.p: FRODSHAII.

SEQUEL TO THE VOLUNTEER DINNER.-Philip Taylor was summoned to Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly at Sutton. P.C. Brew and P.S. Costello proved the case and said the defendant broughta poker from his house to them.—The defendant said every word the constables said was false. He had been to the Volunteer's dinner at Frodsham, and had three glasses of beer to his dinner. Then the silver cup came round and he had a drink of whisky punch out of it. He was not drunk.—A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

• WESLEYAN MISSION WORK IN LONDON. In conneciion with the Penketh Wesleyan Sunday School, an address was given on Sunday afternoon, by Sister Joseph'ne, one of the sisters in connection with the Rev. klugh Price 'Hughe's mission in the West End of London, She gave a discription of the work which is being done in London to raise the poor and wretched inhabitants of the alums, and concluded by an appeal to the teachers and scholars for help to carry on this work. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.

The weekly meeting of the above association was held on Wednesday evening, in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. J. Wigfield. A paper was read by Mr. T. Gandy en- titled "Habits of Birds." In a most able manner he gave a description of the habits of birds, and the manner and situation in which their nests are built. At the conclusion of the paper an interesting dis- cussion followed in which the following took part: —Messrs. Wigfield, Garnett, Peers, Snoddy, and Parker. Mr. Gandy replied, and the meeting closed in the usual manner.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

PRAYER MEETINGS.—On Monday the opening gathering of a series of united Nonconformists' prayer meetings was held in the Sion chapel, when the Rev. James Bedell gave an address. There was a fair attendance. PRIIIIITIVE METHODIST TEA PARTY.—The beginning-of another series of tea parties was inaugurated in the Primitive Methodist School on Wednesday evening. Mrs. Edwards, of Booth's-hill, was the hostess. After tea an interesting entertainment took place. SATURDAY NIGIT CONCERTS.—The first of a series of Saturday night penny popular concerts took place in the Bridgewater Rooms' on Saturday evening. The programme was furnished by the members of the Ough- trington Church Choir. Mr. Hugh Cameron occupied the chair. Mr. Thomas Watson the newly appointed evangelist in Oughtrington, delivered a temperance address, and an excellent musical programme was rendered.

LYMAI LOCAL Boknn.—The usual monthly meeting of this Board took place on Thursday night, Mr. H. Cameron presiding.—The Law Clerk stated that the new Act called "The Housing of the Working Classes Act" had come into operation, but it did not much affect them in Lymm, except one clause übder which it was. compulsory that a report under an officer of the Board should be made annually. On the motion of Mr. Dutton it was resolved to adopt the part third of the Public Health Amendment Act.

div.head: STA.RR-BOMCETT BUILDING SOCIETY
div.p: STA.RR-BOMCETT BUILDING SOCIETY

The 4th annual meeting of the Warrington First Starr-Bowket Building Society was held on Wed- nesday evening in the Primitive Methodist School- room, Legh-st. Mr. T. Burton, one of the directors, presided, and there was a good attendance. The SECRETARY (Mr. J. Titchett) submittedthe report of the directors as follows :—" In presenting the fourth annual report and balance sheet, the direci tors have pleasure in congratulating the members on the continued prosperity of the society. The total amount of subscriptions received for the year amounts to .C 1595 13s. 9d.; fines £3 19s. lid.; 're- payments on appropriations £377 14s. 10d. ; entrance fees, transfer fees &c. £24 2s. 6L; Income for the year £2OOl us. Od. The working expenses have been kept down, all ex- penses have been met, and the balance in favour of the society is increased to£lo6 18s. 4d."— The report was adopted unanimously.—The retiring directors, Messrs. Joseph Owen, Robert Sutton, Thomas Burton, and John Walker, were re-elected as were also the auditors, Messrs. W. Mullard and P. Pearson. After the annual meeting an appro- priation meeting was held, at which two appropria- tions were made. Mr. Burton again presided, the scrutineers were Mr. J. Hayward and Mr. D. Ikin, ar.d the ballot balls were drawn by Master E. Gandy and Miss Maggie Hill. The first ballot re- sulted in the .number 419 being drawn, and this entitled Mr. A. Nutt Hudston, butcher, to a loan of £2OO for 124 years free of interest. At the next draw 420 was the lucky number, but it was found that the possessor of this number was not clear on the books, and therefore, under the rules, not en- titled to a loan. The number 444 was next drawn, and this entirled Mr. F. Dell, painter, Latchford, to a loan of £2OO. The usual votes of thanks closed the meeting.
THREE WOMEN CHARGED WITH ROB-
BING A FARR LABOURER OF _415.

At the IV arrington Borough Police Court, yester- day, Annie Cooper, Catherine Bowdon, and Sarah O'Brien were charged with robbing John Phillips, who is employed on Mrs. Davis's farm near Frodsham, of the sum of £l5 on the previous day.—Chief Con- stable Hunt said the prisoners Cooper and O'Brien had been lodging at No. 3 Naylor-st., occupied by Ellen Bourke. Bowdon was very well known, and had a husband living atßuncorn. The complainant was paid by his mistress on the 7th inst seventeen sovereigns as wages. He came with these to Warrington, on the Bth inst., and met Cooper, and drank with her at a public- house, where he purchased half a pint of whiskey, bringing it away. The complainant and Cooper then went to her lodgings, where the other two prisoners were. For some reason Mrs. Burke ordered them out, and the other women proceeded to The Rose beerhouse, where the landlord's, (Mr. Jackson's), daughter, Mary Jackson was in charge. The complainant asked for a quart dale, but the girl, who was very intelligent, said, "No, you have had enough." The complainant paid for beer for the women, and sat down, Cooper seating her- self on one side of him and O'Brien on the other. The bottle of whisky was emptied into the beer, and the three women drank the liquid. The girl doticed that the man all at once seemed to get quite queer. The women jumped up and went out. Mary Jackson saw Cooper put her hand into her breast, and say, " Let's divide." The girl at once acquainted her father, and he did not lose a moment in seeing about the Matter. Joseph Bates saw the women come out in a very suspicious manner, and followed them into the Mersey Notel. He saw in Cooper's hand a red calico bag, and saw gold taken from it, and four sovereigns handed by Cooper to O'Brien. He heard O'Brien say "I am not going to have that for my share." Bates said "You have stolen that money from a man in the Rose Inn." Cooper offered him two sovereigns on condition he.kept silent, bit he refused them and also beer.—Mrs. Bailey, landlady of the Mersey Hotel, saw Cooper attempt to hand something to Bates, which he refused to have, and heard him tell her she had robbed a man. O'Brien was seen to chuck some- thing away. The landlord of the Rose Inn came in, and sent for the police, and went and brought Phillips from the Rose. The women were taken to the police station, where Phillips identified them. Bowden took out a shilling, 2d. in copper, and a pawn ticket, say- ing "This is all I have." A female searcher searched the women, and while she was doing so a sovereign fell from Bowden's breast, which she said she had got from the Post Office that morning. Cooper gave up 2d., and then O'Brien gave up 6d. Nothing further was found on the women. The red purse was found under the seat where they had been drinking at the Mosey Hotel.— Alderman Harrison asked if the remainder of the money had been traced.—The Chief Constable said none of it had been, but the police had an idea where some of it was. Another charge had cropped up against Bowden; and he would apply for a remand until Monday.—Dr. Gornall desired to know where the complainant was made drunk.—The Chief Constable did not think he would be made drunk in the beerhouse, but said this had nothing to do with the case.—Dr. Gornall : It has ev'erything to do with the ease.—Alderman Harrison: I really don't see the con- nection between the two.—Dr. Gomel' : I see a great deal.—The Chief Constable said Warrington was a queer place for assisting the police, especially in such circum- stances as these.—The prisoners were remanded till Monday.

div.head: INFIRMARY BA.LL.
div.p: INFIRMARY BA.LL.

The annual ball in aid of the funds of the Warrington Infirmary, came off on Thursday evening in the Assembly Room of the Lion Hotel, Bridg e-st. About 150 were present,includ- ing a number of the principal local and county gentry; and the proceedings were managed by the following stewards with Mr. Harrison Tinsley as secretary :—The Hon. J. E. Cross, Messrs. Peers Egerton Warburton, T. E. Withington, J. R. Pick- mere, John White, John Dun, E. Greenall, jun., E. J. Nicholson, Thomas Litton, H. Greenall, and. Major Stone, King's Regiment.. Vetter's band from Manchester was in attendance and contri- buted a selection of excellent musie, and dancing was kept up with spirit till a late hour. Supper was provided by Miss Hart, the manageress of the Lion Hotel in her usual excellent style. The decorations were of a profuse and artistic character, the walls being hung with mirrors, flags, &c., and the usual accessories employed on such occasions being inter- mingled with the happiest effect. The work of decorating was executed by Messrs. S. E. and R. Johnson. The ball was .in every respect a great success; and the deserving institution in support of which it was held will profit by it to an extent unprecedented, the attendance being larger than on any former occasions.

div.head: BOLD-STREET WESLE YAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, WARRINGTON.
div.p: BOLD-STREET WESLE YAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, WARRINGTON.
ANNUAL TEA MEETING.

On Monday evening the annual tea meeting and entertainment in connection with these schools took place in the Bold-street schoolroom. There was not a large attendance, about 100 sitting down to tea. The following ladies presided at the tables and rendered assistance :—Mrs. Gunnell, Mrs. Silcock, Mrs. Barlow, Mrs. Raft, Mrs. Toft, Mrs. Lingard, Misses Lawton, Weaver, Jones, Bennett, Lingard, Prince, Barlow, Hall, Sherlock, &c. After tea there was an increased attendance at the meeting, over which the Rev. A. Freeman presided. The SECRE- TARY (Mr. W. A. Gleave) read the annual report, which showed that the schoal was in a flourishing condition, and that its future prospects were bright. Th e CHAIR3IAN,iII an opening address,compl imented the secretary on his report, and also referred to the importance of Sunday School teaching.—Mr. Nichol- son, as the senior teacher of the school also gave an address. He said the teachers and school workers had no doubt difficulties to overcome, but if they were determined they would be able to overcome them. Let them be patient, and they would ulti- mately see the result of their labours. No depart- ment of church work had of recent years so altered its phase, its mode and manners, as success- ful school teaching. They ought to look upon the Sunday school as an important adjunct to the Christian work of the church. The Sunday school work was spreading and growing, and would continue to do so. It was the nursery of the church, and to their Sunday scholars they looked to supply the future meml hers and officers of the church. (Applause.) The Rev. Thomas Ross said the main object of the meeting that night was to try to get a closer connection between the congregation and those belonging directly to the Sunday school, a sympathy and interest between those who took an active part in the work and those who did not. Sunday school work was certainly the highest and best possible work a person could be engaged in The most important class of all, he held, was the infant class, and it was a very responsible and trying post for the teacher, and one which required patience and per- severance. There were teachers and teachers. A teacher of a Sunday school should be pure in heart and life. (Applause.)—An address was also given by Mr. Kent.— The musical programme was gone through very success- fully. It included pianoforte solos by Mr. W. H. Payton and Miss H. Brown; songs by Mr. R. E. Garnett, Mr. G. Parr, Air. r, Conway, Mr. Richardson, Miss Fanshaw, and Miss Hedgcock ; reading; by Mr. A. Bennett, and a violin solo by Miss Perry- The aecompaßiments were played by Mr. W. H. Payton.

div.head: PADGATE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS.
div.p: PADGATE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS.
ANNUAL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

The annual distribution of prizes and entertain- ment in connection with the Padgate Industrial Schools took place on Tuesday evening. There WAS a large attendance. The first item on the pro- gramme was a selection by the band, which was excellently 'played. From the head master's report for the year, it appears that the cost of maintenance of the children has been reduced from the previous year by threepence per head per week—the cost of each child now being 2s. 61d. per week. This is considered eminently satisfactory when compared with other institutions of a similar character. For the past twelve months the cost of provisions had been £846: necessaries, £222 3s. 6d.; clothing, £207 The Rev- G. F. ROBERTS presided, and amongst those present were—The Rev. J. J. Langham, and Mrs. Langham, the Rev. Father Myerscough, Mr. William Houghton, Mr. E. Aukland. Mr. and Mrs. Mines (superintendent and matron of the school), Mr. Bayley (assistant master), Mr. Samuel Sutton, Dr. Peacocke, &c.

The CHAIRMAN in an address, said the schools at pre- sent were working as well as Could possibly be expected. Since the time the schools had been at Padgate 950 children had &een admitted and 949 diseharged. Of those 159 had been sent out by the Committee to employments of various kinds, 80 girls had been sent to service, 53 boys had been sent to service, eight boys had been sent to sea, and 18 boys to the army. (Applause.) From that they would recog- nise the usefulness of the schools. The diminution in the cost of maintaining the schools was very satisfactory He paid a tribute to Mr. and Mrs. Mines who had the management of the schools. He could also congratulate the institution and the Com- mittee generally on the appointment of their chaplain. He had known Mr. Langham for sonic years, and he was sure he would do all he could for the children and their Ispiritual welfare. (Applause.) Mr. Roberts then pro- ceeded to distribute the prizes to the following scholars: —Martin Healey, John Foley, Thomas Carty, Frank Berry, Martin Healey, John Melshall, Joseph Bolton, John Siddle, Thomas Clarke, James O'Brien, John Mal- shall, WM. Jones, Patrick Foy, Geo. McClelland, Thomas Riley, Isaac Wadsworth, James Kelly, Robert Barton, Win. Jones, Thomas Carty, Mary Wright, Sarah J. Jinks Elisabeth Fairhurst,Sarah O'Brien, Frances Eaton, Sarah Ann Woods, Sarah Barton, Annie Charnock, Frances Eaton, Mary Lloyd, Elizabeth Riley, Sarah J. Jinks Jane Hankinson, Sarah O'Brien, Mary Edelston, Elizabeth Riley, Margaret Walsh, Gertrude Bradshaw, Mary Edels- ton, Elizabeth O'Brien. At the conclusion of the distri- bution, on the motion of the Rev. MysEncouon,seconded by the Rev. J. J. LANGHAM, and supported by Mr. Wm. HOUGHTON, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Rev. G. F. Roberta for presiding. Mr. MINES thanked the subscribers for their generosity in providing the money for the prizes. An admirable programme was then rendered by some friends from Warrington, the evening passing very pleasantly.

The Vienna, police are engaged in unravelling a Pan- slavist conspiracy against the life of Prince Ferdinand of Bulgaria. • Patrick Mooney, aged 78, a farmer near Mayo Bridge, County Down, has been arrested on the charge of mur- dering his wife, Peggy, aged 70. On Wednesday two young men went to the homestead to thresh, and found the woman lying dead on an old chaff bed. She was a piteous sight, being covered with wounds, and had evi- dently been beaten to death. The inquest was held on Thursday. Evidence was given that the deceased and her husband lived unhappily, that he was in the habit of beating her, and had threatened to murder her. A. verdict of death from violence was returned., At four o'clock on Thursday morning the Scotch ex- presis from Euston to Perth, known as "the tourist train," narrowly escaped wreck: When approaching Kirtle Bridge, near Carlisle, the driving shaft of the loco- motive broke. The driver shot off steam; still he had no control over the engine, and it ran a quarter of a mile, ultimately leaving the rails and bumping along the sleepers. One of the carriages dashed against some masonry, was overturned, and fouled the other line. In this carriage there were several. passengers, but they escaped injury. The driver and fireman remained on the footplate, and were also unhurt. After a delay of five, the passengers weresent on by special train. • Ow- ihrogutrso the accident the limited mail and the Manchester express were detained several hours at Carlisle.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES

THEFT OF BOOTS FROill A LODGING-HOUSE. James Travis was charged with stealing on the 2nd of July last, from the lodging-house of Mary Clarke, 35, Tpwn Hill,a pair of boots,value lls.,the property of John Dane. The prosecutor said that at half-past five a.m., on the date named he left his bedroom at the lodging-house to go to work, the prisoner sleeping in the room. On witness returning to dinner he found that the boots and the prisoner had disappeared, he having left his own old pair behind.—Mary Clarke corroborated, and said the prisoner had also carried off a waistcoat belonging to 4: another fellow-lodger now in Ireland.—The prisoner ad- mitted that he took the boots because they were a little bit better than his oWn.—Detective-Ser,geant Monaghan deposed to apprehending the prisoner in Horsemarket-st., on Saturday night, and te his admitting the theft of both boots and vest.—He was committed for trial at the Quarter Sessions.

div.head: JVVENILE THIEF.
div.p: A JVVENILE THIEF.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednes- day, Walter Dumbell, a boy, was charged with stealing on the 29th ult, a purse containing 75., the property of John Brady. The complainant and defendant were em- ployed at Cockhedge factory. It appeared that the complainant went to work at 6 a.m. on the 29th ult., with the purse containing the 7s. in his pocket, and in the evening both they and the prisoner had disappeared. The lad was apprehended and admitted the theft stating thatihe had spent the Rioney.—John Dumbell, a tanner, employed by Mr. Fleming, Chorlev-st., said his wife died 16 months since, and left him with four lads, the pri- soner being the oldest but one. Be had been very bad to witness during the last 12 months, and had done tricks like this to him, but to no one else before. He was a good scholar, and in the• sth standard. The Bench ordered that the prisoner have six strokes of the birch rod that morning and six at night.

div.head: ASSAULTING A WIFE WITII A KNIFE.
div.p: ASSAULTING A WIFE WITII A KNIFE.

Before the Warrington Borough magistrates, on Mon- day, William Lawrenson, labourer, residing in a yard off Dial-st., Warrington, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, also with assaulting his wife, on Satur- day night last. P.S. Jones deposed that he was on duty late on the night in question, and heard the sound of a woman's screams issuing from the direction of the above-mentioned yard. He found the cause to be that the prisoner was drunk, and beating his wife, striking her right and left. On witness going in, Mrs. Lawrenson said, " Qh, I'm glad you've come, for my husband was threatening to stab me with a knife." Witness found a table knife lying close to, and observed that the pro- secutrix had been cut on one of her fingers and on her cheek. P.C. Barnett gave corroborative evidence. Mrs. Lawrenson said her husband came home from the circus soon after eleven o'clock on Saturday night. He quarrelled over his supper, and threatened to cut her throat. He picked up the knife, and she warded him off, and backed him down into his chair. This enraged him more than ever, and she was just coming into the house immediately after, when he ran at her and struck her again. Her finger was cut accidentally in strug- gling with him, and he stabbed her in the face also with the knife. The prisoner said he never meant to cut her. Alderman Harrison said the prisoner deliberately got a knife, which proved that he meant it. The Mayor said if the Bench had had clear proof that the wound on the prosecutrix's face was deliberately inflicted, they would have committed the prisoner to the Sessions, but as it was they would send him to prison for a month's hard
CHARGE OF FRAUDULENT REMOVAL

At the Warrington Borough Police Court,yesterday,Jos. Eaton wtscharged with fraudulently removing his goods with a view to avoid the distraint by Messrs.Armitage and Rigby, of the Cockhedge Factory, for rent due on their house, 63, Orford-st. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the pro- secution, and Mr. Forshaw for the defence. Mr. Bailey, cashier for Messrs. Armitage afid Rigby, said the defen- dant had notice on the 24th of November to quit on December Ist. He owed four weeks arrears of rent, and another week's rent had become due. He removed his goods about 8 p.m. on the 27th of November, and sent the key by a little girl. Another witness gave corrobo- rative evidence. Mr. Forshaw contended that the case was one for the County Court, as there had been no removal to avoid distraint. His client had to quit by December Ist., and had to get another house, and merely took his things there. It had not been shown that there had been any concealment in removing the goods.—Mr. Forshaw, in reply to Alder- man Harrison, said it was stated that the defendant was now living in Warrington.—Mr. Bailey recalled said the defendant had left a false address (20, Orford-road), with his employers, and the firm had endeavoured to trace him by it, but could not.—Alderman Harrison: He did not give you it himself.—Mr. Forshaw : He gave it to his employers. It was intended to mislead.—Alderman Harrison said he did not think there was evidence to sustain the ease,to support which the facts should be very strong. The man had received notice, and it was quite possible he might be under a misapprehension as to the facts, It would have been better to proceed in the -fa,--unty dourt.—ne ease as o_isnliSSed, A YOUTH AGED 19 MANES HIS 11TH APPEARANCE. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Thursday, tgilfore Major Litton (chairman) t 0,114 Major Fickmere, 4::11m Whittaker, aged 19, was charged with beini found the previous day frequenting the premises of the London and North-Western Railway Company, Bank :Quay Rail- way Station, with intent to commit a felony.—Railway Detective Atkinson prosecuted, and said for a long time the Company had been troubled with the defendant fre- quenting their station. Witness had cautioned him repeatedly, and this was the third time he had had him before the Court. He was a very dangerous character, and caused a very great deal of trouble, and witness asked the Bench to deal very severely with him. He went into the Booking Hall, when the ticket collec- tors and porters were away and pestered pas- sengers to be allowed to carry their luggage, and occasionally came out with some beastly lan- guage. The Company had outside licensed porters, and then there were the different cab proprietors in the town who had the usual license.—lnspector Spinks said the prisoner had been warned by the police frequently. He was a complete pest at the station.—Chief Constable Hunt said the prisoner was at the head of a lot of youn- ger fry, and when the police approached they ran away. —Detective Atkinson: As soon as they see me approach the station, they generilly give me leg bail.—lt was mentioned that this was the prisoner's 11th appearance in. court.—He stated in reply.to the Bench that he could not enlist as his hands were crippled.—The magistrates discharged the prisoner with a caution that if he were found loitering about again at the station he would be sent to prison for three months, and he promised not to repeat the offence, and to look for work.
