DRUNICENNESS.—James Ward, for being drunk and disorderly in St. James'-street, on Friday night, wasfined 56. and costs.—Eliza !Smith, for a similar offence in Buttermarket-street, was committed for seven days. It was stated that this was the third time in succession the prisoner had been locked up the same day she had been released from prison. This was her 44th appearance. MAINTENANCE ARREARS.—James Sankey was sum- moned to show cause why he should . not be committed to prison for neglecting to pay £2 Bs. 6d., arrears of a maintenance order towards his son, who is on board the ship Clio. He was ordered to pay 2s. 6d. weekly until the arrears had been cleared off, or in default to go to prison for 28 days. Mormay.--Before the Mayor (Alderman Francemb), Alderman Harrison, Alderman Davits, and Major Litton. DESERTION FROM Tint ARMY.—Frederick Clegg, and James Lloyd were charged with being deserters from her Majesty's 4th Hussars, stationed in Dublin. One of the prisoners stated that he did not like his regiment, and deserted to join another be preferred, and had come to Warrington for the purpose of going to the barracks to be enlisted in it. The prisoners were ordered to be sent back to their regiment,. DRUNK IND DISORDERLY.—Henry Lake drunk and dis- orderly on Sunday night in Bridge-street, was fined ss. and costs; in default seven days.—Thomas Cummins and Mary Cummins, drunk and disorderly in StanleyV., on the 26th ult., were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs, and , Margaret Morgan, charged with being disorderly on the ' same occasion, was dismissed with a caution.—William Bailey, drunk and disorderly on the 26th ult., in Naylor- street, was fined ss. and costs.—James Finn drunk and disorderly on the 30th ult., in Buttermarket'-street, was fined ss. and costs.—Thomas Mannion drunk and dis- orderly in Turner-st., on the 26th ult.' was fined ss. and costs.—John Longshaw and Edward Griffin, drunk and disorderly in the Market Place,on the 26th nit. ,were each fined ss. and costs.—Margaret Riley, aged 18, at whose being brought up on such a charge at so early an age, the magistrates expressed some surprise, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the 25th inst., in Winwiek-st.—Annie Daley, drunk and dis- orderly Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, Was fined ss. and costs. PLAYING CARDS FOR MoNEY.--dohn Longshaw, John Naylor, and Thomas Finch, were charged with playing cards for money in the public Market Place at 9 40 a.m., on the 25th inst.—lt appeared from the evidence that the defendants had been sitting up all night in the Market Place—one of them stating that they .were in a canvas enclosure which had a coke fire in it—and,4during the night they had had three bottles of whisky, and when the constable found them gambling Naylor and Finch were playing with Longshaw to see who should pay for the whisky. They were each fined 3s. 6d. costs. Tnimskzes OF LICENSES.—The license of the Green Dragon Inn, Bridge-st., was transferred from Peter Baguley to Charles George Ford, that of the Royal Ex- change Inn, Golden Square, from Edward Bullock to Wm. Bolton, that of the Alexandra, Scotland-road, from James Taylor to Win. Gregory, and the off license of James Green, provision dealer, Chorley-st., to Robert Whitfield.
FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), and Mr. J. H. Gornall:
INDECENT CoNnucr.—Ellen Morrell, was charged with indecent behaviour, in Marsh House-lane, the previous night, and was dismissed on promising to leave the town.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. TIIESDAY.—Berore Messrs Edward Greenall and James

Marson. MISCELLANEOUS.-Willi4m Gaskell, was charged with being drunk while in charge of a horse and cart at Ac- ton Grange, on the 21st December, and was fined ss. and costs.—John Haddock, a farm labourer, was brought up on remand from Daresbury Petty Sessions, charged with stealing a tin can and a gallon of sweet oil, the pro- perty of Mr. Joseph Hayes, farmer, Little Leigh, but as the evidence against him was not sufficiently strong, the prisoner was discharged.—At the same Court, the same morning, before Mr. James Marson, Thomas Evans, a labourer, was charged with being drunk at Rixten, on Monday, and was fined, ss. and costs.—James Mullen, an old offender, was charged with a similar offence at the same time and place, and was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs. Neither of the defendants were able to pay the fine, and they were accordingly committed to prison for seven days.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAL—Before Mr. J. Rylands (chairman) and Mr. W. H. Bleckly. CHARGE OF ASSAULT.—George Travis was charged with assaulting and beating John Day, at Haydock, on Saturday night. The complainant appeared with his head bandaged up. Mr. Browne, solicitor, appeared for the defendant. The complainant stated that he was in the Owl's Nest public-house on the night in question, chatting with a friend, and on coming out was followed by the defendant, who asked him where "that chap" was going. Witness replied that he did not know, upon which the defendant threw him over, and kicked him for a quarter of an hour about the head and hip.—ln cross-examination the complainant denied that he had got hold of the defendant's dog and threatened to break its leg, or thrown the defendant on the floor. Witness's friend held the dog on the table. Witness did not take defendant's hat: a woman brought it to witness's house. Wm. Chesworth, miner, and Js Seddon, miner, gave evidence, from which it appeared that the two men quarrelled about the breed of some dogs, and the com- plainant threatened to break the defendant's dog's leg, and got up to do so, when the defendant got hold of him, and a struggle ensued. The complainant went home with the defendant's• hat, and the defendant went to the complainant's house for it, whereupon the com- plainant came to the door and struck him with a poker. The defendant closed with him and gave him a good "walloping."—The case was dismissed. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Hodgson' drunk and disorderly at renketii, on the 24th ult.' was fined ss. and costs.—William Webster, disorderly at Orford, on Christ- mas Day, was bound over to keep the peace for six months.—Robert Routledge, was charged with 'being drunk and disorderly in Manchester-road, Rixton. The prosecuting constable, said on taking prisoner his break- fast into the lock-up that morning, he threw his bread and butter down the closet and attempted to throw the tea in witness's face. The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was fined ss. and costs.—Sarah Ann Lambert, was sum- moned on a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Manchester-road, Rixon, but did not appear, and a war- rant was issued.

ROBBING A FELLOW•WORIGIAN.—WiIIiam Birkett, of 20, Crinshill-st., Liverpool, was charged with stealing an axe and a plane, belonging to Wm. Allen. The men were employed in the construction of a new house at Ditton, and on Tuesday last the prosecutor left work at noon, Afterwards the prisoner was seen cartying.the tool's away, and when caught said he was only taking them home to work with. div.head: POST OFFECE DISPUTE.
div.p: THE POST OFFECE DISPUTE.

It is stated by the Comptroller of the Government Savings Banks that many letters have been received from suspended clerks expressing regret at their hasty action. Sir Arthur Blackwood, secretary, addressing the clerks in the department at Queen Victoria-st., on Mon- day, said it was open for the men to seek an interview with Mr. Raikes when he returned to town towards the end of the week; but meantime the department would take steps to cope with the work, and the suspended officials must understand that obedience was the first law of the service.

A requisition to the Postmaster-General,. asking him to grant an Interview, was on Tuesday signed by the clerks of the Postal Savings Bank Department who were suspended onSaturday for refusing to work overtime. They express themselves as willing to return to duty on condition the granting of an inquiry into the subjec matter of the dispute. On Thursday afternoon a deputation of the suspended savings' bank clerks was received by the Postmaster- General, who was accompanied by Sir A. Blackwood and other officials. The deputation apologised for their con- duct, alleging they acted under a wrong impression of their duties which impression had been removed by Sir A. BlackwoLd's recent speech. Mr. Raikes expressed pleasure at the frank manner in which the clerks had apologized for their insubordination. On that account those who, by Saturday next, notified to the Depart- ment their desire to return to their duties would be allowed to do so on Monday next. If any remained out they would be dealt with separately.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON "A" V. SUTTON.-_-A slight mist covered the Wilderspool enclosure when the visitors commenced hostilities towards the pavilion goal, and after free kicks had followed to either side, Golden was found at fault, and the homesters caused play to locate in the visitors' quarters'. Renna, by a good dribble, brought about relief, 3nd transferred the scene of warfare to Warring- ton quhrters. Jolley, by a rush, somewhat neutralised, but over-running the ball,lost a seemingly fine chance of scoring, and directly afterwards, from a pass by Mather, a strong run by Webster looked a certain try, but Travis tackled him finely. Some fine kicking by the rival backs was then witnessed, the wind-up being a strong attack headed by Craghan, Molyneaux, Isherwood, and Lloyd, McCulla saving daringly ; and a minor was ultimately conceded. Following the drop-out, a smart dodgy run by Lalley caused no little amusement, but Sutton, chiefly by the instrumentality of Rimmer, succeeded in getting to the home lines, where Sampson effected a capital save. Warrington were now pressed, and a series of uninteresting packs ensued, the homesters luckily getting off with a minor. Barnes, Donoghue, and Knowles then, got away to midfield, and from a loose scrimmage Law- less ran well into the visitors' 25, and threw across to Lally, who almost got in at the corner flag, another minor being gixen. Warrington were again aggresive until a free kick brought brought about the much desired relief. Exchange kicking between Jolley and Golden resulted in great advantage to the Warring- tonians, and then Mather, from a pass by Rowe, got splendidly away, and threw across, but the ball and chance were both missed. Success at last attended the homesters' efforts, as from a free kick by Jolley, Lloyd got possession, and passing to Knowles, the latter ran over cleverly, whilst Webster improved the point by landing a goal. Re-starting, some fine work by Sampson cleared his lines, and Mather, Jolley, and Rowe ran the ball to neutral territory, where the whistle blew for half-time. Resuming, the play settled down in the visit- ing "25," a fine run by Carrigan, who was effectually floored by Sampson, cadsing the Warringtonians to beat a hasty retreat. Rowe passed wide to Lally, wbo ran capitally along touch, and Jolley dashed away with the ball at his toes until pulled up by Wilson ;an a minor was forced. Golden then got the ball away finely, but another minor wasconceded. Some uninteresting packs then occupied the time fon awhile, until a sharp run by Rowe proved dangerous to the visitors, and Jolley almost dropped a goal. Sampson was next called upon to de- fend, which he did surprisingly well, but another rush forced a minor. Lloyd, Donoghue, and Knowles after- wards got the leather well into the visitors' quarters, but beyond some splendid work by Sampson, nothing of any interest took place, and Warrington retired winners of an unexciting game by 1-0-5 to 0-0-2. Teams Warrington: Sampson, full back; Webster, Jolley, and Laney, three-quarters; Rowe and Mather, half backs; Molyneaux, Craghan, Lloyd, Isherwood, Knowles, Donoghue, Barnes Lawless, and Philips, forwards. Sutton: Golden, full back; Travis, Johnson, and Rim- mer, three-quarters; McCulla and Wilson, half backs; Travis, Renna Thompson, Dale, Carrigan, Harrison, Colquitt, Ralplison, and Ashcroft, forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. HARTLEPOOL HOVERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. HARTLEPOOL HOVERS.

The Warringtonians journeyed the long distance to Hartlepool on Saturday morning, to bring off the first of their arranged engagements. The morning was cold and damp, and anything but agreeable for railway travelling, whilst to mend matters two of the Warrington players (Berry and Daniels) lost the connection at Manchester.
This caused a re-organization of the team. Jolley was drafted to the position of three-quarter, Povey, who was taken as reserve, and Speakman, the umpire, both being put into harness.

The match was in aid of the Hartlepool Hospital, and fully 5,000 were present when 11111 kicked off, the War- rington quarter flag being the sce,ne of operations. The ground was very heavy going, ,p,nd after the first few minutes the players presented ,pitiable sight. Ashton dribbled well, but Emmerson stayed the endeavour to rslieve. After James Bate Cad successfully cleared the danger, smith tricked his opposing half, and punting to Boscow, the Warrington back with a long screw kick caused play to rage at thehome quarters. Frank Turner was foremost in a rush, but Scott and Emmerson making their marks in quick succession, the visiting defence was harassed. Home, Emmerson, andJolley exchanged kicks with advantage to the visitors, and then a fine piece of play by the Warrington half backs was supplemented by the quick following up of the Virgrringtnn forwards, and Horne being in difficulties, play was taken =der the home posts. A grand spell of short passing by the hornestem took play to the Warringtoniine- but Achtnn Efans, Fair Turner, Povey, and-Randles came away ma combined rush, McPherson luckily saving. Runs by Fair Turner and James Bate improved Warrington's position, and on one occasion Scott saved in marvellous style. Evans put in a grand kick, but Scott quickly re- lieved, and making his mark took the place without suc- cess. A tricky run along the touch by James Bate was loudly applauded, and Jolley secured a wide pass, but the tackling was too safe to allow of his travelling far. A spell of passing by the Warringtonians certainly de- served a better fate. A fine run and kick by Evans was cleared by Horne, and although Ashton, Davies, and Dil- loa once more returned to the attack, no point could be scored. Massey had the better of Emmerson in some exchange kicking, and then Boagey for the homesters put in a grand dribble for the Rovers without suc- cess. On the call of half-time, Fair Turner took play on the Hartlepool line, but the leather could not be forced over, and half-time arrived without any point WhatlvOr having been KAned, FmnlT Turner re-started, and play at the onset hovered dangerously near the Rovers' goal. Faulty play by the visiting backs gave the homesters a chance of relieving, and matters assumed a serious aspect. Their forwards, however, were equal to the occasion, and, working with a will, soon had the oval out of danger, and despite a mark by Scott, James Bate and Boscow with a couple of kicks placed Warring- ton on the aggressive. Frank Turner dribbled well, and a rush being made by the home forwards the oval was worked acrossthe halfway line. From some loose play Em- merson in a difficult position dropped a grand goal amidst great enthusiasm. From this point the Warringtonians went at their work with a will, and play was almost confined to the home half. Safe tackling prevented any return to the kick off, and Horne made his mark, but still it did not give relief. Thorniley, Ashton, and Dillon were foremost in 'a forward rush, but the defence was severely taxed a moment later when a short passing thovement, initiated by John Bate, found Massey punting over, Horne luckily saving. Following the drop out, a line-out took place beyond the half way, and Fair Turner securing,punted well down the field, and Evans following up secured possession, and a strong run landed a try behind the posts, Davies being at fault with the kick at goal. Fair Turner again put in a tremendous kick, and a moment later Evans had a shotat goal,which was only productive of a minor. Evans foiled Emmerson in his endeavour to get away, and then a sharp movement by the Warrington forwards was short of the finishing touch. Randles almost notched a score from a strong run, but the fates were against Warrington, and al- though they had considerably the best of this half, in the end they had to retire defeated by one goal (dropped) to a try and two minors. Teams :—Warrington: Full back, Boscow; three- quarter backs, J. Jolley, J. W. Evans, and dn. Massey (captain) ; half backs, Jas. Bate and J. T. Bate; for- wards, H. Ashton, Frank Turner, T. Davies, W. Speak- man, Fair Turner, W. Rand le,s, .1. T. Thorniley, E. Dillon, and Povey. Hartlepool Rovers : Full back,J. W. Borne; three-quarter backs, D. M'Pherson, W. G. Monoghan, and A. E. Emmerson • half backs, G. Smith, and A. C. Scott; forwards, F. C. Lohden' G. E. Boagey, J. Snow- don, A. Hill, J. Coates, C. M. Huntley, W.ltiend (cap- tain), J. J: Rennie, and H. Coates. Referee, Mr. J. A. Blackwood, D.C.R.U.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

The international game between England and Wales, on Saturday, drew together a big crowd. The ground at Newport had been so well cared for that the game was seen at its best, and every man may be said to have had full opportunity of showing his skill. From the first the Englishmen seemed to have the issue in their hands, and when half-time arrived they had little cause for anxiety. They also more than held their own after the change of ends, though the home side gave them more trouble and scored their only point. A victory by two goals and a try to one goal is pretty substantial, especially seeing that the game was contested on foreign soil.

There was no mistake about the superiority of the Englishmen over their rivals. They were smarter for- ward and stronger behind. The backs did remarkably well. Alderson more than fulfilled expectations, his improvement being very marked. Lockwood was as smart as usual,and Christopherson added to his reputa- tion as a great three-quarter. Berry and Leake were very clever at half, the first-named gaining hosts of friends by his well-timed passes and unselfishness. Mitchell proved as safe as ever at full back. The for- wards were superior to the Welshmen, and proved this repeatedly in the scrimmages, and there was not a failure among them. Gwynn, the Oldham three-quarter, who.

has been chosen to assist Lancashire in their next tw6 matches, wasas clever as any of the Welsh backs; and Bancroft came off with flying colours at full back. England need have little fear as to the remaining inter- nationar fixtures,

The game at Swinton, on Saturday, was reduced to a tarce, St. Helens Recreation not reaching there until four o'clock. What little football took place was therefore of no importance. That only two "20's "was possible was ridiculous. True, Swinton had the satisfaction of scor- ing the only point of the game, but this was a poor con- solation under the circumstances.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

Everton have added Aston Villa and Notts to their League victims, and the championship now appears to be a certainty for them. They have a very fine record, though it by no means approaches that of the North End in the first year of the tournament. Our best clubs are now more nearly on an equality. The Blackburn Rovers ran clean away from Derby County, eight goals to no- thing being a terrible defeat.

Wolverhampton look like finishing up a good second to Everton, having added two victories to their list in the new year—Accrington and West Bromwich Albion. Acceington are having a big share of ill-luck, as they have lost all their last three League matches by a goal. They are seeking to strengthen their team, and have captured two or three new men. The North End have also added another to their stock, but he is hardly so much as known on this side of the border. Only Everton appear to have the knack,of picking up really good men, and they have. a very large supply.

An extraordinary scene took place, on Saturday, at Leigh, on the occasion. of the Lancashire Alliance foot- ball match between the Leigh Association and Hindley. Great interest was centred in the match, as Leigh are at present at the head of the Alliance and Hindley are close up. There were about 2,000 spectators, about half of whom hailed from Hindley. About five minutes from the start Hewitt scored a goal for Leigh amid great enthusiasm. Hindley then twice put the ball through the Leigh pal, but in • each case the referee—Mr. W. Ashurst, of Little Lever, who has had considerable experience -in football matters, and who had been mutually chosen by the two clubs—disallowed the goal on the ground ,of off-side play. This infuriated a large section of the spectators, and suddenly about 400 per- sons jumped over the ropes and made for the referee, who was roughly handled. A man named Whitehead came to his assistance, but the mob turned upon him and kicked him brutally. In the confusion the referee escaped and took refuge in a private house, while White- head, whose injuries were very serious, was conveyed to the house of Dr. Jones. Meanwhile, the two captains held a consultation, and after considerable difficulty the crowd were induced to leave the playing portion of the field, and Mr. D. Pemberton, of Leigh, agreed to act as referee. The game then proceeded amid great excite- ment, and Hindley scored an equalising goal. Eight minutes from time a dense fog came Over the ground, and the refereQ stopped the same with the score one each,

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

considerable interest centres in the meeting of the St. Helens Y.M.C.A. and Warrington teams in the first round of the competition for the handsome 200 guineas chal- lenge shield offered by the National Physical and Recrea- tion Society. It will be remembered that last season' Warrington succeeded in reaching the final tie but were then defeated by Liverpool, the present holders of the shield. This is the first season in which the St. Helens team has entered the contest—indeed, the splendid and handsomely fitted up gymnasium possessed by the St. Helens Young Men's Christian Association was only opened in February last. The tie between St. Helens and War- rington will be played at the St. Helens gymnasium next Friday night, and the following members have been selected to take part in the contest: St. Helens : Messrs. G. Ashcroft, G. Butcher, B. Light- foot, T. Marsh, W. H. Point% H. Twiss, E. F. Thilwynd, ' and E. A. B. Woodward. Warrington: Messrs. J. E. Warren, J. Podmore, F. Locker,. James Holmes, Jno. Holmes, George Vernon, A. Vernon, and D. Walsh. The ; respective instructors are Messrs. J. H. Harrison (St. Helens), and E. Alexander (Warrington).

div.head: SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE.
div.p: THE SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE.
RIOTING AT MOTHERWELL.

The Scotch railway strike has reached an acute stage. Great excitement prevailed throughout Monday in Glasgow, but the most serious effects of the struggle were experienced in the mining district of Motherwell, where the colliers have all along manifested sympathy with the strikers. On Monday afternoon the evictions at Motherwell were carried out amidst scenes of wildest excitement. All the miners in the district ceased work, and it was calculated that fully 20,000 persons gathered in the streets. The rendezvous of the crowd was at the Motherwell Railway Bridge, their object being to await the arrival of the evictors. Stone throwing was indulged in, and disorder became so great that the authorities decided to clear the bridge. The military and police were accordingly called out. The majority of the crowd there- upon hastily retreated, but the more daring resisted,and the Sheriff at once proceeded to read the Riot Act. The police immediately afterwards charged the crowd, using their batons vigorously, with the result that many per- sons were knocked down and trampled upon. After the charge it was found that half-a-dozen people had been more or less severely wounded by the policemen. The crowd, being dislodged from the bridge, attacked the station, smashing and wrecking the signal boxes; and trains, instead of stopping at the platforms, were run through to save them from the showers of stones. Some of the unoccupied signal-boxes were entered by the rioters, who manipulated the points and signals and ultimately destroyed the signal lines. The military who were assembled to protect the station fired a couple of blank cartridges. This had a salutary effect upon the crowd. The evictions then proceeded withotit further interference beyond frequent outbursts of hooting and jeering. Several:other works closed on Tuesday because of the difficulty in getting material and the impossibility of sending off their finished goods. In Edinburgh, Glasgow, Leith, and other places indignant complaints are being made about the continuance of the strike and its serious effect on trade and industry. The Leith Town Council adopted a resolution on the subject, urging that public safety and trade interests demanded a settlement of the dispute by a board fairly representing the railway com- panies and their servants. Mr. John Burns, addressing mass meetings in the large centres of industry, strongly counselled the men to remain on, strike, expressing the greatest confidence in their coming victory. The rail- way servants disclaim any responsibility with regard to the riot. Two of the most conspicuous figures in it—a labourer and an ironworker—have been sentenced to sixty days' imprisonment each. Disturbances took place at Blantyre and Coatbridge, but they were easily put down by the police, and at the latter place six MeR were arrested.

A-special correspondent at Glasgow, telegraphing on Wednesday night, describes the attitude of the men on strike as being quite determined, wnile their behaviour so far, has been recognised by the police as being peace- able and orderly. The same cannot, however, be said of the miners, who are kept in 'check by large bodies of police, one detachment having been imported from Lancashire. Traffic remains _very mueh in the same condition, and at Polmadie, the great locomotive centre ever fifty engines, with their tenders full of coal, are lying up. Mr. Cuninghame Graham addressed a:meet- ing of railway men, on Wednesday, but in We course of his remarks attacked a number of public men, and met with no favour.

The h6pe that the Scotch railway strike might quickly end, now efforts at mediation have been resumed, was blighted on Thursday. M. Haldane, M.P., was the , bearer to the North British directors at Edinburgh of a message from the men suggesting that a settlement should be effected on the basis ot! a ten hours day. The communication was received by Mr. Walker, the general manager, and placed before the Board. The directors adopted a resolution thanking the portion of the staff that had remained loyal for its zeal and energy, and then confirmed the memorandum agreed to in December authorising the general manager to meet a deputation from each grade of railway servants on condition that the men resumed work. The decision of the directors caused much feeling among the men on . strike, and at the mass meetings in Edinburgh and Glasgow it was re- solved to continue the struggle even more resolutely. Further help for the strikers was announced from many quarters, and among the amounts promised was one of £5OO from the Seamen and Firemen's Union.

div.head: TRE SEVERE WEATHER.
div.p: TRE SEVERE WEATHER.

Further severe weather is reported from different parts of the country and the Continent. A horse-dealer's assistant, named William Williamson, had been frozen to death at Preston, and a Paris telegram reports three deaths in the public street from cold, and the freezing of three children to death in a wood in the Department du, Nord.

div.head: FISHERIES QUESTION.
div.p: THE FISHERIES QUESTION.

• According to a despatch from Wa.shington, published in New York yesterday, the Behring Sea fisheries ques- tion is now in a more favourable position than at any time since last May, when the negotiations were " clouded " by the issue of the order for seizing British sealing v.essels. The report that the United States Government has issued orders for the concentration of a strong navaliorce in the Pacific is also contradicted.

div.head: HARTLEPOOL CONTEST.
div.p: THE HARTLEPOOL CONTEST.

The " London Gazette" of Tuesday night contains a notice, signed by Mr. Leonard Courtney, deputy speaker of the House of Commons, that at the.end of si. days he will issue a writ for the election of a new member for Hartlepool, in the place of the late Mr. Richardson. A crowded meeting of the supporters of Sir William Gray, the Unionist candidate, was held at East Hartle- pool on Tuesday night. Sir William, who declared that he had not changed his opinions, that he was still a Liberal, and that it was the other side that had changed, received a respectful hearing; but there was some op- position to the other speakers. and the name of Mr. Furness, the Liberal candidate, when mentioned, was loudly cheered. A vote of approval of Sir William Gray's candidature was carried.
Both Liberal and Unionist candidates were very busy at Hartlepool on Thursday,and the contest is now in full swing.

div.head: MINERS' ANNUAL CONFERENCE.
div.p: MINERS' ANNUAL CONFERENCE.

The annual Conference of the National Miners' Federa- tion was opened in Birmingham, Mr. Picard, M.P., pre- siding over delegates .representing between 140,000 and 150,000 members. A resolution expressing sympathy with the Scotch railway strikers and strong censure of the action of the companies was passed. The President, in his address, congratulated the members of the Federa- tion on the advance in miners'wages since they last met, and on the prospect of their present scale of pay being maintained.

On Thursday resolutions were adopted that no Em- ployers' Liability Bill would meet the needs of persons engaged in dangerous occupations which did not eon tam a clause providing for common employmegt, or which allowed workpeople to contract out of its provisions Mr. Aspinall, Lancashire, moved a resolution in favour of the eight hours working day, from bank to bank, secured by Act of Parliament. Mr. Cowey, Yorkshire, seconded the motion, and a discussion followed.

div.head: FIRE AT A LEEDS BAZAAR,.
div.p: THE FIRE AT A LEEDS BAZAAR,.
NINE DEATHS.

The Press Association Leeds correspondent telegraphs that two more of the girls who were burned in the acci- dent at the Christmas party at Wortley have died at the Leeds Infirmary. Their names are Elizabeth Tingle, aged 12,and Harriet Riley, aged 14. These with Florrie br)ok, aged 10, whose death was reported on Sunday, bring the total number of victims to nine. From in- quiries made at the Leeds Infirmary on Tuesday it was ascertained that the children still under treatment there as a result of the disastrous affair at Wortley are all improving with the exception of Emily: Tyrer, whose injuries are much more serious than those of the other survivors.

The coroner's inquest on the bodies of the nine girls burnt to death in Leeds on New Year's Day was resumed on Wednesday. After some further evidence, the in- quiry was adjourned for a week to allow of the attend- ance of two importance witnesses who are at present ill. Most of the injured girls in the hospital are progressing favourably.

div.head: ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
A FIREMAN KILLED,
Shortly after six o'clock on Wednesday morning an alarming accident otutirrstrnearruxtonvancauiGutr-

the London and North-Western Railway,three miles from Chorley. A special goods train from Carnforth to Liverpool, when passing the junction became divided, and the engine left the wagons. The en- gine proceeded about a mile, and the signalmen at Balshaw Lane crossing, finding something wrong, placed fog signals on the line and blocked the goods engine. Immediately afterwards the wagons came along the line at a good speed, and collided with the standing engine, with the result that four heavy wagons were thrown off the metals, the do- bris partially covering the down line. Just at this moment the London express to the North came along, and James Allen, fireman of the goods en- gine, who was in the four-foot way, was cut into pieces, his body being dragged sixty yards. The passenger train was able afterwards to proceed to Preston, the passengers apparently not knowing that anything had happened.

div.head: DISTRESS IN IRELAND.
div.p: THE DISTRESS IN IRELAND.

At the beginning of the week a long letter was issued on the subject of distress in Ireland, signed by the Lord Lieutenant and Mr. Balfour. They premise at the out- set that without doubt money can be usefully spent among the poor on the western seaboard, where there exists a state of things which may well appeal to the charitable. The letter goes on to deal with the perman- ent ill effects which have often followed charitable expenditure, and combats the theorythat the inhabitants of the congested districts have been entirely dependent on the potato for food. In appealing for charitable aid the writers express the opinion that it should be confined to families who, laving no able-bodied men among them, cannot derive benefit from public works; to providing meals at sChool 'for children, and clothes for those unable to procure them. Mr. Balfour has since intimated to the press that the rapid and generous response to the appeal for the relief of distress in Ireland renders it quite impossible for him ' to deal personally with the mass of correspondence which individual acknowledgment would entail, but he hope; to publish a list of subscriptions immediately. The requisition asking the Mayor of Liverpool to convene a town's meeting on the subject has been very numerously signed.
-Mr. Balfour has already received upwards of £6,000 in response to his appeal.

div.head: CHARGE OF WIFE DESERTION.
div.p: CHARGE OF WIFE DESERTION.
MARRIED IN HASTE AND REPENTING IN HASTE.-ALLEGED EXTRAORDINARY SIM- PLICITY.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yester- day, Thopas Cooper, labourer, employed by Mr. Houghton, wire manufacturer, was charged with deserting his wife Elizabeth Cooper. Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant.—The complainant stated that they were married on the 29th of November, and he deserted her on the 30th.—Alderman Harrison : The day after. Good gracious !—Complainant said her husband charged her with misbehaviour with other men previous to her marriage. He charged her with having been a street-walker, but this was untrue. They agreed to live with their respective mothers till Christmas, and in the meantime they could save money to buy furniture.—Two females, Jane Ashton and another gave further evidence, after which Mr. Browne made a statement. He said the complainant and the defendant were two young people who entered into marriage very foolishly. His client was one of the most foolish young men he ever had to do with. This girl came to him after they had known each other a fortnight, and told him she had been to Dr. Cannell and he had informed her she was in the family way. She said unless the defendant mar- ried her she would bring him up for manslaughter. Of course she denied this, and he (Mr. Browne) did not believe Dr. Cannell said anything of the kind. The de- fendant actually believed what she said, and she I induced him to get out the banns at once. The banns I were published within 17 days of their becoming ac- quainted, and they were married within two months. Mr. Browne submitted that as there was separation by mutual consent there was no desertion. He could prove, he said, that it was arranged before they married that they were to go to their mother's hAuses. The defend- ant had proposed to pay her something through a third party. Mr. Browne asked the Bench to dismiss the case, I and promised that his client would allowthe complainant something.—The complainant said the dofendant had threatened that if he made a home for her he would play Jack the Ripper with her—kill her. ' —Alderman Harrison said there was a constructive desertion, because they had only to live apart till ChriStmas. He thought the least the defendant could .offer was 6s. a week. Happier circumstances might arise in future.—The complainant said she could not keep herself and the baby she expected to have on 6s. a week.—Alderman Harrison said the Bench would dis- miss the case entering on the books, that the defendant undertake tri pay 6s. a week till the birth 31 the child, and then to make other arrangements.—Mr. Browne strongly objected to this condition being entered, and asserted that there had been desertion as the parties were not living together after Christmas.—Ultimately the Bench dismissed the case, Mr. Browne promising that his client should make the allowance mentioned.
The bank rate of discount has been reduced from 5 to 4 per cent.

div.head: IRISH FDIFFICULTY.
div.p: THE IRISH FDIFFICULTY.

CONFERENCE AT BOULOGNE. RETIREMENT OF MR. PARNELL. Mr. Parnell left Charing Cross en route for Boulogne on Tuesday morning, accompanied by Mr. T. Harrington, M.P., Mr. Vincent Scully, and Mr. Henry Campbell, M.P. Mr. Vincent Scully was interviewed by a Press repre- sentative before starting; but he declined even to admit that the party were going to France to meet Mr. O'Brien. A conference took place at Boulogne during the day, which was resumed on Wednesday. BOULOGNE, WEDNESDAY NIGHT.—Mr. Parnell and his friends left to-day at two o'clock, amidst a blinding snow- storm, the ex-leader looking, in the opinion of those who know him best, as well as at any time during the last. two years. Shortly before his departure the following communique was handed to the Press; "The conference between Mr. Parnell and Mr. O'Brien terminated to-day. It was agreed by both -sides that the proceedings thereat should be regarded as confiden- tial, but it may be understood that the full interchange of views which has taken place between the Irish mem- bers leads them to entertain the hope that a peacable settlement may be arrived at. Mr. O'Brien will remain some days at Boulogne, and has placed himself in com- munication with Mr. Justin McCarthy!' In the course of a conversation between Mr. 'O'Brien and Mr. Gill this evening, the former said: "I have nothing to add to the communication made to the papers except this. In view of all that is in stake for our unhappy country in this crisis, and in the interests of the goodwill which exists between the two peoples, I would respectfully entreat our friends in a portion of the English Press to excercise a little patience while we are discussing matters of the utmost delicacy and difficulty with our brother representatives of the Irish people." PARIS, WEDNESDAY NIGHT.—The " Figaro "gives the terms of the compromise between Mr. Parnell and Mr. O'Brien as follows. Mr. Justin McCarthy will have to resign. A meeting of all the members of the Irish i party s to be held on the 15th instant in Committee Room 15, to elect a new leader. The presence of the Parnellite members during the vote will seal the msion of the Irish party.

Mr. Parnell, accompanied by his private secretary (Mr. Campbell, M.P.) and Messrs. P. Barrington, M.P., John Redmond, M.P., J. J. Clancy, M.P., and Mr. Vincent Scully, arrived at Charing-cross, at 6.25, on Wednesday evening. In reply to questions by a repre- sentative of the Press, Mr. Parnell said : "I have no communication to make as to the conference at Boulogne. An authorised statement has been delivered to the Press on the other side. To that I have no addition whatever to convey."—The Press Association states that several communications passed between Mr. W. O'Brien and Mr. Justin McCarthy on Wednesday, with reference to the Boulogne conference. After the receipt of the first cablegram the Nationalist leader had a conference, at the National Liberal Club, with Mr. Healy, Mr. Sexton, and Mr. John Barry. Great reticence , is observed as to the result of the negotiations with Mr. Parnell; but the demeanour of Mr. Healy and his friends was one of extreme cheerfulness, and the pre- vailing belief is that a solution of the difficulty has been found. Mr. Healy, it is stated, will address a meeting at Nenagh, on Sunday. A correspondent says :—Mr. O'Brien informed me that he proposed to remain at Boulogne for a couple of days. I am in a position to add that he has telegraphed to Mr. Justin M'Carthy in London asking that gentleman to come at once to Boulogne, and it is hoped that the Chair- man of the Parliamentary Party may be able to come at once. Information derived from a source absolutely re- liable is further to the effect that Mr. Parnell has agreed to retire for an indefinite period from active political work provided that Mr. W. O'Brien shall be elected ses- sional chairman vice Mr. M'Carthy. Mr. O'Brien has himself declared that he would prefer the appointment of Mr. John Dillon to the chairmanship, and Mr. Par- nell has expressed his willingness to accept that arrange- ment, but his retirement depends on the deposition or resignation of Mr. Justin M'Carthy and the appointment of Mr. O'Brien or Mr. Dillon. Whatever arrangement be finally made will be subject to the approval of Mr. Gladstone, to whom it will be communicated confiden- tially. At one of the conferences the question was raised 'as to the guarantees obtainable for Mr. Parnell's good faith ; and promises were afterwards made by the lead- ing supporters of the hon. gentleman that they would withdraw their support should he fail to keep his part of the bargain. Mr. Maurice Healy, in an interview with an Exchange Telegraph Company's correspondent at Mitchelstown, on Thursday, said the Boulogne conference would end in The Special CeFraponaeuv-K7r4,1..._,A4e.c...,„z4awmaz, accompanying Mr. Parnell, says :—At the meeting to be held at Limerick, on Sunday, Mr. Parnell will attend and make an important speech. div.head: PAIGN,
div.p: PAIGN,

The allowance tothe Flan of Campaign evicted tenaats on the Coolroe and Tottenham Estates not having been paid for three months, a public meeting was called for to protest against the present deadlock in the Irish party. Just as the meeting was about to commence Mr. John, Cummins, one of the local managers of the Plan of Cam- paign, announced that he had that morning received a letter from Mr. O'Brien, stating that the cheques would arrive in a few days. The announcement was received with cheers. MR. GLADSTONE AND MR. PARNELL'S RETIREMENT.

Mr. Gladstone, writing to a Plymouth correspondent, who called attention to the statement attributed to Cap- tain Price, M. P., that Mr. Gladstone only suggested that Mr. Parnell should retire for the present—which simply meant that he was to stand aside until the next election —says" I have made no offer of office to Mr. Parnell, and his retirement, of which I spoke to Mr. Morley, was not a retirement for the present, but retirement now.'

div.head: RAILWAY COMMUNICATION WITH ST. HELENS. IMPORTANT RECOMMENDATIONS.
div.p: RAILWAY COMMUNICATION WITH ST. HELENS. IMPORTANT RECOMMENDATIONS.

For some months past the St. Helens Corporation have been in communication with the London and North-western Railway Company with the view of securing an improved service of passenger trains between St. Helens, Liverpool, Manchester, War- rington, Wigan, and Widnes. The Parliamentary Committee of the Corporation appointed a sub-com- mittee, to take charge of the questions affecting the railway communications of the town, and this sub-com- mittee have presented a lengthy detailed report. They state that they carefully examined and dis- cussed the existing arrangements for passenger traffic, and drew up a list of suggestions for iniprovernents therein to which they considered the borough to be entitled. In regard to Liverpool and St. Helens, it was suggested that several trains should be altered so as to provide better connections at St. Helens Junction, and additional trains at night and on Sunday afternoon. In their remarks the committee stated that generally the connection for trains at St. Helens Junction was very bad, and should certainly be improved. An hourly ser- vice to and from Liverpool was suggested as a system to be aimed at. Various alterations and additional trains were suggested with regard to communication with Wigan, Preston, Manchester, Warrington, Widnes, Southport, and Rainford Junction. The sub-committee then arranged an interview with the superintendent for the district, Mr. Shaw, and urged upon him the necessity of the improvement they suggested. They also pointed out to him the unpunctuality of the train service generally, and particularly to and from St. Helens Junction; the delay and inconvenience caused by the stoppage of the trains for the watering of engines at Peasley Cross; the shabby nature of the local carriages and the undue crowding of trains, especially on Saturdays. In regard to these matters, Mr. Shaw promised that hg would. give immediate instructions for the necessary alterations so far as the causes were local; and as to the suggestions for the alterations in the train service, he explained that he was not able to make any such alterations until the reprinting of the time tables in February, but he promised to then arrange a decidedly improved train service giving as full an - effect as possible to the sub-commilte's suggestions, except in the matter of the Sunday traffic, which, he said, was a question for the directors.—The Parliamentary Com- mittee adopted the report, and decided to ask Mr. Shaw to submit to the Council a list of his proposed alterations before they were actually made. The minutes of the Parliamentary Committee also stated that the Town Clerk had submitted notices of the intention to apply to Parliahient during the next session by the Liverpool, St. Helens and South Lancashire Railways Company for an extension of time under their existing Acts, and by the London and North-Western Railway Company, for powers to construct a new rail- way at Peasley Cross, and to deviate and widen portions of their existing railway. It was resolved that assent be given to the first-named application, and that notice of dissent be given to the proposals of the London and North-Western Company, pending an arrangement with that company. At the council meeting on Wednesday afternoon Alder- man R. Pilkington moved, and Alderman J. Harrison seconded, the confirmation of the minutes.—Councillor Leach expressed the opinion that very little was being done in regard to direct communication between St. Helens and Liverpool, and suggested that the committee should endeavour to get local trains between the two places similar to those running between Lime-st. and Bootle and Lime-st. and Garston. The minutes were then passed.
The rumour which has been current that the Arch- bishopric of York had been offered to the Bishop of Man- chester is denied.

Nine Ulster members Of Parliament have memorialised the Postmaster-General to adopt the Larne and Stran- raer rctute for the auxiliary English mail service. Probate has been granted of the will of the late Coun- tess of Rosebery, the net value of the testatrix's personal estate being sworn at £719,876.115. 9d. The sole execu- tor is the Earl of 'Rosebery.

THE SHIP CANAL.
BELFAST TRADE AND THE MANCHESTER sail'
CANAL.

On Saturday afternoon there was launched from tho shipbuilding yard of Messrs. Macllwaine and Maccoll, Belfast, a new steamer called the Manchester, built the order of Messrs. Samuel Lowther and Co., and which has been designed specially to meet the increasing trade between Belfast and Liverpool and Manchester. Wiles fitted out the new vessel will immediately go on tile. station, her first voyage in all probability taking place a' the end of the present month. Her dimensions are length 180 ft., breadth 27ft., depth 131 t. llin. 111 carrying capacity will be about 650 tons. The vesse will carry only a limited number of passengers, but llas been specially adapted for goods traffic. After herd maiden trip, the steamer will ply between Belfast an the Mersey, but when the Ship Canal has been cow pleted she will, after calling at Liverpool, proceed t° Manchester.

div.head: FATAL ICE ACCIDENTS.
div.p: FATAL ICE ACCIDENTS.

A siad drowning fatality oceurred in the river Kennet, near Reading, on Saturday afternoon. Late in the after- noon the thaw was found to' have rotted the ice, but a number of people remained upon it until it gave ay, and five girls were immersed. Four were rescued, put the fifth,Nellie Hopkins, aged 15 years, was drowned in the presence of hundreds of spectators. The bodies of Mary Jane Smith, aged 15, and Robert. d°lln Murray, aged 20, both residing in Lnchmaben, Were found on Saturday in the Castle Loch. ,They were sk•ating on the loch on Friday, and, venturing upon pre- carious ice, fell through. A While skating, at Leicester, on Saturday, a girl named Butcher ventured too near a hole in the ice, and ell through. The body was recovered after three-quarters uf an hour. At Coventry two young Men named Lipscomb, sons of a clergyman, have been drowned while slmting.

-I, At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on leuday, Samuel Gough, furniture dealer, was ged with having on the Ist inst., obstructed "e footpath by allowing six wringing machines 1:1(1 two step ladders to stand on the footpath in arcalt of his shop, in Winwick-st.—P.C. At the Chester City Quarter Sessions yesterda y Week, before his Honor Sir Horatio Lloyd, Recorder, .1..0.hn Bennett, (57), horse dealer; William Smedley, (45d, horse dealer; George Coates, (27), labourer; pa James Coates, (31), farmer, were charged with having, at Chester, on the 20th November, unlaw- hilly conspired with other persons unknown to O- rin £5O by false pretences from William Carter, _arm er, Burtonwood, Warrington. Mr. Malcolm Douglas prosecuted; Mr. E. H. Lloyd defended iShiedley ; Mr. Marshall defended the brothers Co, ales, and Mr. A. D. V. Colt-Williams defended. zennett.—Mr. Malcolm Douglas said the case re- Vealed an amount of simplicity and credulity on the part of the prosecutor one would scarcely expect to find In Cheshire in the nineteenth century. The singular part Of the story was that prosecutor was defrauded of £5O by a common trick, and so green did the men find their 'victim thatthey persuaded him to buy not one but three worthless horses. Prosecutor came to Chester fair on the ,late named with £6O in his pockets. Shortly after noon be found himself near a group of about seven persons, zuongst whom were the prisoners. George Coates was pa charge of a horse, and one of the men, who was not lh custody, asked prosecutor whether he was buying cr tiling. He replied that he was buying, whereupon the '.14411, pointine to the horse in charge of George Coates, "You can buy this if you like for £25." Prosecu- did not bite at that, and the man changed his tactics "IYing want to purchase this horse. I offered £26 ..?_r it, but the man would not have it. If you can get horse for £27 I'll give you £2B for it. Prosecutor (Pagel:lW, and purchased the horse for £27, tendering a Zou note. Coates then went back to the group for the y,llliPose of getting change, which was ultimately pro- ,d from a shop close by, and £27 thus went into rates's pocket.—Mr. Marshall: That is not on the depo-, Mr. Douglas, proceeding, Said the same man eggested to prosecutor that he should buy another horse Or £2O, for which he would give him £22. Prosecutor tgjeed to do this, but when he had paid the £2O the man tv'to 'was to re-purchase the horses had disappeared. Carter was waiting for the arrival of their man, it sPired that the gang had a third worthless cob. A -44,1:1came forward and offered £3O worth of notes for the r?, but the man who had charge of the horse said the t:rks were not good ones. Smedley said, "Won't you Ite the notes P Well, here's the gold," but the gold was Vlt produced. Bennett and Smedley then said to prose- "lf you will buy the cob we will give you £3O for ~ The man in charge suggested that Carter should trive the horse he had given £2O for and £lO in exchange por the ceb. To this he agreed, and when he had paid ,lor the cob the men said they would not re-purchase it they had the other horse too. Prosecutor said "If -L°ll take the other horse I shall want £60." Bennett ""eo said Well, let's trot him out," and pointed out ten who would mount the horse and the cob. They i_ere trotted out, and it was seen that they were worth- broken-down hacks, and prosecutor saw that he :la been swindled. He said he would go for a police- and some of the gang cried out" Chuck him in the Bennett came forward, put £7 into his hand, tald said, "Here's £8 for you ; that's all they are worth!, 37 this means prosecutor was done out of £so—£27 he ga.ve for the first horse £2O for the second, £lO and one °L .the other horses for the cob. This made £57, of which he received £7 back from Bennett.—The advo- ;fates for the prisoners having addressed the jury, his ,°,tiour summed up, and the prisoners were found 14,‘"ItY, Bennett and Smedley being sentenced to six oaths' imprisonment each, and the brothers Coates to month each.

div.head: Utter 5 to the Obttor.
div.p: Utter 5 to the Obttor.
WHAT HAS BECOME OF THE SHIPPING TRADE TO RUNCORN?

Sir,—lt was only last August Mr. Collier said the docks at Runcorn were too small to accommodate the trade, and they were going in for more docks at once. We find the docks now almost deserted by ships that once came in their hundreds, and the channel silted up with sand. What a change! Rave our worthy Codi- missioners no power to see the channel is kept open and the interests of the town are protected? If something is not done, it will be a case of being compelled to help the poor dock labourers and their wives and families in their need mid distress.—Yours truly, A RATEPAYER.

div.head: RUNCORN PARISH. CHURCH..
div.p: RUNCORN PARISH. CHURCH..

Sir,—ln the Parish Magazine for this month the Vicar says—" There is not as much help forthcoming for the Christmas decorations of the churches nor as many com- municants. We don't want un-denominational benevo-

lence but pan-denominational. The Church Army wants more sympathy than it gets from our ordinary church people. As thedaily service at five p.m. at St. Michael's is not attended by even the necessary two or three, it

- will be suspended for the present. The tea party at St. Michael's was almost forgotten by the clergy, and quite forgotten by the church offiC,ers. We expect to begin our confirmation classes after January 11th." Are the ladies beginning to see that decorations are not becoming in a place of worship? How many of his flock will under- stand what he says about benevolence? The Church Army is evidently not wanted in Runcorn or five p.m. services, the seven a.m. (low fasting) celebrations were suggested to catch the men who came off their night work. Why not try five a.m. sermons? The parsons seem to be void of sense on these points.. St. Michael's school tea party was crowded to excess in the late Canon Barclay's day. Comparisons are odious to the Runcorn clergy. As to confirmation, I would ask churchmen to read articles six and twenty, and then tell me if they can find it in the New Testament. Listen to the testimony of men of learning. R. P. Blakeney, L.L.0.D.D., says Confir- mation was not instituted by Christ. In the Church of England it is merely an ecclesiastical ordinance." James Begg, D.D., says" Confirmation was never instituted by Christ or His Apostles." W. Smith, D.C.L., in his Bible Dictionary, a standard work, is silent on it. Richard Watson the eminent divine says "Confirmation rests upon no Scriptural authority at all." G. A. Jacob, D.D. says "It completes that which is necessarily incomplete in infant baptism, wherein the personal requisites of repen- tance and faith cannot be found. But it was not ordained by Christ, nor is it of Apostolic origin." The martyr John Wyeliffe, D.D., says Confirmation was unauthor- ized by the Apostles, is a blasphemy against God. Some are of opinion that this slight and brief confirmation per- formed by the bishop, with the rites which are attached to it with so much solemnity, was introduced at the suggestion of the devil, with a view to delude the people concerning the faith of the church, and to gain more credence to the solemnity,or as to the necessity of bishops." 'Me Syrians had no knowledge of confirmation, and re- garded it. when proposed, not only as superfluous and unnecessary, but as an insult. Cranmer, who is sup- posed to have written the first Homily, part of article thirty-five, says "Let us diligently search for the well of life (John 4c. 14v.) in the books of the Old and New Testament, and not run to the stinking puddles of men's traditions (devised by man's imagination) for our justi- fication and salvaticn." If confirmation be unscriptural and false, is it not clearly a duty to protest against and refuse to countenance it in any way, more especially by restraining your children from observing it. Yours Scc., ' ROBERT FOULKES. Froclsham, Jan. 6,1891.

PUBLIC CHARITY DINNERS AT WARRINGTON. Sir,—l am one who heartily subscribes to the principle laid .down in your excellent article on Saturday week, on "The Gospel of Wealth," that it is the duty of men of means to devote their surplus capital to charitable and philanthroPic objects. Hence I observe with much sat- isfaction from your reports of the public treats, given in the form of substantial meals, by the Mayor and others to the poor of the district, that at least some of our bet- ter-to-do citizens realize to some extent the truth of the hackneyed saying, though one that can never be too *web quoted, that wealth brings with it its responsi- bilities as well as its privileges. But lam nevertheless inglined to doubt whether this exceedingly conspicuous method of dispensing charity, the provision of public dinners and teas and the like is exactly that which is the best calculated to meet the object in view. It seems to me that it savours too much of the appearance of making an exhibition of poor people and of their capacities of eating and drinking: for the delectation of a few well-meaning but curious sight-seers, in better circumstances than them- selves. Consider the matter in what light we will, there must be to the mind of every poor man and woman endued with more or less fineness of feeling and independence of spirit, a something humiliating in being compelled to accept charity; and the humiliation must be felt with aggravated keqpness when they are obliged to accept that charity loublicly. The force of this remark will ke more appreciated when it is considered that this class of people, who are essentially the deserving class— not the vagabonds and impostors who live by preying upon the charitable—are presumably those who form the great majority of the guests at thesepublic feasts. ere ii one feature in connection with them to which

I would:particularly draw attention, as contributing more than any other to give them the semblance of poverty parades and of exhibitions of the gastronomical abilities of the poor. This is the practice on the part of many well-to-do people of making a point of going to watch the- poor people feed on these occasions, just as they would, no doubt, to see the animals in Wombwell's menagerie feed on its occasional visits to the town. These persons, I am sure, have no desire to do anything that would cause unnecessary pain to the poor participants in these meals, but it does seem to me that there is in this custom something that partakes of unseemliness, unmannerliness, and utter want of that same charitable consideration for the poor, so far as their minds are con- c9rned, which is so commendably shown for their bodies. At these public meals to the poor, no matter what other dishes may be absent there is one dish, we may depend upon it, that is always very prominently before those seated at the tables and that has to be profusely partaken of, though the least appreciated of all, that is humble pie, though that it forms so integral a part of the feast may probably be a matter of perfect unconscious- ness to the spectators. Doubtless this unsavoury and indigestible dish is made to many somewhat more pala- table by the presence of an assiduous mayor and mayoress, and several town councillors and other notabilities act- ing as superintendents or waiters round the festive board; but surely the presence of a numller of persons in the mere capacities of onlookers, watching every bite consumed by the hungry guests, and perhaps shriving amusement from the extent of appetites now meeting; with such exceptional satisfaction, must make the objec- tionable dish more unsavoury and indigestible still. If there have to be so many waiters on these occasions,-let others, who can perform no service except this undesir- able sort of eye-service, keep away at all events. Next week, with your permission, I will make a few observations whir& view tr. improvements in the future. —Yours truly, Warrington, Jan. 7, 1891.
MANLIUS

div.head: MR JOHN GANDY AND THE FERNLEY
div.p: MR JOHN GANDY AND THE FERNLEY
LECTURE.

Sir,—l have no intention to take any part in the dis- cussion of the special point at issue between Mr. Gandy and Mr. Peers, touching the vagaries of Count Tolstoi. But I feel compelled to correct the very inaccurate statements of my my friend Mr. Gandy, so far as he professes to quote from tho Fernley Lecture.
I cannot conceive how he shouldhave fallen into two such glaring cases of misapprehension.

1. Professor Beet makes no such statement as that the Gospels "were not written by their reputed authors Matthew, Mark, Luke and John." ' He simply says that the several writings are anonymous, not like the let- ters of St. Paul, with the author's name attached. But that is a very differeut thing from saying that they were not written by their reputed authors. A book may be anonymous, though it may be well known who wrote it for all that; a fact which Professor Beet distinctly recog- nises a few pages further on in his work, where he states that the Ist Epistle of John and the Gospel now bearing his name "are undoubtedly from the same pen" (p. 99 and on page 198 he evidently approves of the ancient and general opinion that Mark was the author of the second Gospel. _ . _ . . .

2. My friend's next case of misapprehension is worse still. He makes Professor Beet say that the gospels were written "by annonymous writers at unknown dates, that in fact no one knows when, or where, or by whom they were written." Again I must state that Professor Beet says nothing of the kind. What he does say on page 92 is, hat"t the names commonly attached to the four gospels, although found in our earliest copies, are doubtless of later date and do but embody a very ancient tradition." But it is only the names so attached that he is speaking of as being of later date, not of the writings themselves—and that "no one knows when, where, or by whom they were written." Professor Beet expresses no doubt whatever upon this subject, and therefore my friend may allay his astonishment at the Professor's "attempt to prove the gospels to be true and authentic." In this month's number of the "Contem- porary," the Professor has an article touching upon this very subject, in which historical evidence is adduced as to the truth of the four gospels and their authors. I very urgently recommend a careful study of this excel- lent paper on "The certainties of Christianity." I regret to have to differ so deeply with my friend as to other portions of his letter. I think he betrays a very sad defect of logical method in dealing with New Testa- ment facts. His strictures upon our Lord's disciples and the Apostle Paul are mrked by utter one-sidedness— leaving out of consideration altogether the very elements in each case necessary to enable him to form anything like a sound judgment. It is readily conceded that our Lord had often to chide His disciples for their dullness of understanding, and their frequent grievous mistakes whilst He was with thcm, and even some time aftee His resurrection; but how does it follow from this that they are not to be trusted in their subsequent teachings after the bestowal of the Holy Spirit upon them at Pentecost? Has my friend really forgotten Christ's promise to then:- that the Father would send His spirit in His name, who . should teach them all things, and bring to their remem- brance all that He had said unto them? that whilst He had many things to say unto them which they could not then bear, when the Spirit of truth was come he should guide them into all truth ? And is it of these spirit- taught men who because they were once so dull and mistaken—that our friend says he must" decline to concede much to ? "

Again, as to the authority of St. Paul, would he have us to believe that when Christ revealed Himself to him, declaring that He had appeared unto him to appoint him a minister and a witness both of the things he then saw, and of the things wherein He would appear unto him (Acts xxvi., v. 16) that this divinely-appointed Apostle's teaching is not to be trusted? And are we at liberty to reject the ambassador who delivers a message which he affirms was neither "received from man, nor was he taught it but by revelation of Jesus Christ ?" (Gala. 1., 12.) I rather think that a king would regard himself as grossly insulted whose ambassador was rejected on the plea that his majesty had not delivered his own mes- sage. And I maintain that to slight the teaching of so clearly an authorised servant and apostle -as St. Paul was, is to incur all the responsibility of rejecting the words of the Lord Himself.

In closing, let me remark that I thoroughly endorse Mr. Gandy's sentiment, that it would be well if a more gewmal interest were taken in the literature of a similar stamp to that of Professor Beet's work. It would arrest, •to a vast extent, the influence of a many modern cranks and crazes,and help to relegate a crowd of sceptical follies to the level of fancies worthy only of a Quixote or a MUnchausen.—Yours &e., Penketh, 7th January, 1891.
JNO. DIGNUM.
IS TOLSTOI "A LOGICAL PHENOMENON"?

Sir,—Mr. Gandy accuses me of making an assump- tien. He does not definitely say what it is, but I infer that it consisted in assuming that his founder, John Wesley, was learned and able enough to read andsunder- stand in a plain way, the plain language of our English Bible. In this I may have been mistaken. But it is no part of my office to fence with Mr. Gandy on the ques- tion of Christ's teachings. That I leave to the Christians. My position, which I am prepared to defend, is an affir- mative answer to the question at the head of this letter. I have lately been amusing myself by classifying men as to their dealings with the Bible, and I am rather anxious to see how Jong it would take Mr. Gandy to find his place therein. To you, sir, I may whisper that it is not in the first or second division, nor has he arrived at that state of logical consistency which would 'entitle him to a place in the fourth and lust. As there is but one Tolstoi, and Gandy is his prophet, Where Tolstoi is there will Gandy be also. This being the case, one can quite understand his being so eager to take up the cudgels in' defence of the logical consistency of his master. Now, whilst to some extent f agree with Mr. 'Gandy in his admiration for Tolstoi, I cannot close my eyes to the glaring inconsistency of any man rejecting large and im- portant portions of the saJred Scriptures and accepting and believing the rest. With me the rejection of a part as not being of divine origin (and only under such condi- tions can I conceive rejection possible) necessarily im- pugns and invalidates the rest. lam for entire accept- ance or entire rejection. Before we begin to analyse the attitude of men with regard to the Bible, let us synthetise a little and classify them according to their Natural Affinities. By this means we get a broader aud more comprehensive view of the whole question. I divide men in regard to the Bible into four great classes, thus, as—l.—Believers—ll.—Recorf- cilers—lll.—Mutilators—lV.—Rejectors. Each of these four great divisions has its typical example in men now livin,g, except perhaps the first, for unsophisticated be- lief has, I think, died out or only lingers here and there in dark corners among the ignorant and fanatic. If any living specimen of this class still exists among the educa- ted and intelligent I know not of it. Of the H. class, the Reconcilers, I take Mr. Gladstone as the type, while the lll.—Mutilators—are well illus- trated by Count Tolstoi, tie W.—Rejectors—being well represented by' Professor Huxley. As to the characteristic features of the four classes— the Believers were, so far as an unswerving and un- mitigated belief in the Bible can be said to be consistent, were consistent. They accepted the Book as the Word of God and believed the world was made in seven natu- ral days—man being specially created in one of them— and that, at furthest,the world was but some seven thousrnd years old. And this they believed and averred, quite irnorant of the fact that down in the bowels of the' earth they were maligning, there lay, like some un- sprung mine, subversive geological evidences awaiting only the quickening touch of modern investigation to scatter ruin and confusion among their simple sect. Ignorance added fervour to their faith. Mr. Gladstone as the type of the Reconcilers is certainly not an unsophisticated believer. He is an excellent example of the disturbing influence ,of modern know- ledge on Biblical interpretation. Mr. Gladstone would
"IN DARKEST ENGLAND, AND THE
WAY OUT." LECTURE AT EARLESTOWN.

Under the auspices of the Earlestown Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society, a lecture was deli. vered on Thursday evening, in the Wesleyan Chapel, by the Rev. T. W. Stafford, of St. Helens, on "In Darkest England, and the Way Out." There was a numerous audience, Mr. J. Burgess presiding. The lecturer said he was not there to Pronounce an eulo- gism upon General Booth, or to descant upon the de- voted heroism of his departed wife. It would be his pur- I pose to examine certain propositions laid down by Gene- ral Booth in his already famous volume, and to consider during the short space of time allowed him, his methods, his Statements, and his aims. It would readily- appear to any thoughtful person, that it would be im- ,ossible for him to enter upon a detailed examination of the scheme. He did not propose to commit himself to any incidents in that scheme; he thought if the general principles of the scheme commended themselves to us, that ought to be sufficient. That book, written by a man who had a passion for saving souls, practically ad- mitted that under certain conditions, preaching the Gos- pel was so much wasted breath. To talk about heaven to these poor wretches who peopled outcast England,was like dangling a £5 note before them, then drawing it back when the hand is outstretched to receive it. "in Darkest England, and the way out." was a revelation which had shocked and convulsed Christian Eng- land from the centre to the circumference. They knew nothing about the state of heathen England ; the vast majority of our church and chapel going people were as ignorant, as it was possible to be, of the conditions of those people whom Booth has des- cribed as the submerged tenth. General Booth knew what he was talking about, and he states that the num- ber of outcasts, equalled the population of Scotland. How was this submerged tenth, reinforced? They were reinforced by men who were what they were, and, could not help themselves. Was it not true that a steady process of degeneration of society was going on? Moral degradation went hand in hand with physi- cal degradation. To account for these people being hopelessly sunken • in vice, General Booth pro- pounds two principles, heredity, and environment. Booth's book opened up to him a most interestiug theo- logical problem, viz., the influence of Heredity on the moral characters of men. He believed there was no doctrine which demanded a larger attention than that doctrine of human depravity. There were thousands ef boys whose mothers saturated themselves with strong drink, before the boys were born, who may be said to have suckled in a taste for strong drink. The law of Heredity had an important bearing upon moral responsi- bility. It was a fair question to ask, if these poor out- cast wretches were responsible for their sin. If they were, then Booth's scheme would be so much waste paper. General Booth preached hope for them, and that was evidence, he thought, that heredity did not bind the will. The next fact was that of ea- vironment. England would be revolutionised, not by Acts of Parliament, not by Christian churches, but by homes. Any national regeneration, must proceed along the lines of brightened homes. The taproom was the poor man's only parlour. It was not Merely' the drink, which drew men there; it was the social influence of the public-house which drew. They could get rid of the evil in parts, without going to Booth's scheme, if they were prepared to counteract the social influence of the public-house, with a social influence of the Church. If they were to draw the people to their churches and chapels they. must meet the devil on his own lines— Booth's idea was to establish every conceivable institution for the social restoration of the submerged tenth. The scheme was a gospel of hope; there was a tone of buoy- ant hopefulness, a splendid optimism, running through the whole book. England was very dark, but there was a way out—might God hasten the day. (Applause.) Votes of thanks to the chairman and lecturer closed the meeting.
