have us believe that he believes that the statement found in the Bible that the earth was created in seven days (with the evening and the morning specially noticed), can be reconciled with the fact that science demonstrates the period to have been more than as many millions—nay, that the process of world-making is still going on by the quiet operation of natural law. Again, the very definite Bible announcement of the specific creation of man and animals, is held to be quite compa- tible with the hypothesis (which he accepts) of the slow evolution of one species from the other, two modes of procedure which appear, to ordinary intellects, to be dia- metrically opposed to each other, and to be as incompa- tible as good and evil. But there are intellects that soar far above such petty details as the disagreement of the text with the fact; minds that by persistently closing the avenues of perception, can accomplish the miracle of reconciling the irreconcilable, and seeing in the text meanings undreamt of by its Author. It appears never to have occurred to these over-zealous folk that,upon the assumption that the Divine mind had thought the first of Genesis sufficiently explicit and well worded to con- vey to mankind what information it was deemed neces- sary for them to know—if this satisfied the mind that inspired it—no mere man is justified in paraphrasing it or altering its meaning. But if it is found in these latter days not to be consistent with observed facts, what does that imply ? Carelessness on the part of its Author in the selection and supervision of His agents employed in its transcription? If this narrative had been deemed to be of the great importance attributed to it by the Recon- cilers, would not greater care have beentaken to render it more intelligible and less liable to misinterpretation, nor to need the nineteenth century corrective of secular discoveries to render it at all understandable? No work of his Maker should need amendment by man. The Reconciler's mode of dealing with the Bible is one which he would'not sanction when applied to any other book.- It consists essentially in closing your eyes, and seeking within your internal coneciouzness for meaning you will to find there. Then, the wish being father to the thought, the miracle is wrought, and the evening and the morning of the first day becomes a geological period of some few million years! This in my eyes .is a tam- peringwith the truth, and truth is much too sacred a thing to be tampered with. In Tolstoi we have an example of the mutilating class. These do not claim to alter the text, but they use the shears freely and snip off whole passages and chapters which are not to their liking. When thus clipped into shape, ato Tolstoi; when the Fall, the Creation of Man, Adam and his Garden have thus found their place in the waste-paper basket by his vigorous ' excision, then and then only is he prepared to accept the rest. It would be interesting if the Count would tell us where we are to begin to believe. Let his next book, neglecting for a while his novel writing,be on,the Limits of Biblical Belief, and then perhaps we shall know where we are. lam not aware that Tolstoi has used his scissors upon the New Testament. This I believe he accepts as a divine revelation and admits the Divine Nature of Christ. But where is the authority for this belief, if the Old Testament is merely the clippable product of the vain imaginings of men? The dogma of the Fall having itself fallen before the censorial shears of Tolstoi ; what becomes of the remedial efficacy of the Death on Calvary; and indeed what was that but a needless arid meaningless waste of suffering? If the mutilators' view be taken in what, except in degree, does Christ differ from Socrates? Both lived good lives; taught what was good; and died violent deaths for so living and so teaching. Both in my opinion were part of the good weft which runs through the warp of evil in the manifold fabric we call religion. Perhaps Mr. Gandy will explain? We next come to the fourth and last class—the Rejec- tors, and have given Prof. Huxley as the type. They are mostly, if not all, Agnostics, i.e. they do not pretend to know the unknowable. They make no claim to com- prehend anything that passeth all understanding. They content themselves with knowledge that can be known and demonstrated to others. Their rejection of the Bible as a divine revelation is justified somewhat in this way :—I. By the entire incompatibility of the nar- rative of Genesis as to the specific creation of the earth and its inhabitants (itself a mere transcript from an older pre-Chaldean fable) with observed and undisputed physical facts. 11. By the time said to have been taken up in this specific creation being so glaringly inade- quate, when viewed by the light of modern science. 111. By the many contradictory and incredible statements in the book itself. IV. By the fact that the new Testa- ment depends for its credentials as a divine revelation upon the Old Testament. The latter being discredited involves the former in a like fate. Any and each of these taken separately is sufficient to destroy the preten- tions of its idolizers, that the Bible is divinely inspired and supervised. Taken together, the adverse evidence is overwhelming. A glance at the four divisions of the classifications will show the evolutionary progression of the series from the believers, who, in the innocence of their hearts and the emptyness of their heads, accepted without question or inquiry the book in its entirety as the Word of God, through the reconcilers who somewhat impiously under- take to correct the proof of their Divine Author and to tinker His text into a fit condition for modern accep- tance, and the Mutilators who destroy the one part ere , they can-accept the ..ast,.._ te_tbe Reae,ctors...who—finding they cannot accept the whole, feel logically and con- scientiously compelled to assume ant attitude of entire non-acceptance. Mr. Gandy has not yet arrived at the full fruition of his own late accession to the blessings of untrammelled thought on these topics. He is on the right road; but halts by the way. However, his face is towards the light. I respect him and every other man who accepts and cherishes, and does his best to promote that glorious heritage of the Reformation, the right—the liberty—aye, the duty of private individual judgment and opinion in matters of religion.—Yours, &c.,
. _ ... JOHN PEERS. [We are at all times willing te insert letters from our readers on topics of public interest; but we must ask our correspondents to keep, as a rule, within half a column.—Ed. Ex.]
SIR JOSEPH EDGAR BOEHM, BART.

This eminent sculptor who died in London in December, 1890, was born in Vienna on July 6th, 1834, of Hungarian parents. His father was director of the -lint in the Austrian empire, Id the possessor of .a cele- nted private collection of 'erks of art. He was edu- ,ted at Vienna, and from 1848 o 1851 in England. He studied
(A'v
so in Italy and for three jars in Paris, but had been in ingland since 1862. He re- dyed the first imperial prize

and exemption from military service in Vienna in 1856, was elected, a member of the Academy of Flotence in 1875, and an associate of the Royal Academy of London, in 1878. Amongst Mr. Boehm's works is a colossal statue of the Queen executed in 1867, and recumbent statues of the late Princess Alice and her daughter, and the late Prince Imperial. A statute of Lord Beaconsfield, for West- minster Abbey, as well as busts of Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Bright, Lord Iddesleigh, and Mr. Ruskin and the equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington for Hyde Park corner, have displayed his genius. He has also produced a colossal statue of the Queen of Sydney; the recumbent statue of General Gordon in St. Paul's Cathedral ; an effigy of the late Prince Leopold in Highland costume for the Albert Chapel, Windsor; a statue of Prince Albert Victor, and another statue of the Queen for the House of Con- vocation of the London University. He also designed the Queen's effigy on the Jubilee coinage.
THE KING OF HOLLAND.

On November 23, 1890, King William 111., of Holland died. He lived 73 years and reigned 40. It is said that he was of the old type of sovereigns, now fast dying out, who did net take a serious view of their profession, but regarded their exalted station as an aid to- wards obtaining the maxi- mum of pleasure and amuse- lent out of life. At the same ime while desirous of having
all personal freedom possible, the Ring, it is fair to add, did not deny it to his subjects. He was a strictly constitutional ruler, liberal in his ideas, and desirous to do all he could

for the welfare of his subjects. The King detested all forms and ceremonies, spoke his mind to all the world, was" hail fellow well met "with every class of the community, and had further the great and rare virtue of being parsimonious with the money of the State while very prodigal with his own. Women were the arbiters of William's life, for good or evil, from his cradle. At 22 it was thought need- ful to marry him, and choice fell upon the Princess Sophia of Wurtemberg,one year his junior. That this marriage proved ill-suited is universally known. Incompatibility of taste and manners made itself felt at once, and on his side still More divergent
tendencies widened the breach, and time-hut increased the difference between the couple. In
1877, regretted by her people, if not by her liege .lord, she was released by death. But scarcely was

she dead than occurred a strange phenomenon. Whether in consequence of his wife's death, or whether by coincidence merely, William of Holland suddenly became a model monarch and man. He further contemplate 4 the wisdom of re-marrying, and his choice fell upon Princess Emma of Waldeck- Pyrmont, and loud and long was the European pity expressed for the young girl of twenty about to make a May and December marriage. But contrary to all expectation the marriage turned out well, and Queen Emma appears to have been happy with the sexagenarian spouse over whom she obtained great influence. There was some.ten years ago born to this couple a little Princess, Wilhelmina, who was the apple of her aged father's eye, and upon whose tender head descends the crown of the N ethekands.

The annual balance sheet of Parr's Banking Com- pany, Limited, which is just being issued states that, including £25,202 3s. sd. brought from previ- ous account, the net balance of profits, after pro- viding amply for all bad and doubtful debts, &c., is £151,71945. Bd. The directors recommend a divi- dend to be now paid of nine per cent., free of income tax, which with the interim half-yearly dividend, declared on July 25th, makes 18 per cent. for the year. The report of the Manchester and Liverpool Dis- trict Banking Company, Limited, for the past year shows a net profit of £224,647. Of that sum the interim dividend in July of 15s. a share and bonus of ss. a share took £lOO,OOO and a like dividend and bonus now will take .2100,000 more, leaving a balance of £24,647 which it is proposed to other- wise deal with.

Both of the banks have joined with the leading London, Provincial, and Scottish Banks in the guarantee against loss to the Bank of England in the liquidation of the estate of the great banking firm of Baring Bros. and Company.

The Howe battleship left Portsmouth yesterday to join the Channel Squadron. STARVED TO DEATH. An aged couple, named Wilson, have been found dead in bed at Saffron Walden, having perished from cold and want.

div.head: NEW RAILWAY.
div.p: THE NEW RAILWAY.
SOME DETAILS OF THE SCHEME.

It can hardly be expected that the members of the Warrington Football Club will grow enthusiastic over the progress that is being made with the pro- motion of the proposed Lancashire, Derbyshire and East Coast Railway. The football field off Wilders- pool Causeway is a veryconvenient centre for agame which has a great number of supporters in Warring- ton and which draws together a vociferoua crowd almost every Saturday during the season. It is a suitable field in every respect for football purposes, and the Club has been at considerable expense in making it one of the best grounds in this part of the country. But this field is the very spot on which the new Company have chosen to start their railway, and as the scheme is being pushed vigor- ously forward, the Football Club will no doubt be soon under the necessity for looking out for" fresh 'grounds' and pastures new," on which its members can disport themselves. Let us hope they will be successful in their search, and that their present loss will be sweetened by ample compensation. The country on the Cheshire side of Warrington is already pretty well intersected with embankments of one kind or another, and the new railway will contri- bute another of these huge ridges which diversify, but do not improve, the landscape.
PROVOSED BRIDGES.

The railway will begin at the Warrington side of the Football Club enclosure at an altitude of 17 feet above the level of the field. It will run from this point in the direction of Wilderspool Causeway, which it will cross by a bridge, 15 feet high and 2.5 feet wide, a few yards on the Wilderspool side of the foundry. After proceeding a short distance farther to the banks of the river, it will by a rather sharp curve re-cross Wilderspool Causeway on another bridge similar to that already Mentioned. This second bridge will be erected a few yards on the Warrington side of the roadway which at present runs down to the river bank from the Wilderspool end of the Causeway. The object of the railway crossing and recrossing the Wilderspool road is of course to " tap the future Ship Canal docks which are to be formed on the present bed of the river. Upon regaining Wilderspool Meadows the neW railway will run through the fields behind the Saracen's Head and will cross the Old Quay Canal on a bridge 40 feet above the water level at a point between the turn- bridge and the present bridge of the railway to Lymm but nearer the turn-bridge. A short distance further and the raiitay will encoun.ter the Ship Canal, and this waterway it will pass over Oh a bridge of the formidable height of 70 feet above the water level. It should be explained, however, that the Water level of the canal ap this point—between Ackers-lane and Lumb Brook— is considerably lower than the level of the ground. The next bridge is one to span Mill-lane a: bye-road which runs from Ackers pits to Blinston's Mill, and this bridge will be 15 feet high and 25 feet wide. Closely following this there will be two more high level bridges one to cross the Chester-road running between Grappenhall and Stockton Heath, and the, other to cross the Bridgewater Canal. The bridge over the Chester-road will be close to where that road is joined by Ackers-lane, and it will be raised to the height of 25 feet above the roadway. About 150 yards beyond the Bridge- water Canal the railway will strike the ground level, and then proceed on its way through the southern parts of the parish of Lymm, Tabley, Knutsford, Chelford, Alderley, and Macclesfield, to Buxton, thence on through Bakewell, Chesterfield, Bolsover, and Taxford to Lincoln.

div.head: BRANCH LINES.
div.p: BRANCH LINES.

There will be several branches near Lincoln, con- necting with the Great Northern and Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire systems, and numerous branches in Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire, con- necting with various collieries and colliery lines. There will be a branch near Knutsford, connecting with the Cheshire Lines at Buxton, and another from Macclesfield to the Midland Railway at Heaton Norris, and from thence to the Warrington and Stockport line to Cheadle. The Bill comprises altogether 25 railways and branch railways. Run- ning powers are sought over existing railways as follows:—The Manchester Ship Canal Railways at Arpley, Warrington; the Midland Railway from Heaton Norris to Throstle Nest, the Cheshire Lines from Throstle Nest to Miinchester (Central), the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire from Brigh- ton to Sheffield, and certain portions of the Great Northern and other railways in Lincolnshire.

div.head: DRINKING CARBOLIC ACID AT PRESCOT WORKHOUSE.
div.p: DRINKING CARBOLIC ACID AT PRESCOT WORKHOUSE.

Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lanca- shire, held an inquest at the .Prescot Union Work- house, Whiston, on Saturday afternoon, touching the death of Annie Cullen, a single woman, 27 years of age, who had been an inmate of the institution for a number of years past. From the evidence given by Mr. Hale, master of the workhouse, Wm. Williams, porter of the institution, and Ada Edmundson. an inmate, it appeared that on New Year's Day, during some festivities in the dining room, the deceased was assisting to clean out the porter's lodge. She several times asked for a drink of whisky, and the witness Edmundson said she told bar that she had not seen any whisky about the place. The deceased, however, made a search, and in a cupboard of the lodge found a. bottle contain- ing liquid, which she appears to have thought waS ' whisky. She drank a quantity of the contents, which turned out to be a solution of carbolic acid. She at once gave an alarm, and Dr. Hall, the union medical officer, and Dr. Cossens applied the stomach pump and tried other remedies, but the unfortunate woman expired in about 20 minutes. A verdict of "Accidental death "was returned.

div.head: EMBEZZLEMENT OF £5,000.
div.p: EMBEZZLEMENT OF £5,000.

Yesterday at the Ayr Sheriff Court, John Stevenson. jun., solicitor, Kilmarnock, pleaded guilty to embezzling nearly £5,000, money entrusted to him by clients for investment. He was remitted for sentence. THE SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE.

Yesterday the traffic at Waverley Station, Edinburgh, further improved. There is no improvement in Dum- frieshire, where there is a scarcity of fuel. The position at Glasgow is more strained. Queen-st. Station is ex- ceedingly quiet, and the early Kilsyth train was not run. Goods and minerals are being moved, but only to a small extent.

On Sunday evening the Te Deum was sung at St. Mary's Catholic Church, Buttermarket-street, for the benefits received during the past year.
THE WYCLIFFE Morro FOR 1891. "Grow up into him," Eph. iv. 15, is the Wycliffe motto for 1891, and from the text, the Rev. John Yonge preached to a large congregation on bunday evening.

LEAGUE OF THE CROSS SOCIAL GATHERING. The annual tea party in connection with the Warrington branch of the League of the Cross place on Monday evening, in the. League Hall, in Bewsey- street. After tea a ball was held, the duties of M.C. being discharged by Mr. John Mullins (President of the League). There were songs by members during the evening, and music was also contributed.

div.head: WESLEYAN CHILDREN'S TREAT.
div.p: WESLEYAN CHILDREN'S TREAT.

The animal tea in connection with the Butter- market-st. Wesleyan Sunday school mission was given on Wednesday evening. The children and teachers, numbering in all about 200, sat down to an excellent repast in the schoolroom. After tea games of various descriptions were entered into with true juvenile hilarity, and orangAs were distributed amongst the children before their departure.

ST. JOHN'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.

At the first meeting of this association after the Christmas vacation, held on Tuesday night. Mr. T. Thompson read a paper, entitled " Notes on the ra- ting and compensation of licensed houses." In his opinion, the only satisfactory way of granting com- pensation was that the amount should be in accor- dance with both the structural or capital value, and the licensing value of the licensed houses. Although differences of opinion were expressed as to whether the structural value ought to be taken into consider- ation in granting compensation, the members were unanimous in paying tribute to Mr. Thompson for his excellent paper. A social gathering to celebrate the re-opening of the Mersey Shoe Factory in Hopwood-st., took place at the Gardeners' Arms, Brick-st., the other evening, when 22 of the employes sat down to a substantial supper provided by Mrs. Cook. After the removal of the cloth, Mr. H. Shinn, who was voted to the chair, made some observations on the progress of the firm. Toasts were given by the Chairman, including "the health of Mr. J. P. Tteirrx'444l.- -and_ukoperity to the firm." Mr. Corgan proposed the h w.s..taiat of the hostess. Several songs were given during the evening, which was spent in an enjoyable man- ner. THE BITTTRIMARKET-ST. CONCEILTS.

The usual penny concert took place in the B utter- market-st. Mission-room on Saturday evening, there being a good attendance. In the absence of Alder- man Holmes, who was announced to preside, Mr. A. N. Price, of Bristol, took the chair. The programme submitted was unusually attractive, and in many instances encores were demanded and responded to. The instrumental music was supplied by Miss A. Dooley (violin), Mr. G. Grminds (euphonium), Miss Kerry and Mr. Price (piano). Recitations were given by Miss Ashworth, Mr. Gemson, and Mr. Fur- ness, and songs by Mr. Griffiths, Mr. Brown, and Misses Hooley and Kerry. A pleasant evening was brought to a close by a vote of thanks to the per- formers, on the motion of Mr. Richardson, seconded by Mr. Isaac Barlow, and the singing of the National Anthem. THE CHA.RIrABLE INVESTIGATION SOCIETY.

This society commenced its operatidns on Tues- day, under the management of Mrs. Harrison, at the King-st. Rooms, when a number of poor women were employed to make up garments or under- clothing, from 1 to 5 p.p., for which they received 6d. in money and their tea. A benevolent lady of Latchford presented the poor women, numbering about forty, each with a flannel petticoat, or rather the materials for them, which they themselves made up, and were permitted to take home with diem to wear. This little society is doing much good in a small way, by inculcating habits of thrift, for most of the women so employed leave their six- pences with Mrs. Hairison for the purchase of the articles they have made up, at the bare cost of the materials, thus enabling them to obtain clothing which they could not otherwise obtain; whilst coals, bread, and milk are supplied to others, whose husbands are out of work through the frost. CRITCHLEY. High Class Tailor. Dold-st.,Warrington.—Advt. MEAT TO AGED PEOPLE AT STOCKTON HEATH.

On New Year's Day the usual treat was given to those inhabitants of Stockton Heath of all denomi- nations who were 60 years of age and upwards. After a bountiful tea, under the kind management of Mr. and Mrs. Speakman, a quarter of a pound of tea was distributed to each of the old ladies pre- sent, whilst the old gentlemen each received a packet of tobacco from Mr. Vere R. Davies. Packets of eatables were, out of the abundance provided, made up for those who could not attend the gather- ing. Upwards of 100 cards of invitation were 'issued, and some 70 or 75 probably were present. The Lea was followed by a concert and reading, to which Mr. and Miss Down, Mr. and Mrs. Logan Wright, Miss Westbrook, Mrs. Synge, Mr. Reddish, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. John Hallows, and the church choir boys contributed either carols, songs, music, or recitations. Mr. Scarisbrick, •of Warring- ton,gave most amusing specimens of ventriloquism, Punch and Judyism, songs, and other comical pre- sentations. The Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington, and many others of the subscribers, were present either at the concert or during the tea, which was presided over by Miss Bailey, Mrs. Crosfield. Mrs. Robert Davies, Mrs. V.ere B. Davies, Mrs. Down, Miss Edgerley, Mrs. Rolfe, Mrs. E. W. Woods, and other ladies. On the motion of the Rev. C. J. Rolfe, who occupied the chair, a vote of thanks to all con- cerned was passed by acclamation. CRITCHLEY'S Tailoring meets the times.—Advt.

THE INDISPOSITION OF THE REV. JOHN GUNNELL. The Rev. John Gunnell, superintendent of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit, who for some months past has been in failing health, left Warrington on Wednesday for Colwyn Bay where he will spend a long rest and holiday. He conducted his last ser- vice prior to his departure in Bold-street Chapel on Sunday afternoon. At the conclusion of the service he said that for 30 years almost without intermis- sion he had worked in the minstry. Now the time had come for him to be laid aside. It was very trying to him to compulsorily turn his back upon the work he loved so well. He, however, was as- sured of their sympathy in many ways, and through so many channels had they shown it to him that he I could not for a moment doubt that he held a place in the heart of every member of the congregation. Ile should perhaps be away, from them for four or five months, his medical attendants advising a somewhat prolonged rest. Ire should carry with him the very grateful memory of the many happy services they had held in that chapel. His case, he should like them to understand, was not serious, but he was assured on'the best authority that unless he had a prolonged absence from work, it might. be a very serious matter for him for the rest of his life. He was not fit for public work in his present con- dition. His successor, the Rev. H. Waterfield, was an admirable preacher and an earnest worker, and he had no doubt the work would be carried on as well in his absence.

div.head: DEATH OF A. LOCAL VOCALIST,
div.p: DEATH OF A. LOCAL VOCALIST,

_ Many of our readers will regret to hear of the early death of Mrs. Fleming, who was better known by her maiden name of Miss Isabella Monks. Mrs. Fleming was married not many months ago, and for some time back she has been in feeble health, her death taking place on Tuesday. The deceased was well known in this locality as a most accomplished and popular vocalist, and she on several occasions ailed important parts at the concerts of the Musical Society. Her interment took place yesterday.
